mount-algidus.s: Mount Algidus (Algidus Mons) is the eastern ridge of the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, crossed by the pass between the Latin plain and the valleys of the interior. In the 5th century BCE the Aequi used it repeatedly to raid Latium, and Roman tradition set several battles…

mount-etna.s: Mount Etna is an active volcano on the east coast of Sicily and the highest mountain in Italy south of the Alps, about 3,300 metres high. Its fertile lower slopes attracted Greek colonists, who founded Catana at its foot in 729 BCE, and its eruptions repeatedly damaged the city.

mount-gerizim.s: Mount Gerizim is a mountain beside Nablus in the West Bank, facing Mount Ebal across the pass where ancient Shechem stood. It is the holy mountain of the Samaritans, who built a temple on it, probably in the 5th century BCE, as their counterpart to the Temple in Jerusalem.

mount-mugh.s: Mount Mugh is a hill in the upper Zeravshan valley of Tajikistan where Divashtich, ruler of Panjikent, made his last stand against the Umayyad Arabs before his capture in 722. In 1932 a shepherd found there an archive of some eighty documents on leather, wood and paper, most…

mount-pagus.s: Mount Pagus, now Kadifekale, is the hill above the harbour of İzmir in western Turkey. Around 300 BCE Antigonus and Lysimachus refounded Smyrna on its slopes, and its summit carried the acropolis of the Hellenistic and Roman city.

mount-pangaion.s: Mount Pangaion is a mountain range in eastern Macedonia, Greece, between the Strymon river and the plain of Drama. In antiquity its gold and silver mines drew Thasian settlers to the facing coast and led Athens to found Amphipolis in 437 BCE.

mount-pilgrim.s: Mount Pilgrim (Mons Peregrinus) was the castle that Raymond of Saint-Gilles built from 1103 on a hill outside Tripoli in Lebanon while besieging the city. It served as the base of the long siege, which ended when his son Bertrand took Tripoli in 1109.

mountstuart-elphinstone.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone was a Scottish administrator of the East India Company. As resident at Pune he played a leading part in the defeat of the Peshwa in the Third Anglo-Maratha War of 1817–1818 and then organised the conquered Deccan territories.

mpu-sindok.s: Mpu Sindok was a king of the Medang kingdom of Java who moved the royal centre from Central to East Java around 929, possibly after eruptions of Merapi or pressure from Srivijaya. He founded the Isyana dynasty, and some twenty inscriptions survive from his reign, which lasted…

mstislav-davydovich.s: Mstislav Davydovich was prince of Smolensk from 1219 to 1230. In 1229 he concluded a trade treaty with Riga and the merchants of Gotland that set rules for German traders in Smolensk and for Smolensk traders in the Baltic.

mstislav-ii-of-kiev.s: Mstislav II of Kiev (Mstislav Iziaslavich) was prince of Volhynia, which he ruled as a separate principality from 1154, and grand prince of Kiev from 1167 to 1169. A son of Iziaslav II, he founded the line of Volhynian princes from which came Roman the Great.

mswati-ii.s: Mswati II was king of the Swazi from 1840 to 1868, and the Swazi people take their name from him. He built up the age-regiment system, expanded the kingdom through raids and alliances with neighbouring Nguni and Sotho chiefdoms, and sought British support against the Zulu…

mubarak-al-sabah.s: Mubarak al-Sabah, called Mubarak the Great, was ruler of Kuwait from 1896 to 1915. He took power by killing his half-brothers, and in 1899 signed a secret agreement placing Kuwait under British protection against Ottoman claims.

mubarak-shah-sharqi.s: Mubarak Shah Sharqi was the second ruler of the Sharqi dynasty of Jaunpur, adopted son of its founder Malik Sarwar. He succeeded in 1399, took the title of sultan and struck coins in his own name, confirming Jaunpur's independence from the weakened Delhi Sultanate.

mubashshir-nasir-al-dawla.s: Mubashshir Nasir al-Dawla was the last ruler of the Taifa of Majorca, governing the Balearic Islands from about 1093 until his death in 1114. A freedman of the previous ruler al-Murtada, he presided over a state that lived largely from corsair raids on Christian coasts and…

mufarrij-ibn-daghfal.s: Mufarrij ibn Daghfal was chief of the Banu Jarrah, a Tayyi Arab clan that dominated Palestine in the late 10th and early 11th centuries. Alternately serving and fighting the Fatimid caliphs, he held the country around Ramla.

muhammad-adil-shah.s: Muhammad Adil Shah was sultan of Bijapur from 1627 to 1656. His reign saw campaigns that extended the sultanate south into Karnataka, though he accepted Mughal overlordship by treaty in 1636.

muhammad-al-ayyashi.s: Muhammad al-Ayyashi was a Moroccan Sufi warrior who led holy war against the Spanish coastal garrisons in the early 17th century. Appointed by the Saadi court as governor near Azemmour, he broke with it around 1614, made Salé his base and attacked Spanish-held La Mamora and…

muhammad-al-badr.s: Muhammad al-Badr was the last Zaydi imam and king of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen. He succeeded his father Ahmad in September 1962 but was overthrown a week later by army officers under Abdullah al-Sallal, who proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic.

muhammad-al-fasi.s: Muhammad al-Fasi was a sharif, said to have come from Morocco, who around 1550 established himself in the Fezzan oases of southern Libya and founded the Awlad Muhammad dynasty. He made Murzuk his capital, and his descendants ruled the Fezzan as sultans, controlling the Saharan…

muhammad-ali-al-abid.s: Muhammad Ali al-Abid was the first president of the Syrian Republic under the French mandate, serving from 1932 to 1936. The son of Izzat Pasha al-Abid, a senior adviser of the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II, he was a wealthy Damascene notable acceptable both to the French and…

muhammad-ali-jinnah.s: Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the leader of the All-India Muslim League and the founder of Pakistan. A barrister born in Karachi, he moved from Hindu-Muslim unity to demanding a separate Muslim homeland, set out in the Lahore Resolution of 1940.

muhammad-ali-khan-wallajah.s: Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah was Nawab of the Carnatic from 1749 to 1795. Backed by the British East India Company against his French-supported rival Chanda Sahib, he won the throne through the Carnatic Wars, which included Robert Clive's defence of Arcot in 1751.

muhammad-al-muzaffar-of-badajoz.s: Muhammad al-Muzaffar of Badajoz was the second Aftasid ruler of the Taifa of Badajoz, reigning from about 1045 to 1068. He fought long wars with the Taifa of Seville and lost Coimbra to Ferdinand I of León in 1064, paying him tribute.

muhammad-al-sanusi-of-dar-al-kuti.s: Muhammad al-Sanusi of Dar al-Kuti was sultan of Dar al-Kuti, in what is now the north of the Central African Republic, from 1890 to 1911. Installed with the backing of the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr, he built a fortified capital at Ndele from 1896 and raided the lands to the…

muhammad-bahr-al-din.s: Muhammad Bahr al-Din, known as Andoka, was sultan of Dar Masalit, on the border of Sudan and Chad, from 1910 to 1951. He succeeded Sultan Taj al-Din, killed fighting the French at Dorothe, and made Geneina his capital.

muhammad-diler-khan.s: Muhammad Diler Khan was an Afghan officer in Mughal service who founded the small state of Kurwai in central India in 1713. He received a territory near the Betwa river, north of Vidisha, and his descendants ruled it as nawabs, later under British paramountcy, until the state…

muhammad-falihi-kaimuddin.s: Muhammad Falihi Kaimuddin was the last sultan of Buton, an island sultanate off south-eastern Sulawesi in Indonesia, reigning from 1937 until his death in 1960. Buton had kept internal autonomy under Dutch rule since its alliance with the Dutch East India Company in 1613.

muhammad-husayn-khan-of-derbent.s: Muhammad Husayn Khan of Derbent was the first khan of Derbent, the walled Caspian city in Dagestan. Formerly the Persian governor of the city, he ruled it and its hinterland as an independent khan after the death of Nader Shah in 1747.

muhammad-ibn-abd-allah-al-birzali.s: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Birzali was leader of the Banu Birzal, a Berber clan brought to al-Andalus as soldiers by al-Mansur. During the civil war that destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba he took control of Carmona around 1013 and made it the base of an independent taifa.

muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.s: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab was a religious scholar of Najd whose call for a strict return to the oneness of God gave rise to the movement known as Wahhabism. Expelled from Uyayna under pressure from the Banu Khalid emir, he moved to Diriyah, where in 1744 he made a pact with…

muhammad-ibn-abil-saj.s: Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj, also called Afshin, was the founder of the Sajid dynasty. From a military family of Ushrusana in Central Asia serving the Abbasid caliphs, he was appointed governor of Azerbaijan in 889 and ruled it almost independently, from Maragha and later Ardabil,…

muhammad-ibn-aid.s: Muhammad ibn A'id was the last independent emir of Asir in south-western Arabia, from the Al A'id family that ruled from Abha. He kept the emirate largely free of Ottoman control despite repeated campaigns, but in 1871–1872 an Ottoman army took Abha and he was killed.

muhammad-ibn-ali-al-idrisi.s: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi was the founder of the Idrisid Emirate of Asir on the Red Sea coast of Arabia. A great-grandson of the Moroccan Sufi teacher Ahmad ibn Idris, he settled at Sabya in the Tihama and used his religious prestige to lead the tribes against the Ottomans,…

muhammad-ibn-ali-al-senussi.s: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Senussi, known as the Grand Senussi, was an Algerian-born scholar who founded the Senussi Sufi order in Mecca in 1837. He set up its first lodge in Cyrenaica at al-Bayda in 1843 and later moved its centre to the oasis of Jaghbub, building a network of…

muhammad-ibn-falah.s: Muhammad ibn Falah was the founder of the Mushasha dynasty of Khuzestan. A Shia scholar from Wasit trained at Hilla, he proclaimed himself the representative of the Hidden Imam, or the Mahdi himself, in the 1430s and gathered a following among the Arab tribes of the marshes.

muhammad-ibn-ilyas.s: Muhammad ibn Ilyas was a Samanid commander of Sogdian origin who made himself ruler of Kerman in south-eastern Iran around 932, founding the Ilyasid dynasty. Ruling from Bardasir, he defended his independence against the Buyids for over three decades.

muhammad-ibn-musafir.s: Muhammad ibn Musafir was lord of Tarom in northern Iran and the founder of the Sallarid (Musafirid) dynasty. From the fortress of Shamiran on the Qezel Ozan he became the leading power in Daylam, marrying into the Justanid dynasty.

muhammad-ibn-muzayn.s: Muhammad ibn Muzayn was the founder of the Taifa of Silves in the western Algarve. A member of a local Arab family, he took control of Silves, then a rich river port on the Arade, around 1027 and ruled it as an independent principality.

muhammad-ibn-nasir-bu-shentuf.s: Muhammad ibn Nasir Bu Shentuf was the last important emir of the Hintata, the Masmuda Berber dynasty that ruled Marrakesh in the early 16th century. Pressed between the Portuguese on the Atlantic coast and the rising Saadi sharifs of the Sous, he was assassinated in 1524, and…

muhammad-ibn-rashid.s: Muhammad ibn Rashid was emir of Jabal Shammar in northern Arabia from 1869 to 1897 and the greatest ruler of the Rashidi dynasty. He exploited the civil war in the second Saudi state to take Riyadh in 1887, and his victory at Mulayda in 1891 made him master of central Arabia.

muhammad-ibn-said-ibn-harun.s: Muhammad ibn Said ibn Harun was the second and last ruler of the Taifa of Santa Maria del Algarve, the small Muslim principality centred on the town later called Faro. He succeeded his father Said ibn Harun and tried to balance between the Taifa of Silves and Seville.

muhammad-ibn-shaddad.s: Muhammad ibn Shaddad was the founder of the Shaddadid dynasty, a Kurdish family that rose as the Sallarid emirate declined. In 951 he seized Dvin in Armenia, though he could not hold it, and he died in 955.

muhammad-ibn-uthman-al-mazrui.s: Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Mazrui was the Omani governor of Mombasa who made the city independent. When the Ya'rubid dynasty of Oman fell in 1741, he refused to recognise the new Busaidi ruler Ahmad ibn Said and ruled from Fort Jesus as a sovereign.

muhammad-ibn-yahya-al-yahsubi.s: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Yahsubi was ruler of the Taifa of Niebla, in the far south-west of al-Andalus. A member of the Arab Banu Yahya family, he succeeded his brother Ahmad and for a time accepted the protection of Seville before resisting it.

muhammad-ibn-yusuf-al-ukhaydir.s: Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Ukhaydir was the founder of the Ukhaydirid dynasty of al-Yamama in central Arabia. A descendant of al-Hasan ibn Ali, he fled the Hejaz around 866 after a failed Alid revolt and took control of al-Yamama, with his seat at al-Khidrima near modern al-Kharj.

muhammad-ibn-zayd.s: Muhammad ibn Zayd was the second ruler of the Alavid (Zaydi) state in Tabaristan, succeeding his brother Hasan ibn Zayd in 884. Governing from Amol with the support of Daylamite warriors, he held the Caspian lands against rivals and Abbasid governors.

muhammad-ibn-ziyad.s: Muhammad ibn Ziyad was the founder of the Ziyadid dynasty of Yemen. A descendant of the Umayyad governor Ziyad ibn Abihi, he was sent by the caliph al-Ma'mun in 818 or 819 to subdue the rebellious tribes of the Tihama.

muhammad-ii-of-kelantan.s: Muhammad II of Kelantan was sultan of Kelantan, on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, from 1837 to 1886. Coming to power after a succession war with Siamese backing, he strengthened royal power from his new capital at Kota Bharu.

muhammad-khan-bangash.s: Muhammad Khan Bangash was an Afghan soldier of fortune who founded the Bangash nawabs of Farrukhabad. Serving the Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar, he received lands in the Ganges Doab and in 1714 founded the town of Farrukhabad, naming it after the emperor.

muhammad-naguib.s: Muhammad Naguib was an Egyptian army officer who served as the figurehead of the Free Officers' coup of July 1952 that forced King Farouk to abdicate. When the monarchy was abolished in June 1953 he became the first president of the Republic of Egypt.

muhammad-nazim-khan.s: Muhammad Nazim Khan was mir of Hunza in the Karakoram from 1892 until his death in 1938. After a British force defeated Hunza and Nagar in 1891 and his half-brother Safdar Ali Khan fled to China, the British installed him as ruler.

muhammad-quli-qutb-shah.s: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was the fifth sultan of Golconda, reigning from 1580 to 1612. He founded the city of Hyderabad in 1591 and built its central monument, the Charminar.

muhammad-rahim-of-bukhara.s: Muhammad Rahim of Bukhara was a chief of the Manghit tribe who took effective power in the Khanate of Bukhara in the 1740s under the protection of Nader Shah. After Nader's death in 1747 he pushed aside the Janid khans and in 1756 took the title of khan himself.

muhammad-rumfa.s: Muhammad Rumfa was ruler of the Hausa kingdom of Kano from about 1463 to 1499. He extended the city walls, built the Gidan Rumfa palace, founded the Kurmi market and strengthened Islam at court, receiving the North African scholar al-Maghili, who wrote him a treatise on…

muhammad-salahuddin-of-bima.s: Muhammad Salahuddin of Bima was the last sultan of Bima, on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia, reigning from 1915 to 1951. Bima was then a self-governing domain of the Dutch East Indies.

muhammad-thakurufaanu.s: Muhammad Thakurufaanu was a Maldivian hero who led the resistance against the Portuguese, who had occupied Malé from 1558. With his brothers he waged a guerrilla war from the northern atolls and in 1573 killed the Portuguese commander and freed the capital.

muhammad-v-of-granada.s: Muhammad V of Granada was the Nasrid sultan of Granada from 1354 to 1359 and again from 1362 to 1391. Deposed in a palace coup, he regained his throne with help from Peter I of Castile.

muhammad-v-of-kelantan.s: Muhammad V of Kelantan has been sultan of Kelantan, in north-eastern Peninsular Malaysia, since 2010. In 2016 he was elected Yang di-Pertuan Agong, the king of Malaysia, under the country's rotating monarchy.

muhammadjan-tynyshbaev.s: Muhammadjan Tynyshbaev was a Kazakh engineer and politician of the Alash movement who served as the first head of government of the Turkestan Autonomy, proclaimed at Kokand in November 1917. He soon handed over to Mustafa Chokay, and the Bolsheviks crushed the autonomy in…

muhammadu-dikko.s: Muhammadu Dikko was emir of Katsina in northern Nigeria from 1906 to 1944. Appointed by the British after they deposed the previous emir, he founded the Sullubawa dynasty that still reigns.

muhammadu-kanta.s: Muhammadu Kanta, also called Kanta Kotal, was the founder of the Hausa kingdom of Kebbi. A commander in the Songhai army of Askia Muhammad, he quarrelled over the spoils of a campaign against Agadez around 1516 and rebelled, defeating Songhai forces and building fortified…

muhammadu-makau.s: Muhammadu Makau was the last Hausa king of Zazzau (Zaria) before the Fulani jihad. When the jihadists took Zaria in 1808, he fled south with his followers to Zuba and kept up a successor state.

muirchertach-mac-lochlainn.s: Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn was king of Ailech in the north of Ireland and, from 1156, high king of Ireland. The most powerful of the Mac Lochlainn kings of the Northern Uí Néill, he dominated the island for a decade and supported church reform, including the new Cistercian…

muirchertach-o-briain-d-1343.s: Muirchertach Ó Briain was king of Thomond, in north Munster, from 1317 to 1343. He won the throne in a civil war among the O'Briens, and in 1318 his side destroyed the army of the Anglo-Norman lord Richard de Clare at Dysert O'Dea, ending Norman attempts to conquer Thomond.

muizz-al-dawla.s: Mu'izz al-Dawla was the youngest of the three Buyid brothers who built a Daylamite empire in Iran and Iraq. Born Ahmad ibn Buya, he entered Baghdad in 945 and received his title from the Abbasid caliph, whom he and his successors kept as a figurehead.

muizz-al-din-husayn-kart.s: Mu'izz al-Din Husayn Kart was the most notable ruler of the Kart dynasty of Herat, reigning from 1331 to 1370. At first a vassal of the Ilkhanate, he ruled as an independent sovereign after its collapse in 1335, defeated the Sarbadars at Zava in 1342 and patronised Persian…

mujahid-al-amiri.s: Mujahid al-Amiri was a freedman of the Amirid household who seized Dénia around 1010, as the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed, and founded the Taifa of Dénia. He added the Balearic Islands to his realm and in 1015–1016 led a seaborne expedition against Sardinia, which was driven…

mujir-al-din-abaq.s: Mujir al-Din Abaq was the last Burid ruler of Damascus, reigning from 1140 to 1154, largely under the control of powerful ministers. Damascus kept a cautious alliance with the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem against the Zengids, yet was besieged by the Second Crusade in 1148.

mukunda-deva-ii.s: Mukunda Deva II was raja of Khurda in Odisha when the British East India Company conquered the region in 1803. He joined a revolt against the Company, and in 1804 Khurda was annexed and the raja deposed and imprisoned.

mulla-ilyas.s: Mulla Ilyas, known as Akhund Baba, was a 17th-century Pashtun religious leader of the Yusufzai Painda Khel in the Dir region of north-western Pakistan. His spiritual standing gave his descendants authority over the Panjkora valley, where they became khans and later Nawabs of Dir.

mullah-mohammad-omar.s: Mullah Mohammad Omar was the founder and supreme leader of the Taliban, which arose among religious students in Kandahar in 1994. Taking the title Commander of the Faithful, he led the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan from 1996, imposing a strict interpretation of Islamic law…

muriq-shpata.s: Muriq Shpata was an Albanian ruler of the Despotate of Arta in north-western Greece, succeeding Gjin Bua Shpata in 1399. His family had taken Arta during the Albanian expansion into Epirus in the 14th century.

murong-bao.s: Murong Bao was the second emperor of the Xianbei state of Later Yan and son of its founder Murong Chui. In 395 he led a great army against the rising Northern Wei and was crushingly defeated at Canhe Slope.

murong-chong.s: Murong Chong was a prince of the deposed Former Yan house who led the Xianbei rising against Former Qin after the Battle of Fei River. Taking over from his brother Murong Hong in 384, he captured and plundered Chang'an in 385 and proclaimed himself emperor of the state later…

murong-huang.s: Murong Huang was the Xianbei leader who founded the Former Yan, declaring himself King of Yan in 337. Building on his father Murong Hui's settlement of western Liaoning, he moved his capital to Longcheng (modern Chaoyang) in 342, sacked the Goguryeo capital the same year and…

murong-jun.s: Murong Jun was the ruler of Former Yan from 348 to 360 and son of Murong Huang. After the collapse of Later Zhao he led his Xianbei armies onto the North China Plain, captured Ran Min in 352 and proclaimed himself emperor.

murong-ke.s: Murong Ke was a prince and general of the Former Yan, son of Murong Huang. In 352 he defeated and captured Ran Min, ruler of Ran Wei, at Liantai, opening the way to Ye.

murong-nuohebo.s: Murong Nuohebo was the last ruler of Tuyuhun, the Xianbei kingdom around Qinghai Lake, reigning as a vassal of the Tang dynasty and married to a Tang princess. When the Tibetan Empire conquered Tuyuhun in 663 he fled with his followers into Tang territory.

murong-wei.s: Murong Wei was the last emperor of Former Yan, succeeding his father Murong Jun as a child in 360. After the regent Murong Ke died, court jealousy drove the general Murong Chui to Former Qin.

murong-xianbei.s: The Murong Xianbei were a branch of the Xianbei nomads who settled in western Liaoning in the 3rd century and adopted farming and Chinese-style government. Their princes founded the Former Yan, Later Yan, Western Yan and Southern Yan states in northern China.

murrough-obrien-1st-earl-of-thomond.s: Murrough O'Brien was the last Gaelic king of Thomond in western Ireland. Under Henry VIII's policy of surrender and regrant he gave up his kingship in 1543, went to court and was created Earl of Thomond, holding his lands under the English Crown in the new Kingdom of Ireland.

murshid-quli-khan.s: Murshid Quli Khan was a Mughal official appointed diwan (revenue minister) of Bengal by Aurangzeb. He moved the revenue office to the town he renamed Murshidabad and in 1717 also became governor.

murska-sobota.s: Murska Sobota is the main town of Prekmurje, the region beyond the Mura river in north-eastern Slovenia, which belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary until 1919. On 29 May 1919, amid the turmoil of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, the local politician Vilmos Tkálecz proclaimed the…

musa-ibn-musa.s: Musa ibn Musa was the most powerful member of the Banu Qasi, a family of Muwallad lords in the upper Ebro valley. Half-brother of Íñigo Arista of Pamplona, he balanced between the Emirate of Córdoba, the Franks and the Christian kingdoms, ruling Tudela, Zaragoza and Huesca and…

musa-ibn-nusayr.s: Musa ibn Nusayr was the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya who completed the conquest of North Africa. His subordinate Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed into Iberia in 711 and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic; Musa followed in 712 with a larger army and took Seville, Mérida and Zaragoza.

mustafa-chokay.s: Mustafa Chokay was a Kazakh lawyer and politician who headed the Turkestan Autonomy, proclaimed at Kokand in 1917 within a hoped-for democratic Russian federation. When the Bolsheviks destroyed Kokand in February 1918 he escaped, eventually settling in Paris, where he edited…

mustafa-pasha-bushati.s: Mustafa Pasha Bushati was the last hereditary pasha of Scutari (Shkodër) from the Bushati family, which had ruled northern Albania almost independently since 1757. He joined Bosnian notables resisting the centralising reforms of Sultan Mahmud II, but in 1831 the grand vizier…

mustapha-bouchelaghem.s: Mustapha Bouchelaghem was bey of the West (Mascara) in Ottoman Algeria in the early 18th century. In 1708 his forces captured Oran from Spain, which had held it since 1509, and he made it his capital.

mustapha-boumezrag.s: Mustapha Boumezrag was the last bey of Titteri, the Ottoman province of central Algeria governed from Médéa. After the French captured Algiers in 1830 he first submitted to the invaders and then turned against them.

mutara-iii-rudahigwa.s: Mutara III Rudahigwa was mwami (king) of Rwanda from 1931 to 1959, installed by the Belgian administration of Ruanda-Urundi in place of his father. He converted to Catholicism and in 1946 dedicated the country to Christ the King.

mwambutsa-iv.s: Mwambutsa IV was mwami (king) of Burundi from 1915 to 1966, reigning under Belgian rule and into independence in 1962. Burundi became a constitutional monarchy, but ethnic and political violence, including the assassination of prime ministers, undermined his authority.

mwanga-ii.s: Mwanga II was kabaka (king) of Buganda from 1884, succeeding Mutesa I. He ordered the killing of Christian converts at his court in 1885–1887, the Uganda Martyrs, and was deposed and restored amid civil war between Muslim, Catholic and Protestant factions.

mwata-yamvo.s: Mwata Yamvo is the title of the paramount ruler of the Lunda Empire, centred in the south of the present Democratic Republic of the Congo. From the 17th century the Mwata Yamvo sent generals and kinsmen to found tributary or offshoot kingdoms, among them Kazembe on the Luapula…

mwezi-iv-gisabo.s: Mwezi IV Gisabo was mwami (king) of Burundi from about 1852 to 1908, the last to rule before effective colonial control. He fought off Swahili-Arab slave traders and rival princes, and for years resisted German forces from German East Africa.

mykhailo-hrushevsky.s: Mykhailo Hrushevsky was a Ukrainian historian, author of a multi-volume History of Ukraine-Rus', and a leader of the national movement. In 1917 he chaired the Central Rada in Kyiv, which proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic and in January 1918 its independence.

mykola-ryabovol.s: Mykola Ryabovol was a Kuban Cossack politician and chairman of the Kuban Rada in the Kuban People's Republic during the Russian Civil War. He led the Black Sea Cossack faction that favoured federation with Ukraine, bringing conflict with General Denikin's Volunteer Army, which…

mykola-skrypnyk.s: Mykola Skrypnyk was a Ukrainian Bolshevik who served in the People's Secretariat of the Soviet Ukrainian government formed in Kharkiv in December 1917. Later, as People's Commissar of Education of Soviet Ukraine, he promoted Ukrainian language and culture under the policy of…

mynyddog-mwynfawr.s: Mynyddog Mwynfawr was a ruler of the Gododdin, the Brittonic people of south-east Scotland, known from the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin attributed to Aneirin. The poem tells how he feasted a war band for a year at his stronghold of Din Eidyn (Edinburgh) before sending it to…

mikhail-of-chernigov.s: Mikhail of Chernigov was prince of Chernigov and, at times, grand prince of Kiev in the years of the Mongol invasion. After the Mongols sacked Chernigov in 1239 he fled abroad, and in 1246 he was executed at the camp of Batu Khan, reportedly for refusing a pagan purification…

milan-i-of-serbia.s: Milan Obrenović ruled Serbia as prince from 1868 and as its first modern king from 1882 to 1889. Under him Serbia fought the Ottomans in 1876–1878 and won full independence at the Congress of Berlin.

matilda-of-ringelheim.s: Matilda of Ringelheim was the wife of Henry the Fowler, king of East Francia, and mother of Emperor Otto I. Educated at the abbey of Herford, she became known for her piety and charity, founded convents including Quedlinburg and Nordhausen, and was venerated as a saint after…

mohammed-iii-of-morocco.s: Mohammed III of Morocco, known as Sidi Mohammed ibn Abdallah, was Alaouite sultan from 1757 to 1790. He restored order after decades of civil strife, founded the port of Essaouira (Mogador) to control foreign trade, recaptured Mazagan from the Portuguese in 1769 and signed…

mary-mother-of-jesus.s: Mary, mother of Jesus, known as the Virgin Mary, is venerated in Christianity, above all in the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Medieval rulers dedicated lands to her: Pope Innocent III dedicated conquered Livonia to her, giving Terra Mariana its name, and the lord of…

maykop.s: Maykop is the capital of the Republic of Adygea in the North Caucasus of Russia, on the Belaya river. It was founded as a Russian fortress in 1857 during the conquest of the western Circassians.

maharashtra.s: Maharashtra is a state of western India, created in 1960 from the Marathi-speaking parts of Bombay State, with Mumbai as its capital. Its territory includes the Konkan coast and much of the northern Deccan plateau.

mikmaq.s: The Mi'kmaq are an Indigenous people of the Atlantic region of North America, living in what are now Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, the Gaspé Peninsula and Newfoundland. They speak an Algonquian language and were members of the Wabanaki Confederacy.

muhammad-daud-syah.s: Muhammad Daud Syah was the last sultan of Aceh. Proclaimed as a child in the 1870s, after the Dutch had taken the capital during the Aceh War, he became a symbol of Acehnese resistance.

mumbai.s: Mumbai, formerly Bombay, is the capital of Maharashtra and the largest city of India, built on a group of islands on the west coast. Portugal ceded the islands to England in 1661 as part of the dowry of Catherine of Braganza, and the East India Company made them its main…

munich.s: Munich is the capital of Bavaria in southern Germany, on the river Isar. Founded around 1158 by Henry the Lion, it became the residence of the Wittelsbach dukes, electors and kings of Bavaria from the 13th century until 1918.

maritsa.s: The Maritsa, called Evros in Greek, Meriç in Turkish and Hebrus in antiquity, is the longest river lying wholly in the Balkans, about 480 kilometres long. It rises in the Rila mountains of Bulgaria, flows through the Thracian plain past Plovdiv and Edirne, and forms the border…

mures-river.s: The Mureș, Maros in Hungarian, is a river of Romania and Hungary about 760 kilometres long. It rises in the Eastern Carpathians, flows west across Transylvania past Târgu Mureș, Alba Iulia and Arad, and joins the Tisza at Szeged.

moamoria-rebellion.s: The Moamoria rebellion was a series of uprisings against the Ahom kings of Assam from 1769 to about 1805. It was led by disciples of the Moamara satra, a Vaishnavite monastery whose followers, many of them of low caste or tribal origin, had been persecuted by the court.

moran-people.s: The Moran are an indigenous people of upper Assam in north-eastern India, who once spoke a Bodo-Garo language now largely replaced by Assamese. They were among the first peoples absorbed into the Ahom kingdom after Sukaphaa's arrival in the 13th century.

marka.s: Marka, also spelled Merca, is a port town on the Benadir coast of southern Somalia, south-west of Mogadishu. A trading town since the Middle Ages, it exported grain and cotton from the Shabelle valley and came under the Ajuran Sultanate, the Geledi Sultanate and the Sultanate…

mir-ali-bey.s: Mir Ali Bey was an Ottoman corsair who led two expeditions down the East African coast in the 1580s. In 1585–86 he persuaded many Swahili towns to reject Portuguese overlordship and accept Ottoman protection.

mariehamn.s: Mariehamn is the capital and only town of the Åland Islands, an autonomous Swedish-speaking region of Finland. Founded in 1861 under Russian rule and named after the Empress Maria Alexandrovna, it lies on a peninsula of the main island with harbours on both sides.

moulay-ali-al-sharif.s: Moulay Ali al-Sharif was a sharif of Tafilalt in south-eastern Morocco who was proclaimed leader there around 1631, as the Saadi Sultanate disintegrated. He is regarded as the founder of the Alaouite dynasty, although its real power was built by his sons Muhammad and…

mirzhakip-dulatov.s: Mirzhakip Dulatov was a Kazakh poet, journalist and politician, a founder of the Alash party. His poetry collection Oyan, qazaq!

makan-ibn-kaki.s: Makan ibn Kaki was a Daylamite military commander who dominated Tabaristan and Gurgan in the 920s and 930s, first in the service of the Alavid rulers and then on his own account. He competed for power with Asfar ibn Shiruya and Mardavij, and was killed in 940 fighting a…

mardavij.s: Mardavij ibn Ziyar was a Gilite military leader who founded the Ziyarid dynasty in northern Iran. Rising in the service of Daylamite commanders, he seized Tabaristan and much of the Jibal around 930, ruling from Isfahan and Rayy and dreaming of restoring the Persian monarchy.

monterey-california.s: Monterey is a city on Monterey Bay on the central coast of California. Founded by Spain in 1770 as a presidio and mission, it was the capital of Alta California under Spanish and Mexican rule.

mexican-american-war.s: The Mexican–American War was fought between the United States and Mexico from 1846 to 1848, following the American annexation of Texas and a border dispute. American forces occupied New Mexico and California and captured Mexico City in 1847.

mangalore.s: Mangalore (Mangaluru) is a port city on the coast of Karnataka, south-western India, at the mouth of the Netravati and Gurupura rivers. It was a capital of the Alupa dynasty and a trading port visited by Arab and later Portuguese merchants.

meos.s: The Meos are a Muslim community of the Mewat region, in parts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh in north-western India. Mostly farmers, they converted to Islam in stages between about the 12th and 17th centuries but long kept many customs shared with their Hindu neighbours.

mau-movement.s: The Mau was a non-violent movement for Samoan self-government. An early Mau a Pule under the orator chief Lauaki Namulauʻulu Mamoe opposed German rule in 1908–1909, and the movement revived in the 1920s against New Zealand rule in Western Samoa, where police killed its leader…

milcom.s: Milcom, or Milkom, was the national god of the Ammonites, worshipped in their kingdom east of the Jordan in the Iron Age. His name is related to the Semitic word for 'king', and he appears in Ammonite inscriptions such as the Amman Citadel Inscription.

madagascar.s: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island, in the Indian Ocean off south-eastern Africa. Settled by Austronesian seafarers from South-East Asia and by people from East Africa during the first millennium CE, it developed many kingdoms, of which the Merina unified most of…

mahavihara.s: The Mahavihara was the great monastery of Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, founded by King Devanampiya Tissa in the 3rd century BCE after the arrival of the monk Mahinda. It became the stronghold of Theravada orthodoxy, competing with the Abhayagiri and Jetavana monasteries.

mahinda-buddhist-monk.s: Mahinda was a Buddhist monk, said to be a son of the Maurya emperor Ashoka, who brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE. According to the chronicles he converted King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale, and the Mahavihara monastery was founded at Anuradhapura soon after.

mahinda-v.s: Mahinda V was the last king of the Anuradhapura Kingdom in Sri Lanka, reigning from 982. His rule was weakened by unpaid mercenaries and revolt, and the Chola Empire under Rajaraja I took Anuradhapura in 993.

mission-san-luis-de-talimali.s: Mission San Luis de Talimali was a Spanish Franciscan mission in modern Tallahassee, Florida, founded in 1656 among the Apalachee. It became the western capital of Spanish Florida, where Apalachee leaders lived alongside Spanish soldiers, friars and settlers.

muses.s: The Muses were the Greek goddesses of poetry, music and the arts, daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, usually counted as nine. Their chief sanctuaries were on Mount Helicon in Boeotia, where Thespiae held the Mouseia festival in their honour, and at Pieria near Mount Olympus.

mappila.s: The Mappilas are a Muslim community of Kerala on the south-west coast of India, descended largely from Arab traders who settled on the Malabar coast and from local converts. Long active in seafaring and the spice trade, they supplied ministers and admirals to the Zamorins of…

mount-hermon.s: Mount Hermon is a mountain cluster on the border of Syria and Lebanon, its highest summit reaching about 2,814 metres. Snow-capped for much of the year, it feeds the sources of the Jordan River and was regarded as sacred in antiquity, with many temples on its slopes.

mastoureh-ardalan.s: Mastoureh Ardalan was a Kurdish poet and historian from Sanandaj in western Iran. Married to Khosrow Khan, ruler of the Ardalan principality, she wrote poetry in Persian and Gorani and a history of the Ardalan dynasty, among the earliest historical works by a woman in the region.

manbij.s: Manbij is a city in northern Syria, north-east of Aleppo and west of the Euphrates. In antiquity it was Hierapolis Bambyce, a famous centre of the cult of the Syrian goddess Atargatis.

mardin.s: Mardin is a city in south-eastern Turkey, built in terraces on a steep hill overlooking the Mesopotamian plain. It was the capital of an Artuqid dynasty from the early 12th century to 1409 and is famous for its stone mosques and madrasas and its Syriac Christian heritage.

max-mallowan.s: Sir Max Mallowan was a British archaeologist of the ancient Near East. He excavated Chagar Bazar and Tell Brak in Syria in the 1930s and later led major excavations at Nimrud in Iraq, recovering many of its famous ivories.

my-chau.s: Mỵ Châu is a princess of Vietnamese legend, daughter of King An Dương Vương of Âu Lạc. She married Trọng Thủy, son of Zhao Tuo of Nanyue, who used her trust to steal the magic crossbow that protected the citadel of Cổ Loa, allowing his father to conquer the kingdom around 179…

mayenne.s: Mayenne is a department of north-western France, in the Pays de la Loire region, named after the river Mayenne that crosses it from north to south. Its capital is Laval.

mandsaur.s: Mandsaur is a city in the Malwa region of western Madhya Pradesh, India. As ancient Dashapura it was the capital of the Aulikara dynasty, and inscriptions found there and nearby, including the silk weavers' inscription of 436 and 473 and the victory pillars of Yashodharman at…

madhya-pradesh.s: Madhya Pradesh is a large state in central India, with its capital at Bhopal. It covers much of Malwa, Bundelkhand and the Narmada valley and includes sites such as Sanchi, Khajuraho and Bhimbetka.

maurice-frydman.s: Maurice Frydman was a Polish-born engineer and spiritual writer who settled in India in the 1930s, where he became a follower of Gandhi and of Ramana Maharshi and took the name Swami Bharatananda. He drafted the 1939 constitution of the princely state of Aundh, which gave…

minturnae.s: Minturnae was an ancient town near the mouth of the Liris, now the Garigliano, in southern Lazio, Italy. Originally an Auruncan settlement, it was destroyed by Rome in 314 BCE, and a Roman colony was founded there in 296 BCE.

minkhaung-i.s: Minkhaung I was king of Ava in Upper Burma from 1400 until his death in 1421, a son of Swa Saw Ke. His reign was dominated by the Forty Years' War against the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy under Razadarit, in which Ava's armies, often led by his son Minye Kyawswa, came close to…

myitnge-river.s: The Myitnge, or Dokhtawady, is a river of central Myanmar that rises in the Shan Hills and flows west to join the Irrawaddy just south of Mandalay. At the confluence stood Ava, or Inwa, capital of Burmese kingdoms for long periods between 1365 and 1842, whose site was…

madrasa-al-firdaws.s: The Madrasa al-Firdaws is an Islamic college and Sufi lodge outside the walls of Aleppo, in Syria, founded in 1235–1236 by Dayfa Khatun, regent of the Ayyubid principality. Built of finely cut stone around a courtyard with a pool and an arcaded portico, it is considered one of…

musavat.s: Musavat, meaning 'Equality', is an Azerbaijani political party founded in Baku in 1911, which led the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic of 1918–1920 under Mammad Amin Rasulzade. Banned after the Soviet takeover in 1920, it continued in exile and was revived in Azerbaijan in…

muryeong-of-baekje.s: Muryeong was king of Baekje from 501 to 523 and restored the kingdom's strength after its retreat to Ungjin. He strengthened ties with the Liang dynasty in southern China and with Yamato Japan.

mahmud-gawan.s: Mahmud Gawan was a Persian merchant from Gilan who became chief minister of the Bahmani Sultanate of the Deccan, serving from the 1460s until 1481. He reorganised the provinces and revenue system, led campaigns that extended Bahmani territory to the west coast, including the…

marico-river.s: The Marico River is a river in South Africa's North West province that flows north from the western highveld to join the Crocodile River, the two together forming the Limpopo. The surrounding Marico district was home to the Bahurutshe and other Tswana people, and in 1837…

mont-orgueil.s: Mont Orgueil Castle is a medieval castle on a rocky headland above Gorey harbour in Jersey, facing the coast of Normandy. Begun in the early 13th century after King John lost mainland Normandy in 1204, it was Jersey's main defence against French attack for some 400 years and…

masjed-soleyman.s: Masjed Soleyman is a city in Khuzestan province in south-western Iran, in the foothills of the Zagros on lands of the Bakhtiari tribes. On 26 May 1908 William Knox D'Arcy's syndicate struck oil there, the first commercial oil discovery in the Middle East, which led to the…

maiden-tower.s: The Maiden Tower is a cylindrical stone tower about 29 metres high in the Old City of Baku, Azerbaijan, standing near the old shoreline of the Caspian Sea. Its date and purpose are disputed: parts may be pre-Islamic, while an inscription links building work to the 12th century.

molepolole.s: Molepolole is a large village in south-eastern Botswana, about 50 kilometres north-west of Gaborone, and the administrative centre of Kweneng District. It became the capital of the Bakwena under Sechele I in the 1860s, and missionaries later founded the Scottish Livingstone…

mojmir-i.s: Mojmír I was the first known ruler of the Moravian Slavs, regarded as the founder of Great Moravia, ruling from about 830 to 846. Around 833 he drove the Slavic prince Pribina out of Nitra and united the lands north of the middle Danube into a single state centred on the…

mahon.s: Mahón, or Maó, is the capital of Menorca in the Balearic Islands, Spain, set at the head of one of the largest natural harbours in the Mediterranean. Known in antiquity as Mago, it is traditionally said to have been founded by the Carthaginians, and in 418 Bishop Severus…

mallorca.s: Mallorca, or Majorca, is the largest of the Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean, with its capital at Palma. Home to the Talaiotic culture in prehistory, it was conquered by Rome in 123 BCE and ruled by Muslim dynasties from 902, including the Banu Ghaniya.

menorca.s: Menorca, or Minorca, is the second-largest of the Balearic Islands, north-east of Mallorca. It is rich in Talaiotic monuments, including T-shaped taulas and the Naveta des Tudons.

macva.s: Mačva is a fertile lowland region in western Serbia between the Drina and Sava rivers, centred on the town of Šabac. In the Middle Ages it formed the Hungarian Banate of Macsó, created around 1254, and was contested by Hungary and Serbia.

muhammad-yunus.s: Muhammad Yunus is a Bangladeshi economist who founded the Grameen Bank and pioneered microcredit, lending small sums to the rural poor without collateral. He and the bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

makaba-ii.s: Makaba II was chief of the Bangwaketse, a Tswana people of present-day Botswana, in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. A successful raider and trader in cattle, ivory and furs, he made the Bangwaketse one of the strongest Tswana states, and European travellers visited his…

muhammad-arsyad-al-banjari.s: Muhammad Arsyad al-Banjari was an Islamic scholar from the Banjar Sultanate in southern Borneo. After some thirty years of study in Mecca and Medina he returned home in 1772, founded a religious school near Martapura and advised the sultan on Islamic law.

martapura.s: Martapura is a town in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, south-east of Banjarmasin on the Martapura river. After a Dutch attack on Banjarmasin in 1612 the court of the Banjar Sultanate moved upstream to Martapura, which remained a royal seat.

mahi-bajaj-sagar-dam.s: The Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam is a large dam on the Mahi river near Banswara in southern Rajasthan, India, built in the 1970s and 1980s for irrigation and hydroelectric power. Named after the independence activist Jamnalal Bajaj, it created a reservoir dotted with islands, and its…

mia-mottley.s: Mia Mottley is a Barbadian lawyer and politician who became the first woman prime minister of Barbados in May 2018, when her Barbados Labour Party won every seat in parliament. Her government oversaw the country's transition to a parliamentary republic in November 2021, and…

malhar-rao-gaekwad.s: Malhar Rao Gaekwad was Maharaja of Baroda from 1870 to 1875. In 1874 he was accused of trying to poison the British Resident, Colonel Robert Phayre, with arsenic.

maharaja-sayajirao-university-of-baroda.s: The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda is a public university in Vadodara, Gujarat, founded in 1949 and named after Sayajirao Gaekwad III. It grew out of Baroda College, established in 1881, and was created on the initiative of the princely family, fulfilling Sayajirao's…

mahikeng.s: Mahikeng, formerly Mafikeng or Mafeking, is the capital of North West province, South Africa. It grew from a settlement of the Tshidi Barolong in the mid-19th century and was the administrative headquarters of the Bechuanaland Protectorate, though outside it, until 1965.

methodism.s: Methodism is a Protestant movement that began in the 18th-century evangelical revival led by John and Charles Wesley within the Church of England, and became separate churches after Wesley's death. Its stress on personal conversion, preaching and organised local societies…

montshiwa.s: Montshiwa was chief of the Tshidi branch of the Barolong in southern Africa in the second half of the 19th century. He settled his people at Mafikeng and resisted the encroachment of the Transvaal Boers and the Boer statelets of Stellaland and Goshen.

mulambwa.s: Mulambwa was Litunga (king) of the Lozi kingdom of Barotseland from about 1780 to about 1830, one of its longest reigns. He reformed the kingdom's laws and strengthened royal authority over the Zambezi floodplain.

morija.s: Morija is a village in Maseru district, Lesotho, founded in 1833 as the first station of the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society, whose missionaries Moshoeshoe I invited into his kingdom. It became a centre of Christian education and printing in Sesotho, and is home to the…

muria.s: The Muria are a Gondi-speaking Adivasi people of the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh, India. They are known for the ghotul, a village dormitory where young people lived, learned and took part in community life, and for their dances and crafts.

maseru.s: Maseru is the capital and largest city of Lesotho, on the Caledon River at the border with South Africa. It was founded in 1869 as a British police camp after Basutoland became a British protectorate, and became the colonial capital.

maun.s: Maun is a town in north-western Botswana, on the Thamalakane river at the south-eastern edge of the Okavango Delta. It became the capital of the Batawana in 1915 and is the administrative centre of the North-West District.

moshoeshoe-i.s: Moshoeshoe I was the founder of the Basotho nation and of the kingdom that became Lesotho. From his stronghold of Thaba Bosiu he gathered refugees from the wars of the 1820s and used diplomacy, missionaries and guns to defend his lands against rivals, the British and the…

mar-biti-apla-usur.s: Mar-biti-apla-usur was king of Babylon for about six years in the late 10th century BCE, after the end of the Bazi Dynasty. The Babylonian king lists record him as the only king of an Elamite dynasty, though his name is Akkadian and his origins are uncertain.

mahendradatta.s: Mahendradatta was a Javanese princess of the Isyana dynasty of East Java who married King Udayana of Bali in the late 10th century and ruled jointly with him. Their son Airlangga became king of Kahuripan in Java, and another son, Anak Wungsu, later ruled Bali.

muzaffar-al-din-gokbori.s: Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri was the ruler of Erbil in northern Iraq from 1190 to 1233, son of Zayn al-Din Ali Kuchuk. He married Rabi'a Khatun, sister of Saladin, and fought at the Battle of Hattin in 1187.

mawlid.s: Mawlid is the celebration of the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad, held by many Muslims on 12 Rabi al-Awwal, the third month of the Islamic calendar. Public celebrations are first recorded under the Fatimids in Egypt, and those staged by Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri in Erbil in the…

magway-region.s: Magway Region is an administrative region of central Myanmar, in the dry zone along the Irrawaddy, with its capital at Magway. Its oilfields around Yenangyaung have been worked for centuries.

manhattan-project.s: The Manhattan Project was the programme led by the United States, with British and Canadian participation, that developed the first atomic bombs during the Second World War. Directed by General Leslie Groves, with J.

manuel-esquivel.s: Manuel Esquivel was a Belizean politician who led the United Democratic Party and served twice as Prime Minister of Belize, from 1984 to 1989 and from 1993 to 1998. His first victory ended the long rule of George Price's People's United Party since before independence.

mwamba-bemba-title.s: Mwamba is the title of one of the senior chiefs of the Bemba of north-eastern Zambia, who rules a large territory next to that of the Chitimukulu, the paramount. Holders of the Mwamba title were among the most powerful figures in the 19th-century Bemba state and often…

murtaza-nizam-shah-i.s: Murtaza Nizam Shah I was sultan of Ahmadnagar in the Deccan from 1565 to 1588. Early in his reign the Deccan sultanates defeated the Vijayanagara Empire at Talikota, and in 1574 he conquered and annexed the Berar Sultanate, ending the Imad Shahi line.

maniots.s: The Maniots are the people of the Mani peninsula in the southern Peloponnese of Greece. In its barren mountains they lived in clans with fortified stone tower houses, known for blood feuds, and they resisted Ottoman control throughout the period of Ottoman rule in Greece.

mascara-algeria.s: Mascara is a city in north-western Algeria, in the Tell Atlas south-east of Oran. Around 1700 it became the seat of the Ottoman Beylik of the West, until the bey moved to Oran after the Spanish left in 1792.

mazouna.s: Mazouna is a small town in north-western Algeria, in the Dahra hills east of Oran. From 1563 it was the first seat of the Ottoman Beylik of the West, before the capital moved to Mascara around 1700.

medea.s: Médéa is a city in the Tell Atlas of northern Algeria, about 80 km south-west of Algiers. From the 16th century it was the seat of the Ottoman Beylik of Titteri, a market town for grain, livestock and wool.

mukunda-deva.s: Mukunda Deva was the last independent Hindu king of Odisha, ruling from about 1559 to 1568. A minister of the Bhoi dynasty, he seized the throne by overthrowing its last rulers.

masaba.s: Masaba was emir of Nupe in central Nigeria, the son of the Fulani scholar Mallam Dendo by a Nupe mother. After struggles with his brother Usman Zaki and rival claimants, he ruled from Bida from 1859 to 1873.

muhu.s: Muhu is an island in western Estonia, between Saaremaa and the mainland, and the third largest in the country. Its people resisted the German crusaders until 1227, when the island was taken in the conquest of Saaremaa.

matiilu.s: Mati'ilu was the last independent king of Arpad, the Aramaean state of Bit-Agusi in northern Syria, in the mid-8th century BCE. He made a treaty with Ashur-nirari V of Assyria and another, preserved on the Aramaic Sefire steles, with Bar-Ga'yah of KTK.

max-von-oppenheim.s: Max von Oppenheim was a German diplomat, orientalist and archaeologist. In 1899 he discovered the site of Tell Halaf in north-eastern Syria, ancient Guzana, which he excavated from 1911 to 1913 and in 1929.

marias-massacre.s: The Marias Massacre was an attack by the United States Army on a camp of Piegan Blackfeet on the Marias River in Montana on 23 January 1870. Troops under Major Eugene Baker struck the peaceful band of Heavy Runner and killed well over a hundred people, most of them women,…

montana.s: Montana is a state of the north-western United States, stretching from the Rocky Mountains to the northern Great Plains. Once home to the Blackfeet, Crow, Cheyenne and other peoples, it saw gold rushes in the 1860s and the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, and became the…

mongolian-peoples-party.s: The Mongolian People's Party is a political party founded in 1920 by Mongolian revolutionaries, among them Damdin Sükhbaatar. With the help of the Soviet Red Army it took Urga in 1921 and set up a government that became the Mongolian People's Republic in 1924.

mahajanga.s: Mahajanga, formerly Majunga, is a port city on the north-west coast of Madagascar at the mouth of the Betsiboka River. It grew as a town of Antalaotra merchants and in the 18th century became the capital and main port of the Sakalava kingdom of Boina.

maiduguri.s: Maiduguri is the capital of Borno State in north-eastern Nigeria. It grew from Yerwa, the new capital founded in 1907 by Shehu Abubakar Garbai of Borno under British rule, and remains the seat of the Shehu of Borno.

maeotians.s: The Maeotians were ancient peoples living along the eastern shore of the Sea of Azov, which the Greeks called Lake Maeotis, and in the lower Kuban valley. Farmers and fishermen, they traded with the Greek cities of the Bosporus, and in the 4th century BCE the Spartocid kings…

miao-people.s: The Miao are an ethnic group of southern China, living mainly in Guizhou, Hunan, Yunnan, Sichuan and Guangxi, and officially one of China's largest minorities. The name covers several related peoples, including the Hmong, who also live in Vietnam, Laos and Thailand.

muslim-league-of-eritrea.s: The Muslim League of Eritrea was a political party founded in 1946 by Ibrahim Sultan Ali during the British administration of Eritrea. Drawing support mainly from Muslim lowlanders and opposing the Unionists who sought union with Ethiopia, it campaigned for Eritrean…

makarios-iii.s: Makarios III was archbishop of the Church of Cyprus from 1950 and the first president of the Republic of Cyprus from 1960 until his death in 1977. Leader of the Greek Cypriot campaign for union with Greece, he was exiled by the British to the Seychelles in 1956–1957.

misima.s: Misima is an island of the Louisiade Archipelago in Milne Bay Province, Papua New Guinea. Gold was found there in the 1880s, attracting prospectors in the early days of British New Guinea, and a large modern gold mine operated on the island from 1989 to 2004.

manuel-rojo-del-rio-y-vieyra.n: Manuel Rojo del Río y Vieyra
manuel-rojo-del-rio-y-vieyra.s: Manuel Rojo del Río y Vieyra was a Mexican-born archbishop of Manila from 1759 and acting governor of the Philippines from 1761. When British forces took Manila in October 1762 he signed the capitulation and agreed to a large ransom, while Simón de Anda y Salazar refused to…

mole-saint-nicolas.s: Môle Saint-Nicolas is a town and harbour at the north-western tip of Haiti, on the Windward Passage. Christopher Columbus landed there in December 1492 on his first voyage.

maasina-rule.s: Maasina Rule was a political and social movement on Malaita and other islands of the British Solomon Islands Protectorate from 1944 to about 1952. Led by local chiefs and returning labourers from the wartime Labour Corps, it organised villages, codified custom and refused…

malaita.s: Malaita is the most populous island of the Solomon Islands, a long mountainous island north-east of Guadalcanal. From the late 19th century many Malaitans were recruited as labourers for Queensland and Fiji and later for plantations in the Solomons.

macliau.s: Macliau was a Breton count of Vannes in the 6th century, known from the History of Gregory of Tours. After a violent struggle with his brother Chanao for power, he took control of the Vannetais, but he was killed in 577 by Theuderic, son of Bodic.

makhambet-otemisuly.s: Makhambet Otemisuly was a Kazakh poet and warrior of the Bukey Horde. With Isatay Taimanuly he led the revolt of 1836–1838 against Jangir Khan and the exactions of the Russian-backed elite, and his fiery verses became classics of Kazakh literature.

mikhail-frunze.s: Mikhail Frunze was a Bolshevik revolutionary and Red Army commander. In the Russian Civil War he defeated Kolchak's forces in the Urals, captured Bukhara in 1920 and drove Wrangel's army from the Crimea later that year.

meena-people.s: The Meenas are a people of Rajasthan and neighbouring parts of India, recognised today as a Scheduled Tribe in Rajasthan. Before the rise of the Rajput states, Meena chiefs held much of eastern Rajasthan, including the areas of Amber and Bundi, which Rajput clans took from…

margaret-iii-countess-of-flanders.s: Margaret III, Countess of Flanders, known as Margaret of Male, was the heiress of Louis of Male, count of Flanders. Her marriage in 1369 to Philip the Bold, duke of Burgundy, brought Flanders, Artois, Nevers, Rethel and the Free County of Burgundy to the Valois dukes on her…

muin-al-din-unur.s: Mu'in al-Din Unur was a Turkish mamluk commander who governed Damascus as atabeg for the last Burid rulers from about 1138 until his death in 1149. To resist Zengi of Aleppo and Mosul he allied with the Kingdom of Jerusalem, yet the Second Crusade besieged Damascus in July…

muin-al-din-suleyman-pervane.s: Mu'in al-Din Suleyman, known by his title Pervane, was the leading statesman of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in the 1260s and 1270s, governing under Mongol overlordship. He took the Black Sea port of Sinop in the early 1260s, and his family held it afterwards as a hereditary…

martabat-tujuh.s: The Martabat Tujuh, 'seven grades', was the constitution of the Sultanate of Buton, adopted under Sultan La Elangi in the early 17th century. Its name comes from a Sufi doctrine of seven stages of divine manifestation, which it used to order the ranks and offices of the state.

mohe.s: The Mohe were a group of Tungusic tribes of Manchuria, recorded in Chinese sources from the 6th century as successors of the earlier Sushen and Wuji. The southern Sumo Mohe joined Goguryeo refugees in founding Balhae in 698, while the northern Heishui Mohe on the Amur long…

miskawayh.s: Miskawayh was a Persian philosopher and historian who served as secretary and librarian to Buyid rulers and viziers. His Experiences of the Nations is a major universal history and an eyewitness source for Buyid Iraq and Iran.

midwestern-united-states.s: The Midwestern United States is a region of the north-central United States, including states such as Illinois, Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Missouri. Before European settlement it was home to the Mississippian culture, centred on Cahokia, and later to…

mariano-guadalupe-vallejo.s: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo was a Californio military commander and landowner, comandante of the northern frontier of Mexican Alta California, where he laid out the town of Sonoma in 1835. Rebels of the Bear Flag revolt seized him at Sonoma in June 1846 and held him prisoner for…

musab-ibn-al-zubayr.s: Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr was a brother of the caliph Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and his governor of Iraq during the Second Fitna. Ruling from Basra, he defeated al-Mukhtar al-Thaqafi at Kufa in 687.

mound-key.s: Mound Key is an island in Estero Bay on the south-west coast of Florida, built up largely of shell mounds by the Calusa. It is identified with Calos, the capital of the Calusa paramount chief, where the Spanish governor Pedro Menéndez de Avilés met the chief Carlos in 1566 and…

momin-khan-i.s: Momin Khan I, born Mirza Ja'far Najm-ud-daula, was a Mughal official of Persian descent who founded the state of Cambay, now Khambhat, in Gujarat. Posted to Cambay in the 1720s, he made it his family's hereditary seat as Mughal power declined, and he was later named governor…

mythen.s: The Mythen are a pair of limestone peaks above the town of Schwyz in central Switzerland: the Grosser Mythen, 1,898 metres high, and the Kleiner Mythen. Their distinctive shape dominates the valley of Schwyz and has long served as a landmark of the region where the Swiss…

menzingen.s: Menzingen is a municipality on an upland plateau in the Swiss canton of Zug. With Ägeri and Baar it formed one of the three rural communes that shared power with the town of Zug in the old canton's Landsgemeinde and rotated its offices.

mapuche.s: The Mapuche are an indigenous people of south-central Chile and south-western Argentina. They resisted Spanish conquest in the long Arauco War, keeping their independence south of the Biobío river after 1598, and dealt with Spain through treaties and parliaments.

mindanao.s: Mindanao is the second-largest island of the Philippines, in the south of the archipelago. Its western and southern parts were home to Muslim peoples and the Sultanate of Maguindanao, which, with the nearby Sulu Sultanate, resisted Spanish conquest for more than three centuries.

morro-do-castelo.s: Morro do Castelo was a hill in central Rio de Janeiro to which the young city was moved in 1567 under Governor Mem de Sá, after the French were driven out. It held the first fort, cathedral and Jesuit college of the city.

manuel-da-nobrega.s: Manuel da Nóbrega was a Portuguese Jesuit who led the first Jesuit mission to Brazil, arriving with the governor-general Tomé de Sousa in 1549. He organised missions among the indigenous peoples, opposed their enslavement and in 1554, with José de Anchieta, founded the college…

maximian.s: Maximian was a Roman emperor, raised by Diocletian to be his colleague and ruler of the west, as Caesar in 285 and Augustus in 286. He fought the Germanic peoples on the Rhine but failed to suppress the usurper Carausius in Britain.

marcianopolis.s: Marcianopolis was a Roman city in Moesia, near modern Devnya in north-eastern Bulgaria, founded by Trajan and named after his sister Marciana. It became the capital of the province of Moesia Secunda.

marne.s: The Marne is a river of north-eastern France, about 500 km long, that rises on the Langres plateau and flows through Champagne to join the Seine just south-east of Paris. Towns such as Châlons-en-Champagne and Meaux grew on its banks.

melus-of-bari.s: Melus of Bari was a Lombard nobleman of Apulia who led revolts against Byzantine rule in southern Italy. After a failed rising in 1009, he returned in 1017 with Norman mercenaries, the first Normans to fight in the region, but was crushed by the catepan Basil Boioannes at…

mar-scotland.s: Mar is a historic province of north-east Scotland, between the rivers Dee and Don in Aberdeenshire. It was ruled by a mormaer and later by the earls of Mar, one of the oldest Scottish earldoms, recorded from the 12th century.

mirobriga.s: Miróbriga was a Celtic and Roman town near present-day Santiago do Cacém in the Alentejo, southern Portugal. Pliny the Elder called its people Mirobrigenses 'surnamed Celtici'.

macbeth-king-of-scotland.s: Macbeth, in Gaelic Mac Bethad mac Findlaích, was King of Scotland from 1040 to 1057. Mormaer of Moray, he killed King Duncan I in battle in 1040 and took the throne, ruled securely enough to make a pilgrimage to Rome in 1050, and was killed by Duncan's son Malcolm III at…

mensheviks.s: The Mensheviks were the moderate faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, formed when it split with Lenin's Bolsheviks in 1903. Led by Julius Martov and others, they favoured a broad party and a bourgeois-democratic stage before socialism.

maranon-river.s: The Marañón is the main headwater of the Amazon, rising in the Andes of central Peru and flowing about 1,700 km north-west and then east through deep canyons before joining the Ucayali to form the Amazon proper. Its valleys bordered the homeland of the Chachapoya culture.

megabazus.s: Megabazus was a Persian general of Darius I in the late 6th century BCE. Left in Europe after Darius's Scythian campaign, he conquered Perinthus, much of Thrace and the Paeonians, and secured the submission of Macedon.

mangalesha.s: Mangalesha was king of the Chalukyas of Badami from about 592 to 610, ruling after his brother Kirtivarman I. He defeated the Kalachuris of Mahishmati and conquered Revatidvipa on the Konkan coast, and he dedicated the Vishnu cave temple at Badami in 578.

my-son.s: Mỹ Sơn is a group of ruined Hindu temples in a valley of Quảng Nam province, central Vietnam, built by the kings of Champa from the 4th to the 13th century. Dedicated mainly to Shiva, it was the chief religious centre of the Cham kingdom.

mahoba.s: Mahoba is a town in Bundelkhand, in southern Uttar Pradesh, India, and the headquarters of the district of the same name. It was one of the capitals of the Chandela dynasty, whose kings built large artificial lakes there such as the Madan Sagar.

mainamati.s: Mainamati is a range of low hills near Comilla in eastern Bangladesh with the remains of more than fifty Buddhist sites of the 7th to 12th centuries. The best known, the Shalban Vihara, was a large monastery built by a Deva dynasty king in the 7th or 8th century, and the area…

mattium.s: Mattium was the chief settlement of the Chatti, a Germanic people of what is now northern Hesse. Tacitus records that Germanicus burned it in 15 CE during his campaigns across the Rhine, but Rome never brought the Chatti under lasting control.

modhera-sun-temple.s: The Sun Temple at Modhera in northern Gujarat, India, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Surya, built in 1026–1027 under the Chaulukya king Bhima I. It consists of a sanctum, an assembly hall and a large stepped tank, the Surya Kund, all richly carved, and it is aligned so that…

mularaja-ii.s: Mularaja II was a child king of the Chaulukya dynasty of Gujarat, ruling from about 1175 to 1178 under the regency of his mother Naikidevi. In 1178 the Chaulukya army defeated Muhammad of Ghor at the Battle of Kasahrada near Mount Abu, one of the few defeats suffered by the…

mularaja.s: Mularaja was the founder of the Chaulukya, or Solanki, dynasty of Gujarat, ruling from Anahilavada (Patan) from about 941 to 996. By tradition the nephew of the last Chavda king, he seized the throne around 942 and built a kingdom across northern Gujarat, fighting the…

mahabharata.s: The Mahabharata is one of the two great Sanskrit epics of ancient India, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa and composed over several centuries between roughly 400 BCE and 400 CE. Its central story is the war at Kurukshetra between the Pandava and Kaurava branches of…

mahendravarman-chenla.s: Mahendravarman, born Chitrasena, was a king of Chenla in present-day Cambodia around the end of the 6th and start of the 7th century. Together with his relative Bhavavarman I he conquered much of Funan, and he left Sanskrit inscriptions across north-east Cambodia, southern…

mahodayapuram.s: Mahodayapuram, also called Makotai, was the capital of the Chera Perumals of Kerala from about the 9th to the early 12th century. It lay near modern Kodungallur in Thrissur district, around Tiruvanchikulam, and housed the royal court, temples and an astronomical observatory…

malayalam-language.s: The Malayalam language is a Dravidian language spoken mainly in Kerala and Lakshadweep in south-western India, by about 35 million people. It developed from the western dialects of Old Tamil and emerged as a distinct literary language between the 9th and 13th centuries,…

molokai.s: Molokaʻi is one of the main Hawaiian Islands, lying between Oʻahu and Maui. Known for the sea cliffs of its north coast and the fishponds of its southern shore, it was often contested between the chiefs of Oʻahu and Maui.

meskhetian-turks.s: The Meskhetian Turks are a Turkish-speaking Muslim people originally from Meskheti, the region of south-western Georgia around Akhaltsikhe along the Turkish border. Many descend from the Muslim population of the Ottoman Childir Eyalet.

mississippi-band-of-choctaw-indians.s: The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians is a federally recognised Native American nation in east-central Mississippi, United States, formed by descendants of Choctaw who stayed in their homeland after the removals of the 1830s. Left landless and marginalised for decades, they…

mississippian-culture.s: The Mississippian culture was a Native American mound-building civilisation that flourished in the Mississippi valley and the south-eastern United States from about 800 to 1600 CE. Based on maize farming, it formed chiefdoms centred on towns with large earthen platform mounds,…

mwana-pwo.s: Mwana Pwo, "young woman", is a type of wooden dance mask of the Chokwe people of Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. Representing an idealised female ancestor, with scarification marks and a fibre headdress, it is worn by a male dancer at masquerades…

mori-terumoto.s: Mōri Terumoto (1553–1625) was a Japanese daimyo who ruled much of western Honshu from Hiroshima, which he founded. One of the five regents appointed by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, he was the nominal commander of the western army at Sekigahara in 1600, though he stayed at Osaka Castle.

murata-seifu.s: Murata Seifū (1783–1855) was a samurai official of the Chōshū domain who led its Tenpō-era reforms from 1838. He reduced the domain's heavy debts, cut spending and encouraged and regulated the production of paper, salt and wax, while developing trade through the port of…

mayurasharma.s: Mayurasharma was the founder of the Kadamba dynasty of Karnataka in the mid-4th century CE. According to the Talagunda inscription, he was a Brahmin scholar who, insulted by a Pallava horseman at Kanchipuram, took up arms, defeated the Pallava frontier forces and forced them…

moctezuma-i.s: Moctezuma I, also called Motecuhzoma Ilhuicamina, was the fifth ruler (tlatoani) of Tenochtitlan, reigning from 1440 to 1469. With his adviser Tlacaelel he expanded the Aztec Triple Alliance far beyond the Valley of Mexico, conquering Chalco, Coixtlahuaca and lands towards the…

matthew-baillie-begbie.s: Matthew Baillie Begbie was an English-born lawyer who became the first judge of the colony of British Columbia in 1858. Travelling on circuit on horseback through the goldfields, he enforced British law among the miners and earned a reputation for firmness.

mikve-israel-emanuel-synagogue.s: The Mikvé Israel-Emanuel Synagogue in Willemstad, Curaçao, houses the oldest Jewish congregation in continuous existence in the Americas, founded by Sephardic Jews from Amsterdam in the 1650s. The present building, known as the Snoa, was dedicated in 1732 and is the oldest…

morant-bay-rebellion.s: The Morant Bay rebellion was an uprising of poor black farmers in Saint Thomas Parish, Jamaica, in October 1865, led by the Baptist deacon Paul Bogle. Protesters attacked the courthouse at Morant Bay, killing several officials.

mount-pelee.s: Mount Pelée is an active volcano at the northern end of Martinique in the French Antilles. Its eruption on 8 May 1902 sent a pyroclastic flow over the town of Saint-Pierre, then the island's commercial capital, killing about 28,000 people in minutes, with only a handful of…

maliseet.s: The Wolastoqiyik, also known as the Maliseet, are an Algonquian-speaking First Nation of the Saint John River valley in New Brunswick and neighbouring Quebec and Maine. They lived by hunting, fishing and farming, allied with the French and the Wabanaki Confederacy in the…

moreton-bay.s: Moreton Bay is a large bay on the coast of south-east Queensland, Australia, sheltered by Moreton and North Stradbroke islands, into which the Brisbane River flows. A penal settlement for reoffending convicts was founded on its shores at Redcliffe in 1824 and moved to the site…

mount-morgan-queensland.s: Mount Morgan is a town in central Queensland, Australia, south-west of Rockhampton, which grew around one of the world's richest gold mines. Gold was found there in the early 1880s, and the Mount Morgan mine produced gold and later copper for about a century, until the 1980s.

macquarie-harbour.s: Macquarie Harbour is a large, shallow inlet on the remote west coast of Tasmania, entered through a narrow passage known as Hells Gates. From 1822 to 1833 its Sarah Island held one of the harshest penal stations of the British Empire, for convicts who had reoffended in the…

mount-bischoff.s: Mount Bischoff is a mountain in north-western Tasmania near the town of Waratah. The prospector James 'Philosopher' Smith discovered tin there in 1871, and the Mount Bischoff mine became for a time one of the richest tin mines in the world, bringing prosperity to the colony in…

mount-lyell.s: Mount Lyell is a mountain in the West Coast Range of Tasmania, near Queenstown. Gold was found there in the 1880s, and from the 1890s the Mount Lyell Mining and Railway Company worked its huge copper deposits, smelting the ore on site.

melbourne.s: Melbourne is the capital of Victoria and the second-largest city of Australia, on Port Phillip Bay at the mouth of the Yarra River. Founded in 1835 by settlers from Van Diemen's Land, it boomed after the gold rushes of the 1850s to become one of the largest cities of the…

mimnermus.s: Mimnermus was a Greek elegiac poet from Colophon or Smyrna, active around 630 BCE. His surviving fragments lament the brevity of youth and the miseries of old age and celebrate love and pleasure.

mabo-v-queensland-no-2.s: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) was a 1992 decision of the High Court of Australia in a case brought by Eddie Mabo and other Meriam people of the Torres Strait. The court rejected the doctrine that Australia had been terra nullius, land belonging to no one, at British settlement, and…

manuel-l-quezon.s: Manuel L. Quezon was a Filipino statesman and the first president of the Commonwealth of the Philippines, from 1935 until his death.

mincio.s: The Mincio is a river of northern Italy that flows out of Lake Garda at Peschiera, passes Mantua, where it widens into lakes, and joins the Po. It formed a strong defensive line, part of the Quadrilateral of Austrian fortresses in the 19th century, and was crossed in battles…

martino-della-torre.s: Martino della Torre was a Milanese nobleman and leader of the popular party who in 1259 was made lord of the people of Milan, beginning the transformation of the commune into a lordship. His family, the della Torre, dominated Milan until 1277, when Archbishop Ottone Visconti…

modena.s: Modena is a city in Emilia-Romagna, northern Italy, on the Via Emilia. Roman Mutina, it became a commune in the 12th century and from 1288 belonged mostly to the Este, who made it their capital after losing Ferrara in 1598.

maremma.s: The Maremma is a coastal region of south-western Tuscany and northern Lazio in Italy. Once home to Etruscan cities, it became marshy and malarial after antiquity and was thinly settled for centuries, a land of pasture and cattle herded by mounted butteri.

march-of-treviso.s: The March of Treviso was a medieval name for the region of north-eastern Italy around Treviso, Padua, Vicenza, Feltre and Belluno, between the Alps and the Venetian lagoon. Dominated by the da Romano family in the 13th century, it was known for its courtly culture as the Marca…

mastino-i-della-scala.s: Mastino I della Scala was the founder of Scaliger power in Verona. Chosen leader of the commune after the death of Ezzelino III da Romano in 1259, he held the office of captain of the people and was effectively lord of the city by 1262.

mastino-ii-della-scala.s: Mastino II della Scala was lord of Verona from 1329, nephew of Cangrande I. He extended Scaliger rule to Brescia, Parma and Lucca, but a coalition of Venice and Florence defeated him in 1336–1339, stripping him of Padua, Treviso and other cities.

mashonaland.s: Mashonaland is the region of northern and north-eastern Zimbabwe inhabited mainly by the Shona people. Claimed by the Ndebele kingdom, it was occupied in 1890 by the Pioneer Column of the British South Africa Company, which founded Fort Salisbury, later Harare.

monrovia.s: Monrovia is the capital of Liberia, on Cape Mesurado at the mouth of the Saint Paul River. It was founded in 1822 by free African Americans settled by the American Colonization Society and named in 1824 after President James Monroe.

montgomery-alabama.s: Montgomery is the capital of the US state of Alabama, on the Alabama River. In February 1861 delegates of seceding states met there to form the Confederate States of America, and it was the Confederate capital until May 1861.

mangaia.s: Mangaia is the southernmost of the Cook Islands, an ancient volcanic island ringed by a raised coral cliff called the makatea. It had a warlike traditional society ruled by a high priest and victorious war leaders.

mars-mythology.s: Mars was the Roman god of war and, in early times, also a guardian of farmland, second in importance only to Jupiter in the state religion. Regarded as the father of Romulus and Remus, he was honoured with festivals in March, the month named after him, and with the Campus…

midlands.s: The Midlands is the central region of England, between the South and the North, usually divided into the East Midlands and the West Midlands. In the Iron Age it was home to peoples such as the Corieltauvi and Cornovii, and in the early Middle Ages it formed the core of the…

monastery-of-san-juan-de-la-pena.n: Monastery of San Juan de la Peña
monastery-of-san-juan-de-la-pena.s: San Juan de la Peña is a monastery in the Pyrenees south-west of Jaca, in Aragon, built beneath a great overhanging rock. Its origins lie in the 10th century or earlier, and in 1071 it became the first monastery in the Iberian Peninsula to adopt the Roman liturgy.

monastery-of-san-pedro-de-siresa.n: Monastery of San Pedro de Siresa
monastery-of-san-pedro-de-siresa.s: San Pedro de Siresa is a monastery church in the Hecho valley of the Aragonese Pyrenees, documented from the 9th century and among the oldest religious foundations of Aragon. Eulogius of Córdoba visited its library around 848 and took manuscripts of classical authors back to…

mahaut-countess-of-artois.s: Mahaut was countess of Artois from 1302, after her father Robert II was killed at the Battle of the Golden Spurs. Her nephew Robert III of Artois repeatedly challenged her inheritance, but royal courts upheld her claim.

madeleine-de-la-tour-dauvergne.s: Madeleine de La Tour d'Auvergne was a French noblewoman, heiress to the counties of Auvergne and Boulogne, who married Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, in 1518. She died weeks after giving birth to their daughter Catherine de' Medici, later queen of France.

marie-countess-of-champagne.s: Marie was countess of Champagne by her marriage to Henry the Liberal, and the eldest daughter of Louis VII of France and Eleanor of Aquitaine.
