mhlontlo.s: Mhlontlo was a king of the Mpondomise in the Eastern Cape of South Africa. He accepted a Cape magistrate in 1873, but in 1880 his followers killed the magistrate Hamilton Hope at Sulenkama and rose in revolt during the wider Basotho Gun War.

mpondomise.s: The Mpondomise are a Xhosa-speaking southern Nguni people of the Eastern Cape in South Africa, living around Tsolo and Qumbu. Their royal genealogy is shared with the Mpondo, from whom they separated many generations before written records, and they were respected by…

mzimvubu-river.s: The Mzimvubu is one of the largest rivers of the Eastern Cape in South Africa, rising in the Drakensberg and reaching the Indian Ocean at Port St Johns. Its upper valleys were the home of the Mpondomise, and its lower course ran through Pondoland.

min-bin.s: Min Bin was king of Mrauk U in Arakan from 1531 to 1554 and its most powerful ruler. He built up a strong navy with Portuguese mercenaries, controlled Chittagong and raided Bengal, and fortified his capital, beating off an invasion by Tabinshwehti of Toungoo in 1546 to 1547.

midhat-pasha.s: Midhat Pasha was an Ottoman statesman and reformer. As governor of the Danube province and of Baghdad from 1869 to 1872 he introduced the new provincial system, settled tribes, and founded schools, newspapers and public works.

mumuye.s: The Mumuye are a people of Taraba State in north-eastern Nigeria, speaking an Adamawa language. They lived in the hills south of the Benue and long resisted the Fulani emirate of Muri, which was founded among them and the Jukun in the 19th century.

muhammad-tayrab.s: Muhammad Tayrab was sultan of Darfur from about 1752 to 1786. After wars with Wadai to the west, he led a large army east in 1785, drove the Musabba'at ruler Hashim out of Kordofan and annexed the province.

menelaus.s: In Greek mythology, Menelaus was king of Sparta, the brother of Agamemnon and husband of Helen. When Helen left with the Trojan prince Paris, he and Agamemnon led the Greek expedition against Troy.

meghalaya.s: Meghalaya is a state in north-eastern India, formed from Assam in 1972, with its capital at Shillong. Its hills are home mainly to the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo peoples, who follow matrilineal descent, and include some of the wettest places on earth, such as Mawsynram and Sohra.

m-visvesvaraya.s: M. Visvesvaraya was an Indian civil engineer and statesman who served as diwan of Mysore from 1912 to 1918.

myrsilus.s: Myrsilus was a tyrant of Mytilene on Lesbos around 600 BCE, during the city's struggles between aristocratic factions. He is known mainly from the poems of his enemy Alcaeus, who greeted his death with a famous call to drink.

mozabites.s: The Mozabites are a Berber people of the Mzab valley in the Algerian Sahara, followers of the Ibadi branch of Islam. Their ancestors, refugees after the fall of the Rustamid state, founded the valley's five fortified towns from the 11th century.

mudhoji-ii-bhonsle.s: Mudhoji II Bhonsle, known as Appa Sahib, was ruler of the Maratha kingdom of Nagpur from 1816 to 1818, first as regent for his cousin Parsoji, whom he is believed to have had murdered. Having signed a subsidiary alliance with the British, he attacked their residency at…

malazgirt.s: Malazgirt is a town in Muş Province in eastern Turkey, north of Lake Van, known in Byzantine and medieval sources as Manzikert. It lies in the ancient Urartian and Armenian highlands on routes between Anatolia and Iran.

makhanda.s: Makhanda, known until 2018 as Grahamstown, is a town in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. It was founded in 1812 as a British military post during the frontier wars against the Xhosa and named after Colonel John Graham.

mir-jafar.s: Mir Jafar was the commander of the army of Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, who secretly allied with the British East India Company and held back his troops at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. Installed by Robert Clive as nawab, he depended on the Company, which replaced him in…

mixton-war.s: The Mixtón War was a rising of the Caxcan and other indigenous peoples of north-western Mexico against Spanish rule in New Galicia from 1540 to 1542. The rebels, fortified on mountain strongholds such as the Peñol of Mixtón, beat back early Spanish attacks, and the…

mhlatuze-river.s: The Mhlatuze is a river in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, flowing east to the Indian Ocean at Richards Bay. Around 1819 Shaka's Zulu army decisively defeated the Ndwandwe of Zwide on its banks, a victory that broke Ndwandwe power and made the Zulu the dominant state in the region.

mkuze-river.s: The Mkuze is a river in northern KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, flowing east through a gorge in the Lebombo Mountains to the Lake St Lucia system on the Indian Ocean coast. In the late 18th and early 19th centuries its valley, with that of the Pongola, was the heartland of the…

mabhoko.s: Mabhoko, known to the Boers as Mapoch, was king of the Ndzundza Ndebele in present-day Mpumalanga, South Africa, in the mid-19th century until his death in 1865. He rebuilt the kingdom after its defeat by Mzilikazi and made his fortress at KwaMaza, with its caves, a refuge…

mampuru-ii.s: Mampuru II was a claimant to the throne of the Pedi kingdom in present-day Limpopo, South Africa, and the rival of his half-brother Sekhukhune I. In 1882 he had Sekhukhune killed and took refuge with the Ndzundza Ndebele under Nyabela, whom the South African Republic then…

mascouten.s: The Mascouten were an Algonquian-speaking people of the western Great Lakes region, known to the French as the 'Fire Nation'. In the 17th century they were at war with the Neutral and other Iroquoian peoples and later lived in present-day Wisconsin.

matignon-accords-1988.s: The Matignon Accords were signed in June 1988 at the Hôtel Matignon in Paris by the French government of Michel Rocard, the Kanak independence leader Jean-Marie Tjibaou and the loyalist leader Jacques Lafleur. Ending years of violent conflict in New Caledonia, they divided the…

milford-connecticut.s: Milford is a city on Long Island Sound in New Haven County, Connecticut, United States, at the mouth of the Wepawaug River. It was founded in 1639 by English Puritans led by Peter Prudden and joined the New Haven Colony in 1643.

magdalena-river.s: The Magdalena is the principal river of Colombia, flowing about 1,500 km north between the Central and Eastern Cordilleras to the Caribbean near Barranquilla. Spanish expeditions, including that of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada in 1536, used it to reach the Andean interior and…

muzo.s: Muzo is a town in the department of Boyacá, Colombia, in the western foothills of the Eastern Cordillera. The mines around it, worked before the Spanish conquest by the Muzo people, have long produced some of the world's finest emeralds.

monterrey.s: Monterrey is the capital of the state of Nuevo León in north-eastern Mexico. It was founded by Diego de Montemayor in 1596, after earlier settlements in the area had failed, and remained a small frontier town of the New Kingdom of León for most of the colonial era.

manhattan.s: Manhattan is an island at the mouth of the Hudson River and the central borough of New York City. Inhabited by the Lenape, it was bought from them in 1626, by tradition for goods worth 60 guilders, by Peter Minuit of the Dutch West India Company, and became the site of New…

miguel-hidalgo-y-costilla.s: Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla was a Mexican Catholic priest who began the war of independence against Spain. On 16 September 1810, in the town of Dolores, he called on his parishioners to rise, an event known as the Grito de Dolores.

my-tho.s: My Tho is a city in the Mekong delta of southern Vietnam, capital of Tien Giang province, on the northern branch of the Mekong. It was founded in the late 17th century by Ming loyalist refugees from China under Duong Ngan Dich, settled there with the permission of the Nguyen…

murashu-archive.s: The Murashu archive is a collection of about 730 cuneiform tablets of a Babylonian family business, the house of Murashu, found at Nippur in 1893. Dating mostly from about 455 to 403 BCE, under the Persian kings Artaxerxes I and Darius II, the texts record the firm's…

masyaf.s: Masyaf is a town in western Syria, on the eastern slopes of the coastal mountains west of Hama, dominated by a medieval castle. The Nizari Ismailis acquired the castle in 1140–1141, and under Rashid al-Din Sinan it was the headquarters of their Syrian branch, the 'Assassins'…

merkurios.s: Merkurios was a king of Makuria in Nubia around the end of the 7th and the beginning of the 8th century; an inscription implies that his reign began in 697. His rule is linked with the union of Nobadia and Makuria and with the Nubian church's adherence to the Coptic…

marasimha-ii.s: Marasimha II was a king of the Western Ganga dynasty of southern Karnataka, ruling from about 963 to 975 as an ally and feudatory of the Rashtrakuta emperor Krishna III. He fought on the Rashtrakutas' behalf in northern India and crushed the Nolamba dynasty.

mat-salleh.s: Mat Salleh, or Datu Muhammad Salleh, was a chief of Bajau and Suluk descent from the Sugut river region of northern Borneo who led a rebellion against the British North Borneo Company from 1894. His followers burned the company's settlement on Gaya Island in 1897.

murut.s: The Murut are an Indigenous people of the interior of northern Borneo, mainly in south-western Sabah in Malaysia and neighbouring parts of Sarawak, Kalimantan and Brunei. Traditionally hill rice farmers and hunters living in longhouses, they practised headhunting until the…

motsu-ji.s: Mōtsū-ji is a Tendai Buddhist temple at Hiraizumi in Iwate prefecture, northern Japan, founded according to tradition in 850 and rebuilt on a grand scale by Fujiwara no Motohira and Hidehira in the 12th century. Its great halls were later lost to fire, but its Pure Land…

minamoto-no-yoshitsune.s: Minamoto no Yoshitsune was a Japanese general, younger half-brother of Minamoto no Yoritomo, whose victories at Ichi-no-Tani, Yashima and Dan-no-ura in 1184–1185 destroyed the Taira clan in the Genpei War. After falling out with Yoritomo he fled to the Northern Fujiwara at…

mahaparinirvana-sutra.s: The Mahaparinirvana Sutra, or Nirvana Sutra, is a Mahayana Buddhist scripture set during the last days of the Buddha. It teaches that the Buddha is eternal and that all beings possess Buddha-nature and can attain enlightenment.

mbelwa.s: Mbelwa, also called M'mbelwa, was the ruler of the northern Ngoni of Malawi from the 1850s until his death in 1891. A son of Zwangendaba, he led one branch of the Ngoni after his father's death and settled it in the Mzimba highlands, from where his kingdom raided the Tumbuka,…

mzimba-district.s: Mzimba is a district and town in the Northern Region of Malawi, covering highlands west of Lake Malawi; it is the country's largest district. From the 1850s it was the heart of the northern Ngoni kingdom of Mbelwa, whose descendants remain paramount chiefs there.

muse-myanmar.s: Muse is a town in northern Shan State, Myanmar, on the Shweli river opposite the Chinese town of Ruili in Yunnan. Lying on the route of the old Burma Road, it has become Myanmar's main crossing for overland trade with China, and the surrounding area has seen repeated fighting…

magnus-the-good.s: Magnus the Good was king of Norway from 1035 and of Denmark from 1042 to 1047, the son of Olaf II, Norway's patron saint. Nobles who had turned against Danish rule brought him back as a boy from exile in Kievan Rus'.

marfa-boretskaya.s: Marfa Boretskaya was a wealthy Novgorod noblewoman, widow of the posadnik Isaak Boretsky, who led the party opposed to Moscow. In 1470–1471 her faction sought an alliance with Casimir IV of Poland-Lithuania to preserve Novgorod's independence.

medracen.s: The Medracen is a royal mausoleum of the Numidian kings near Batna in north-eastern Algeria. A large stepped circular tumulus ringed by engaged Doric columns, it probably dates from the 3rd century BCE.

micipsa.s: Micipsa was king of Numidia from 148 to 118 BCE, the eldest legitimate son of Masinissa. He first shared power with his brothers Gulussa and Mastanabal and, after their deaths, ruled alone from Cirta, keeping the kingdom a loyal ally of Rome and encouraging Greek and Punic…

mong-cai.s: Móng Cái is a city in Quảng Ninh province in north-eastern Vietnam, on the border with Dongxing in China's Guangxi region. A long-standing frontier market town, it was the centre of the Hải Ninh area, whose largely Nùng and Chinese-speaking population formed the French-backed…

malawi-congress-party.s: The Malawi Congress Party is a political party founded in 1959 as the successor to the banned Nyasaland African Congress. Under Hastings Kamuzu Banda it won the 1961 elections, led Nyasaland to independence as Malawi in 1964 and ruled as the sole legal party from 1966 until…

mount-hiei.s: Mount Hiei is a mountain of 848 metres on the border of Kyoto and Shiga prefectures in Japan, overlooking Kyoto and Lake Biwa. From the late 8th century it was the seat of the great Tendai monastery of Enryaku-ji, regarded as the guardian of the capital against evil from the…

mount-fuji.s: Mount Fuji is an active stratovolcano on Honshu and, at 3,776 metres, the highest mountain in Japan. Long revered as sacred and depicted by artists such as Hokusai, it last erupted in the Hōei eruption of 1707, which buried surrounding farmland, including much of the Odawara…

masud-beg.s: Mas'ud Beg was a Khwarazmian Muslim administrator in the Mongol Empire and the son of Mahmud Yalavach. From the 1240s he governed the settled lands of Transoxiana and Turkestan on behalf of the Great Khan and later of the Central Asian khans, keeping the cities' revenues…

merbok-river.s: The Merbok River is a river in Kedah, north-western Malaysia, flowing west into the Strait of Malacca south of Gunung Jerai. From about the 4th century its estuary was a landfall for ships crossing the Bay of Bengal, and the ports and shrines of Old Kedah grew up along its banks.

meidum.s: Meidum is an archaeological site in Egypt on the desert edge west of the Nile, about 100 km south of Cairo. Its pyramid, completed under Sneferu in the 26th century BCE, was converted from a step pyramid into a true pyramid and later lost much of its outer casing.

menkaure.s: Menkaure was a king of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty in the 26th century BCE, probably a son of Khafre. He built the third and smallest of the main pyramids at Giza.

martinus-theunis-steyn.s: Martinus Theunis Steyn was a lawyer and the last president of the Orange Free State, serving from 1896 to 1902. He allied the republic with the South African Republic and led it into the Second Boer War in 1899, staying in the field with the commandos after the British…

messenians.s: The Messenians were the people of Messenia in the south-western Peloponnese. Conquered by Sparta in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, most were reduced to helots and rebelled repeatedly, while refugees settled at Naupactus and at Zancle in Sicily, renamed Messana.

meseta-central.s: The Meseta Central is the high inland plateau that covers much of central Spain, at an average altitude of about 600 to 700 metres. Divided by the mountains of the Central System into a northern and a southern half, it is drained by the Duero, Tagus and Guadiana rivers.

missolonghi.s: Missolonghi, or Mesolongi, is a town on a lagoon at the mouth of the Gulf of Patras in western Greece. During the Greek War of Independence it was the centre of the revolution in western Greece and withstood several sieges, until its defenders broke out in April 1826 and the…

muradid-dynasty.s: The Muradid dynasty ruled Tunisia as hereditary beys under Ottoman suzerainty from 1613 to 1702. Founded by Murad Bey, a Corsican-born mamluk, it grew stronger under Hammuda Pasha Bey and eclipsed the deys of Tunis.

mandelieu-la-napoule.s: Mandelieu-la-Napoule is a town on the French Riviera in the Alpes-Maritimes department, just west of Cannes at the mouth of the Siagne. Its harbour of La Napoule is guarded by a medieval castle restored in the early 20th century by the American artist Henry Clews.

mount-lykaion.s: Mount Lykaion is a mountain in south-western Arcadia in the Peloponnese, rising to about 1,400 metres. Its summit held an ash altar of Zeus Lykaios, the site of ancient sacrifices and athletic games, and local legend made it the birthplace of Zeus.

machanidas.s: Machanidas was ruler of Sparta from about 211 BCE, governing in the name of the boy king Pelops. Allied with the Aetolians and Rome during the First Macedonian War, he attacked the Achaean League and its Macedonian allies.

margus-of-keryneia.s: Margus of Keryneia was the first sole general (strategos) of the Achaean League, elected in 255 BCE when the league replaced its two joint generals with one. He had helped the people of Bura overthrow their tyrant and was a leading statesman alongside Aratus.

maximinus-thrax.s: Maximinus Thrax was Roman emperor from 235 to 238, a soldier of humble Thracian origin proclaimed by the army after the murder of Severus Alexander. His heavy taxation to pay for wars on the Rhine and Danube provoked the revolt of the Gordians in Africa and the hostility of…

manas-river.s: The Manas is a transboundary river of the eastern Himalayan foothills that flows from Bhutan south into Assam, India, where it joins the Brahmaputra. After 1682 it marked the western frontier of the Ahom kingdom against the Mughal Empire.

mir-jumla-ii.s: Mir Jumla II was a Persian-born merchant, general and statesman who served the Golconda Sultanate and then the Mughal Empire. Made governor of Bengal by Aurangzeb, he invaded Cooch Behar and the Ahom kingdom in 1661–1663, occupied the Ahom capital Garhgaon and imposed the…

mayamara-satra.s: The Mayamara Satra, often called the Moamaria satra, is a Vaishnavite monastery of Assam founded by Aniruddhadeva in the early seventeenth century. Its followers, many of them Morans, Kacharis and lower-caste peasants, were persecuted by Ahom kings who favoured Shaktism, and…

momai-tamuli-borbarua.s: Momai Tamuli Borbarua was a senior official of the Ahom kingdom of Assam in the reign of Pratap Singha (1603–1641) and the first holder of the office of Borbarua. He reorganised the paik system of compulsory labour into khels, professional guilds that supplied the state with…

magnus-decentius.s: Magnus Decentius was a relative, probably the brother, of the Roman usurper Magnentius, who made him Caesar in 350 and gave him command in Gaul. During the civil war with Constantius II, Alemannic forces under King Chnodomar defeated him, and the Alemanni overran much of the…

macrianus-alemannic-king.s: Macrianus was a king of the Alemannic Bucinobantes, who lived opposite Mainz, in the later fourth century. The emperor Valentinian I tried to seize him in 372 and to replace him with Fraomarius, but failed, and in 374 met him on the Rhine near Mainz to make peace.

mallobaudes.s: Mallobaudes was a Frankish king and a senior officer in the Roman army in the fourth century. As commander of the imperial guard under Gratian he shared command with Nannienus at the Battle of Argentovaria in 378, where the Alemannic Lentienses were destroyed.

madriu-perafita-claror-valley.s: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley is a glacial valley in south-eastern Andorra, covering almost a tenth of the country's territory. Inscribed in 2004 as Andorra's only UNESCO World Heritage Site, it preserves a cultural landscape of summer pastures, stone shepherds' huts,…

marcelo-t-de-alvear.s: Marcelo T. de Alvear was an Argentine politician of the Radical Civic Union who served as president from 1922 to 1928, between the two terms of Hipólito Yrigoyen. His presidency fell in a period of prosperity and orderly constitutional government, and he later led the wing of…

mauricio-macri.s: Mauricio Macri is an Argentine businessman and centre-right politician, president of the Boca Juniors football club and head of government of the city of Buenos Aires from 2007 to 2015. As president of Argentina from 2015 to 2019 he lifted currency controls and settled with…

mercosur.s: Mercosur, the Southern Common Market, is a South American trade bloc founded by Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay through the Treaty of Asunción in 1991. It created a customs union with a common external tariff and became the region's largest trading arrangement, with…

miguel-juarez-celman.s: Miguel Juárez Celman was an Argentine politician of the National Autonomist Party and president from 1886 to 1890. His government encouraged heavy foreign borrowing and speculation, which ended in the financial crisis of 1890.

mothers-of-the-plaza-de-mayo.n: Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
mothers-of-the-plaza-de-mayo.s: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo are an Argentine association of mothers of people who disappeared under the military dictatorship. From April 1977 they marched every Thursday in the Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires, wearing white headscarves, to demand news of their children,…

micion.s: Micion of Kephisia was an Athenian statesman who, with his brother Eurycleides, directed the city's affairs in the later third century BCE. In 229 BCE they secured the withdrawal of the Macedonian garrisons from Piraeus and Attica by paying their commander Diogenes, and they…

miltiades.s: Miltiades was an Athenian general who ruled the Thracian Chersonese before fleeing to Athens from the Persians in 493 BCE. As one of the ten generals he persuaded the Athenians to fight and led them to victory at Marathon in 490 BCE.

munychia.s: Munychia is a steep hill in Piraeus, the port of Athens, with a harbour of the same name below it. Its fortified summit commanded the harbours: in 403 BCE Thrasybulus defeated the Thirty Tyrants there, and from 322 BCE a Macedonian garrison on Munychia held Athens under…

mahatthai.s: The Mahatthai was one of the two great ministries of the Siamese state from the Ayutthaya period, headed by the Samuha Nayok and responsible for civil affairs and later the administration of the northern provinces. Traditionally attributed to the reforms of King…

maha-thammarachathirat.s: Maha Thammarachathirat was king of Ayutthaya from 1569 to 1590. Formerly governor of Phitsanulok, he sided with Bayinnaung of Burma, who installed him as a vassal king after taking Ayutthaya in 1569.

mingyi-swa.s: Mingyi Swa was crown prince of Toungoo Burma, son of King Nanda Bayin. He led the Burmese invasion of Ayutthaya in 1592–1593 and was killed at the Battle of Nong Sarai, according to the chronicles in an elephant duel with King Naresuan.

marananta.s: Marananta was a Buddhist monk, said to have come from Central Asia or India, who brought Buddhism to Baekje from the Eastern Jin dynasty of China. According to the Samguk sagi he arrived in 384 and was received by King Chimnyu, who soon built a temple for him.

mireuksa.s: Mireuksa was a Buddhist temple at Iksan, South Korea, built under King Mu of Baekje in the early seventh century and among the largest temple complexes of its time in East Asia. Its stone pagoda, the oldest and largest surviving in Korea, was restored between 2001 and 2019.

mongchon-toseong.s: Mongchon Toseong is an earthen-walled fortification in the Songpa district of south-eastern Seoul, dating from the early Baekje period, around the third century CE. Its walls, more than two kilometres long, enclosed a large settlement, and it is thought to have formed part of…

mahmud-shah-bahmani.s: Mahmud Shah was sultan of the Bahmani Sultanate from 1482 to 1518, coming to the throne as a boy after the death of Muhammad Shah III. Real power passed to the nobles, above all Qasim Barid at Bidar, while the provincial governors of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Berar and Golconda…

muhammad-shah-iii-bahmani.s: Muhammad Shah III was sultan of the Bahmani Sultanate from 1463 to 1482, succeeding his brother Nizam Shah as a boy. With Mahmud Gawan as chief minister the kingdom reached its greatest extent, taking Goa and pressing to the eastern coast.

musunuri-nayakas.s: The Musunuri Nayakas were Telugu chiefs who led the revolt that drove the Delhi Sultanate out of the Kakatiya lands of Andhra and Telangana in the 1330s. Under Prolaya Nayaka and his cousin Kapaya Nayaka they ruled from Warangal, but wars with the Bahmani Sultanate cost them…

margaret-of-anjou.s: Margaret of Anjou was queen of England as the wife of Henry VI from 1445. As her husband's mental illness left him unable to rule, she became the driving force of the Lancastrian cause in the Wars of the Roses, raising armies against the House of York.

mun-of-balhae.s: Mun, personal name Dae Heummu, was the third king of Balhae, reigning from 737 to 793. He made peace with Tang China, adopted Tang institutions and learning, and moved the capital first to the Central Capital and around 756 to Sanggyeong, laid out on the plan of Chang'an.

mu-of-balhae.s: Mu, personal name Dae Muye, was the second king of Balhae, reigning from 719 to 737, and son of its founder Dae Joyeong. He expanded the kingdom over Mohe tribes in Manchuria and northern Korea and used his own reign title.

mount-paektu.s: Mount Paektu is a volcanic mountain on the border between North Korea and China, at 2,744 metres the highest peak in the Korean peninsula, with the crater lake Heaven Lake at its summit. Revered in Korean and Manchu tradition as a sacred ancestral mountain, it erupted…

mudan-river.s: The Mudan River is a river of north-east China, about 700 kilometres long, rising in Jilin province and flowing north through Heilongjiang to join the Songhua. Its valley was the heartland of Balhae, whose Upper Capital Sanggyeong stood near modern Ning'an, and it later lay in…

mwanawina-iii.s: Mwanawina III was Litunga, king of the Lozi of Barotseland, from 1948 until his death in 1968, and a son of Lewanika. As Northern Rhodesia moved towards independence he sought to keep Barotseland's special status, and on 18 May 1964 he signed the Barotseland Agreement with…

mambari.s: The Mambari were traders from the Ovimbundu kingdoms of the central highlands of Angola, and people of mixed Portuguese and African descent, who travelled inland to the upper Zambezi in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They exchanged cloth, beads and guns for ivory,…

max-gluckman.s: Max Gluckman was a South African-born British social anthropologist, director of the Rhodes-Livingstone Institute in Northern Rhodesia and founder of the Manchester School of anthropology. His study The Judicial Process among the Barotse of Northern Rhodesia (1955) showed that…

mbunda-people.s: The Mbunda are a Bantu people of south-eastern Angola and western Zambia. Groups of them migrated east into Barotseland from the late eighteenth century, during the reign of Litunga Mulambwa, who welcomed them; they were valued as warriors and diviners and helped the Lozi…

mulena-mukwae.s: The Mulena Mukwae is the title of the royal princess who rules the southern part of Barotseland from Nalolo, under the Litunga, the Lozi king, who rules from the north. Chosen from the royal family, she has her own court, council and Kuomboka ceremony, and her role reflects…

ma-huan.s: Ma Huan was a Chinese Muslim interpreter and traveller who accompanied three of the Ming treasure voyages of Zheng He in the early fifteenth century. His book Yingya Shenglan, "The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores", completed around 1451, describes the countries visited,…

maladhar-basu.s: Maladhar Basu was a Bengali poet from Kulingram in Burdwan who composed the Sri Krishna Vijaya, a Bengali version of parts of the Bhagavata Purana telling the life of Krishna, between 1473 and 1480. He wrote under the patronage of Sultan Rukunuddin Barbak Shah, who gave him…

malik-i-maidan.s: The Malik-i-Maidan, 'monarch of the plains', is a huge bronze cannon on a bastion of the walls of Bijapur. It was cast in 1549 at Ahmadnagar by Muhammad bin Hasan Rumi and later brought to Bijapur, where it became the most famous gun of the Adil Shahi fortifications.

mallu-adil-shah.s: Mallu Adil Shah was the third sultan of Bijapur, succeeding his father Ismail Adil Shah in 1534. His brief reign ended within months when he was deposed and blinded by nobles who placed his brother Ibrahim Adil Shah I on the throne.

mount-helicon.s: Mount Helicon is a mountain in Boeotia, central Greece, rising to about 1,750 metres between Lake Copais and the Gulf of Corinth. In Greek myth it was sacred to the Muses, whose sanctuary in the Valley of the Muses held festival contests, and the spring Hippocrene was said to…

machares.s: Machares was a son of Mithridates VI of Pontus who governed the Bosporan Kingdom as his father's viceroy. During the Third Mithridatic War he made peace with the Roman general Lucullus in 70 BCE and sent him supplies.

mount-mithridates.s: Mount Mithridates is a hill in the centre of Kerch in eastern Crimea, the acropolis of the ancient Greek city of Panticapaeum, capital of the Bosporan Kingdom. Excavations on its slopes have uncovered temples, public buildings and houses from the sixth century BCE onwards.

machado-de-assis.s: Machado de Assis was a Brazilian novelist, short-story writer and poet, widely regarded as the greatest writer in Brazilian literature. Born in Rio de Janeiro to a poor family of mixed descent, he rose to fame with ironic and psychologically subtle novels such as The…

meerut.s: Meerut is a city in western Uttar Pradesh, India, about 70 kilometres north-east of Delhi. On 10 May 1857 Indian sepoys of the Bengal Army mutinied in its cantonment after the punishment of soldiers who had refused the new greased cartridges, killed British officers and…

montagu-declaration.s: The Montagu Declaration was a statement made in the British House of Commons on 20 August 1917 by Edwin Montagu, Secretary of State for India. It announced that British policy was the gradual development of self-governing institutions with a view to the progressive realisation…

muhyiddin-of-brunei.s: Muhyiddin was the fourteenth sultan of Brunei, reigning from 1673 to 1690. Raised to the throne in opposition to the usurper Abdul Hakkul Mubin, he won the Brunei civil war of 1660–1673 with help from the Sultanate of Sulu.

melayu-islam-beraja.s: Melayu Islam Beraja, or Malay Islamic Monarchy, is the national ideology of Brunei, proclaimed at independence in 1984. It presents the state as a Malay nation guided by Islamic values under the rule of the sultan, combining Malay language and culture, Islam of the Shafi'i…

majd-al-dawla.s: Majd al-Dawla was the Buyid ruler of Ray from 997 to 1029, succeeding his father Fakhr al-Dawla as a child. For many years real power was held by his mother, Sayyida Shirin, who kept the Ghaznavids at bay.

marvdasht.s: Marvdasht is a city and plain in Fars province, south-western Iran, north of Shiraz. The fertile plain, watered by the Kur and Pulvar rivers, contains the ruins of Persepolis, Naqsh-e Rustam and Istakhr, centres of Achaemenid and Sasanian power.

muayyad-al-dawla.s: Mu'ayyad al-Dawla was a Buyid ruler, a son of Rukn al-Dawla, who governed Isfahan from 976 as a loyal ally of his brother Adud al-Dawla. In 980 he drove out his other brother Fakhr al-Dawla and took Hamadan and Ray, and he then expelled the Ziyarid ruler Qabus, who had…

maurice-dunand.s: Maurice Dunand was a French archaeologist who directed the excavations at Byblos in Lebanon for about half a century from 1925. Working layer by layer across the site, he uncovered remains from the Neolithic to the Crusader period, including the Temple of the Obelisks, which…

middle-kingdom-of-egypt.s: The Middle Kingdom of Egypt was the period of reunified rule that followed the First Intermediate Period, beginning when Mentuhotep II of the Eleventh Dynasty reunited the country. Under the Twelfth Dynasty, with kings such as Senusret III and Amenemhat III, Egypt conquered…

manuel-chrysoloras.s: Manuel Chrysoloras was a Byzantine scholar and diplomat who taught Greek in Florence from 1397, the first sustained teaching of the language in Italy for centuries. His pupils included Leonardo Bruni and Guarino da Verona, and his grammar, the Erotemata, was widely used.

maslama-al-majriti.s: Maslama al-Majriti was an astronomer and mathematician of al-Andalus, born in Madrid and active in Córdoba. He revised the astronomical tables of al-Khwarizmi for the meridian of Córdoba and wrote on the astrolabe, and he founded a school of astronomers and mathematicians.

muhammad-ii-of-cordoba.s: Muhammad II al-Mahdi was an Umayyad caliph of Córdoba who seized power in a revolt in February 1009, deposing Hisham II and overthrowing the Amirid regime of Sanchuelo. His rule set off the Fitna of al-Andalus: ousted by Sulayman with Berber support later that year, he…

madinat-al-zahira.s: Madinat al-Zahira was the palace and administrative city built by Almanzor from about 979 near Córdoba, to which he moved the offices of government, leaving the caliph Hisham II isolated in his palace. It was the seat of the Amirid regime until 1009, when it was sacked and…

margaret-atwood.s: Margaret Atwood is a Canadian novelist, poet and critic. Her novels include The Edible Woman, Cat's Eye, The Handmaid's Tale, a dystopia published in 1985, and The Blind Assassin, which won the Booker Prize in 2000; she won it again in 2019 for The Testaments.

mark-carney.s: Mark Carney is a Canadian economist and politician who was governor of the Bank of Canada from 2008 to 2013 and of the Bank of England from 2013 to 2020. Elected leader of the Liberal Party, he became prime minister of Canada in March 2025 and won the federal election of April…

marshall-mcluhan.s: Marshall McLuhan was a Canadian literary scholar and theorist of communication at the University of Toronto. In The Gutenberg Galaxy and Understanding Media he argued that the forms of media shape societies more than their content, coining the phrases 'the medium is the…

makhanda-prophet.s: Makhanda, also called Nxele, was a Xhosa prophet and war leader. In the Fifth Frontier War he led an assault by some 10,000 Xhosa on the British garrison at Grahamstown on 22 April 1819, which was repulsed.

mihranid-dynasty.s: The Mihranid dynasty was a princely family of Persian origin that ruled Caucasian Albania from the early seventh century until the early ninth. Claiming descent from the Sasanian noble house of Mihran, its princes, above all Javanshir, balanced between Persia, Byzantium, the…

mount-sinai.s: Mount Sinai is a mountain of about 2,285 metres in the south of the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, traditionally identified as the biblical mountain where Moses received the Law. Saint Catherine's Monastery, founded under Justinian I, stands at its foot, and the mountain has drawn…

moncayo-massif.s: The Moncayo Massif is a mountain range on the border of Aragon and Castile and León in Spain, whose highest summit, at 2,314 metres, is the highest point of the Iberian System. In antiquity iron ores mined on its slopes supplied the Celtiberian smiths of Turiaso and Bilbilis,…

mauryas-of-konkan.s: The Mauryas of Konkan were a dynasty that ruled the Konkan coast of western India in the sixth and seventh centuries, claiming descent from the Maurya emperors. Their island capital, Puri, has been identified with Elephanta or a nearby site.

mahakuta-group-of-temples.s: The Mahakuta group of temples is a complex of Shaiva temples near Badami in northern Karnataka, India, built by the Chalukyas of Badami in the sixth and seventh centuries around a sacred spring-fed tank. Its principal shrine is the Mahakuteshwara temple.

malaprabha-river.s: The Malaprabha is a river of northern Karnataka, India, a tributary of the Krishna. It rises in the Western Ghats in Belagavi district and flows east for about 300 kilometres to join the Krishna near Kudalasangama.

metrodorus-of-chios.s: Metrodorus of Chios was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BCE in the atomist tradition of Democritus. He was known for a radical scepticism, declaring that none of us knows anything, not even whether we know or not.

maria-temryukovna.s: Maria Temryukovna was a Kabardian princess, the daughter of Prince Temryuk of Kabarda, who was baptised and married Ivan IV of Russia in 1561 as his second wife. The marriage sealed Kabarda's alliance with Muscovy and brought Kabardian princely families into the Russian nobility.

marion-mahony-griffin.s: Marion Mahony Griffin was an American architect and artist, among the first women licensed as architects in the United States and an early member of Frank Lloyd Wright's studio. Her striking drawings presented the plan for Canberra with which her husband and partner Walter…

matadi-kinshasa-railway.s: The Matadi–Kinshasa Railway, built from 1890 to 1898 as the Matadi–Léopoldville railway, links the seaport of Matadi to Kinshasa, bypassing the rapids of the lower Congo River. Its construction through difficult country cost the lives of many African and Asian labourers.

mark-twain.s: Mark Twain, the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, was an American writer and humorist, author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. A critic of imperialism in his later years, he served as a vice-president of the American Anti-Imperialist…

matadi.s: Matadi is the chief seaport of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and capital of Kongo Central province, on the Congo River about 150 kilometres from the Atlantic, below the rapids that block navigation upstream. Founded in 1879 in the time of Henry Morton Stanley, it became…

matins-of-bruges.s: The Matins of Bruges was the uprising in Bruges before dawn on 18 May 1302 in which Flemish townsmen led by Pieter de Coninck and Jan Breydel massacred the French garrison installed by Philip IV of France. It began the Flemish revolt that led to the defeat of the French…

maubeuge.s: Maubeuge is a town on the Sambre in the Nord department of northern France, formerly part of the County of Hainaut. It grew around a seventh-century convent founded by Saint Aldegund and became a cloth town.

midi-france.s: The Midi is the common French name for the south of France, the regions bordering the Mediterranean and the Pyrenees, including Languedoc, Provence, Roussillon and Gascony. Historically the land of the langue d'oc, it kept a strong tradition of written Roman law and an Occitan…

montsegur.s: Montségur is a castle on a rocky peak in the Ariège department of southern France, in the foothills of the Pyrenees. Rebuilt around 1204 as a Cathar refuge, it became their main stronghold during the Albigensian Crusade.

mehmed-iv-giray.s: Mehmed IV Giray was khan of Crimea in 1641–1644 and again in 1654–1666. He supported Poland-Lithuania against Muscovy in the Russo-Polish War, and in 1659 his cavalry helped Hetman Ivan Vyhovsky defeat a Muscovite army at Konotop.

murad-giray.s: Murad Giray was khan of Crimea from 1678 to 1683. He fought for the Ottomans against Muscovy and Cossack Ukraine and led Crimean cavalry in the Ottoman campaign against Vienna in 1683.

muravsky-trail.s: The Muravsky Trail was the main route used by Crimean Tatar raiders from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century to strike north into Muscovy. Running along the watershed between the Dnieper and Don basins from the Perekop isthmus towards Tula, it avoided major river crossings.

mudejar.s: Mudéjars were Muslims who remained under Christian rule in the Iberian kingdoms as the Reconquista advanced, from the 11th to the early 16th century. Protected by terms of surrender, they kept their religion and law in return for tribute and formed much of the rural population…

mesta.s: The Mesta was the association of sheep owners of Castile, chartered by Alfonso X in 1273. It organised the seasonal migration of merino flocks between summer pastures in the north and winter grazing in the south and held wide privileges over grazing rights.

medina-del-campo.s: Medina del Campo is a town in the province of Valladolid in central Spain. Its great fairs, flourishing in the 15th and 16th centuries, made it a centre of the wool trade and of European credit and exchange.

milan-kundera.s: Milan Kundera was a Czech-born novelist whose first novel, The Joke of 1967, satirised life under communism. After the Prague Spring his books were banned, and he emigrated to France in 1975, later writing in French.

milan-rastislav-stefanik.s: Milan Rastislav Štefánik was a Slovak astronomer who became a French air force officer and general in the First World War. With Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and Edvard Beneš he led the Czechoslovak National Council and helped organise the Czechoslovak Legions.

martin-slovakia.s: Martin is a town in northern Slovakia, known until 1950 as Turčiansky Svätý Martin. A centre of the Slovak national movement, it was the seat of the cultural society Matica slovenská, founded in 1863.

maeatae.s: The Maeatae were a confederation of peoples in Scotland near the Antonine Wall, recorded by Cassius Dio around 200 CE, when they and the Caledonians fought the Romans and provoked the campaigns of Septimius Severus. Their name may survive in Dumyat hill near Stirling, and the…

moine-mhor.s: Mòine Mhòr, Gaelic for 'great moss', is a raised bog in Kilmartin Glen in Argyll, one of the largest remaining in Britain and a national nature reserve. The rocky hill of Dunadd, the chief fortress of the kings of Dál Riata, rises from the bog beside the River Add.

manius-acilius-glabrio.s: Manius Acilius Glabrio was a Roman politician and general, consul in 191 BCE. In that year he defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III at Thermopylae, driving him from Greece, and then campaigned against his Aetolian allies.

marcabru.s: Marcabru was a Gascon troubadour active from about 1130 to 1150 at the courts of William X of Aquitaine and Alfonso VII of León and Castile. More than forty of his poems survive, many of them sharp moral satires attacking false love and the vices of the nobility.

minnesanger.s: The Minnesänger were the German lyric poets of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries who composed Minnesang, songs of courtly love modelled partly on the troubadours and trouvères. Leading figures included Heinrich von Morungen, Reinmar, Walther von der Vogelweide and Wolfram…

monpazier.s: Monpazier is a small town in the Dordogne department of south-western France, founded as a bastide in 1284 by Edward I of England as duke of Aquitaine. Its regular grid of streets around an arcaded central square survives almost intact, and it is often cited as the…

marsilius-of-padua.s: Marsilius of Padua was an Italian political thinker whose treatise Defensor pacis (1324) argued that political authority comes from the people and that the Church should hold no coercive power. Condemned by Pope John XXII, he fled to the court of Louis IV of Bavaria,…

march-of-verona.s: The March of Verona was a frontier territory in north-eastern Italy, created by Otto I in 952 from lands around Verona, Aquileia and Friuli and given to his brother Henry I, Duke of Bavaria. It controlled the Alpine routes into Italy along the Adige.

marie-de-france.s: Marie de France was a poet of the later twelfth century, probably active in England at the court of Henry II, and the earliest known woman poet in French. Her twelve Lais, short verse tales of love and the supernatural, are presented as retellings of Breton lays.

matter-of-britain.s: The Matter of Britain is the body of medieval legend about the early history of Britain, above all King Arthur and his knights, Merlin and the Holy Grail. Built on Welsh and Breton traditions and Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain of about 1136, it was…

michel-colombe.s: Michel Colombe was a French sculptor from Tours, the leading sculptor in France at the beginning of the Renaissance. His best-known work is the tomb of Duke Francis II of Brittany and Marguerite of Foix, made in 1502–1507 for Anne of Brittany and now in Nantes Cathedral.

montereau-fault-yonne.s: Montereau-Fault-Yonne is a town in the Seine-et-Marne department, south-east of Paris, where the Yonne flows into the Seine. On 10 September 1419 Duke John the Fearless of Burgundy was killed there on the bridge during a meeting with the Dauphin Charles, driving Burgundy into…

morvan.s: The Morvan is a wooded upland massif in Burgundy, in central-eastern France, lying across the departments of Nièvre, Yonne, Côte-d'Or and Saône-et-Loire. Made of granite and covered with forests and lakes, it formed a natural western limit of the Duchy of Burgundy.

mary-of-guise.s: Mary of Guise was a daughter of Claude, first duke of Guise, of a cadet branch of the house of Lorraine, and the wife of James V of Scotland. Mother of Mary, Queen of Scots, she governed Scotland as regent from 1554, keeping it allied with France.

matilda-of-flanders.s: Matilda of Flanders was the daughter of Baldwin V, count of Flanders, and the wife of William the Conqueror, whom she married around 1051. She governed Normandy during his absences in England and was crowned queen of England in 1068.

museo-di-capodimonte.s: The Museo di Capodimonte is an art museum in Naples, housed in the Royal Palace of Capodimonte, begun in 1738 by Charles of Bourbon to display the Farnese collection he had inherited from his mother Elisabeth Farnese. Its holdings include paintings by Titian, Raphael,…

margaret-of-parma.s: Margaret of Parma was an illegitimate daughter of Emperor Charles V. Married first to Alessandro de' Medici and then to Ottavio Farnese, duke of Parma, she was governor of the Habsburg Netherlands for her half-brother Philip II from 1559 to 1567.

monitorium-of-parma.s: The Monitorium of Parma was a papal brief issued by Pope Clement XIII on 30 January 1768 declaring null the church reforms of the Duchy of Parma, introduced by the minister Guillaume du Tillot, and threatening their authors with excommunication. Parma responded by expelling…

mont-blanc-department.s: Mont-Blanc was a department of France created in November 1792 after French revolutionary troops occupied the Duchy of Savoy, with Chambéry as its capital. It took its name from the highest mountain of the Alps.

matilda-of-england-duchess-of-saxony.n: Matilda of England, Duchess of Saxony
matilda-of-england-duchess-of-saxony.s: Matilda of England was the eldest daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. In 1168 she married Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, and lived at his court in Brunswick, where she was a patron of literature.

manado.s: Manado is the capital of North Sulawesi province in Indonesia, a port at the northern tip of Sulawesi. The Dutch East India Company built a fort there in the seventeenth century, and the surrounding Minahasa region became largely Christian under Dutch rule.

mare-liberum.s: Mare Liberum ('The Free Sea') is a Latin treatise by Hugo Grotius, published in 1609, arguing that the sea is international territory open to the ships of all nations. Written in defence of the Dutch East India Company's right to trade in the East Indies against the Portuguese…

maarten-tromp.s: Maarten Tromp was a lieutenant-admiral of the Dutch Republic and one of its most successful naval commanders. In 1639 he destroyed a Spanish armada at the Battle of the Downs, ending Spain's attempts to reinforce Flanders by sea.

matanzas.s: Matanzas is a port city on the northern coast of Cuba, east of Havana, founded by the Spanish in 1693. Its bay was the scene of a celebrated Dutch triumph in September 1628, when Piet Heyn of the Dutch West India Company trapped the Spanish treasure fleet there and seized its…

maurice-prince-of-orange.s: Maurice of Nassau, Prince of Orange from 1618, was stadtholder of Holland and Zeeland from 1585 and later of most other provinces of the Dutch Republic. A son of William the Silent, he reformed the army with his cousin William Louis, introducing regular drill, smaller units…

michiel-de-ruyter.s: Michiel de Ruyter was a Dutch admiral, the most celebrated commander of the Dutch navy. During the Second and Third Anglo-Dutch Wars he won the Four Days' Battle in 1666, led the Raid on the Medway in 1667, when the English flagship Royal Charles was towed away, and fought off…

mount-mao.s: Mount Mao (Maoshan) is a mountain in southern Jiangsu, China, south-east of Nanjing, sacred in Daoism. Revelations received in the 360s by the medium Yang Xi became the scriptures of the Shangqing school, and in the late fifth century Tao Hongjing settled on the mountain and…

mount-lu.s: Mount Lu (Lushan) is a mountain range in northern Jiangxi, China, near Jiujiang and Poyang Lake. In the late fourth century the monk Huiyuan founded the Donglin Temple there, making it a major centre of Chinese Buddhism, and poets and painters celebrated its scenery for…

martyrs-of-cordoba.s: The Martyrs of Córdoba were forty-eight Christians executed in Umayyad Córdoba between 850 and 859, most after publicly denouncing Islam or as apostates from it. Recorded chiefly by Eulogius of Córdoba and Paul Alvarus, who supported the movement, the executions divided the…

madrasa-of-granada.s: The Madrasa of Granada (Madrasa Yusufiyya) was founded in 1349 by the Nasrid emir Yusuf I as the city's first public institution of higher learning, teaching law, theology and other sciences. After the Christian conquest the building became the city hall; its restored prayer…

muhammad-iii-of-granada.s: Muhammad III was the third Nasrid emir of Granada, reigning from 1302 to 1309. A patron of building, he constructed the main mosque of the Alhambra.

muhammad-iv-of-granada.s: Muhammad IV was Nasrid emir of Granada from 1325 to 1333, coming to the throne as a boy of ten. With the help of Marinid forces from Morocco he besieged and recaptured Gibraltar from Castile in 1333, but he was murdered shortly afterwards by discontented commanders.

muhammad-ix-of-granada.s: Muhammad IX, called al-Aysar (the Left-handed), was Nasrid emir of Granada four times between 1419 and 1453. Supported by the Abencerraje family, he was repeatedly deposed and restored in civil wars with rival claimants, some backed by Castile, such as Yusuf IV in 1432.

muhammad-vi-of-granada.s: Muhammad VI, known to the Castilians as el Bermejo (the Red), was Nasrid emir of Granada from 1360 to 1362. He seized power by killing Ismail II, whom he had helped to depose Muhammad V.

muhammad-xiii-of-granada.s: Muhammad XIII, known as al-Zaghal (the Valiant), was Nasrid emir of Granada from 1485 to 1487 and held the eastern part of the emirate until 1489. A brother of Abu al-Hasan Ali, he fought both the Castilians and his nephew Boabdil.

manuel-iii-of-trebizond.s: Manuel III was Emperor of Trebizond from 1390 to 1417, the son of Alexios III. Faced with Timur's advance into Anatolia, he accepted Timur's overlordship, and after Timur defeated the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402 Trebizond enjoyed a respite from Ottoman pressure.

michael-panaretos.s: Michael Panaretos was a Greek official and historian of the Empire of Trebizond in the fourteenth century, who served Emperor Alexios III at court and on embassies. His short chronicle, covering the empire from its foundation in 1204 to about 1390, is the only surviving native…

metagenes.s: Metagenes was a Cretan architect of the sixth century BCE, the son of Chersiphron of Knossos, with whom he built the archaic Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. According to Vitruvius he devised a way of moving the temple's heavy architrave blocks by setting them inside large wooden…

manuel-jose-arce.s: Manuel José Arce (1787–1847) was a Salvadoran soldier and politician who became the first president of the Federal Republic of Central America in 1825. Elected after a disputed vote in congress, he drifted towards the Guatemalan conservatives and in 1826 had the liberal…

madara-rider.s: The Madara Rider is a large rock relief carved about 23 metres up a cliff near the village of Madara in north-eastern Bulgaria, probably in the early 8th century. It shows a horseman spearing a lion, with a dog running behind, surrounded by Greek inscriptions recording events…

madara.s: Madara is a village and archaeological site near Shumen in north-eastern Bulgaria. Its cliffs hold the Madara Rider relief and Greek inscriptions of the Bulgar khans, and the area was an important pagan sanctuary and fortified place of the First Bulgarian Empire, close to its…

maria-lekapene.s: Maria Lekapene (died c. 963) was a Byzantine princess, granddaughter of the emperor Romanos I Lekapenos, who married Tsar Peter I of Bulgaria in 927.

merogaisus.s: Merogaisus was a Frankish king who, together with Ascaric, broke the peace with Rome on the lower Rhine around 306. Constantine the Great captured both kings and had them thrown to the beasts in the amphitheatre at Trier, an event praised in a Latin panegyric of 310.

marcomer.s: Marcomer was a Frankish king of the late 4th century who, with Sunno, raided Roman territory across the lower Rhine in 388. The Frankish general Arbogast, serving Rome, campaigned against them across the river in 392.

main-recess.s: The Main Recess (Hauptrezess) of 1712 was a constitutional settlement of Hamburg, reached after years of conflict between the council and citizens and with mediation by an imperial commission. It declared the council and the assembly of propertied citizens jointly sovereign…

manifesto-of-the-algerian-people.s: The Manifesto of the Algerian People was a declaration drawn up by Ferhat Abbas and presented to the French authorities in February 1943, after the Allied landings in North Africa. It condemned colonial rule and called for an Algerian constitution guaranteeing equality, an end…

messali-hadj.s: Messali Hadj (1898–1974) was a founder of Algerian nationalism who led the North African Star, then the Algerian People's Party and the Movement for the Triumph of Democratic Liberties. He was the first major figure to demand full independence for Algeria.

mohammed-dib.s: Mohammed Dib (1920–2003) was an Algerian novelist and poet from Tlemcen, writing in French. His trilogy Algeria, beginning with La Grande Maison (1952), portrayed poverty and growing political awareness among Algerians under colonial rule.

morice-line.s: The Morice Line was a fortified barrier built by France from 1956 along Algeria's border with Tunisia, named after the defence minister André Morice. Made of electrified fences, minefields and radar, backed by mobile troops, it cut the FLN's fighters inside Algeria off from…

michelin.s: Michelin is a French tyre manufacturer founded in 1889 by the brothers André and Édouard Michelin in Clermont-Ferrand. It pioneered detachable pneumatic tyres and published the Michelin guides.

muhammad-abu-likaylik.s: Muhammad Abu Likaylik was a Hamaj military leader in the Funj Sultanate of Sennar. In the late 1740s he conquered Kordofan from the Musabba'at, and in 1762 he deposed Sultan Badi IV, becoming regent.

marinus-of-tyre.s: Marinus of Tyre was a Greek geographer and mapmaker of the Roman period, active around 100 CE. His work is lost but known through Ptolemy, who used and criticised it in his Geography.

manuchihri.s: Manuchihri was a Persian poet from Damghan who served at the court of the Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud I. He is celebrated for his lively descriptions of nature, wine and the seasons, and is credited with developing the musammat, a strophic verse form.

masud-iii-of-ghazni.s: Mas'ud III was a sultan of the Ghaznavid dynasty who reigned from 1099 to 1115, succeeding his father Ibrahim. His reign was a period of relative peace and prosperity, with campaigns into northern India and a stable frontier with the Seljuks, to whom the Ghaznavids were linked…

mawdud-of-ghazni.s: Mawdud was a sultan of the Ghaznavid dynasty and son of Mas'ud I, reigning from 1041 to 1050. After his father's murder he defeated his uncle Muhammad and took the throne, avenging Mas'ud.

minhaj-i-siraj-juzjani.s: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani was a Persian historian born in 1193 who served the Ghurids and then the Delhi Sultanate, where he became chief judge. Around 1260 he completed the Tabaqat-i Nasiri, a general history in Persian dedicated to Sultan Nasir al-Din Mahmud, which is the main…

muhammad-ibn-suri.s: Muhammad ibn Suri was a chieftain of Ghor in central Afghanistan and an ancestor of the Ghurid dynasty. In 1011 Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Ghor and captured him; he died in captivity, and his son was left to rule Ghor as a Ghaznavid vassal.

micheon-of-goguryeo.s: Micheon of Goguryeo was the fifteenth king of Goguryeo, reigning from 300 to 331. In 313 he captured the Chinese commandery of Lelang and soon after took Daifang, ending more than four centuries of Chinese administration in north-western Korea.

munjamyeong-of-goguryeo.s: Munjamyeong of Goguryeo, also known as King Munja, ruled Goguryeo from 491 to 519 as the grandson and successor of King Jangsu. In 494 the last ruler of the kingdom of Buyeo surrendered to him, completing Goguryeo's absorption of the state from which its founder was said to…

maniakh.s: Maniakh was a Sogdian merchant and diplomat in the service of the Turkic Khaganate. In 568 he led the first Türk embassy to the Byzantine emperor Justin II at Constantinople, proposing an alliance against the Sasanian Empire and direct trade in silk that would bypass Persia.

mamai.s: Mamai was an emir and military commander of the Golden Horde who, during the Great Troubles after 1359, ruled its western half through a series of puppet khans. Not being a descendant of Genghis Khan, he could not take the throne himself.

mengu-timur.s: Mengu-Timur was khan of the Golden Horde from 1266 or 1267 until 1280, a grandson of Batu. He struck coins in his own name, marking the Horde's effective independence from the Great Khan, and granted trading privileges to the Genoese at Caffa.

mokjong-of-goryeo.s: Mokjong of Goryeo was king of Goryeo from 997 to 1009. His reign was dominated by his mother, the queen dowager, and her favourite.

munjong-of-goryeo.s: Munjong of Goryeo was king of Goryeo from 1046 to 1083, a thirty-seven-year reign often seen as the height of the dynasty. He refined its institutions, revised the stipend land system in 1076 and fostered Buddhism and Confucian learning.

myocheong.s: Myocheong was a Korean Buddhist monk and geomancer of the Goryeo period. He urged King Injong to move the capital to Pyongyang, to take the title of emperor and to defy the Jurchen Jin dynasty.

main-neckar-railway.s: The Main-Neckar Railway is a railway line in Germany linking Frankfurt, Darmstadt and Heidelberg, with a branch to Mannheim. It was built jointly by the Free City of Frankfurt, the Grand Duchy of Hesse and the Grand Duchy of Baden and opened in 1846.

martynas-mazvydas.s: Martynas Mažvydas was a Lutheran pastor and the author of the first printed book in the Lithuanian language, a catechism published in Königsberg in 1547. Educated at the University of Königsberg, he served as a pastor in Ragainė in Ducal Prussia.

mogilev.s: Mogilev, or Mahilyow, is a city in eastern Belarus on the Dnieper. Part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, it grew into an important trading town and received Magdeburg rights in 1577.

marie-adelaide-grand-duchess-of-luxembou.s: Marie-Adélaïde, Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, reigned from 1912 to 1919, succeeding her father William IV under the succession law he had changed in her favour. Her apparent sympathy for the German occupiers during the First World War and her interventions in politics made her…

macarius-metropolitan-of-moscow.s: Macarius was Metropolitan of Moscow and All Rus' from 1542 to 1563 and a leading adviser of the young Ivan IV, whom he crowned as tsar in the Dormition Cathedral on 16 January 1547. Earlier archbishop of Novgorod, he compiled the Great Menaion Reader, a vast collection of…

moskva-river.s: The Moskva River is a river of western Russia, about 470 kilometres long, which rises on the Smolensk–Moscow Upland and flows east through Moscow to join the Oka at Kolomna. The city of Moscow grew on its banks from a small settlement first mentioned in 1147, and control of…

mahipala-i-pratihara.s: Mahipala I was a Gurjara-Pratihara emperor who ruled from Kannauj from about 913 to about 944. Early in his reign the Rashtrakuta king Indra III sacked Kannauj and forced him to flee, but he recovered the capital and much of his territory.

munger.s: Munger, formerly Monghyr, is a city on the south bank of the Ganges in Bihar, India. In the early medieval period it was an important centre of the Pala Empire, where royal grants were issued from a victory camp, and near it the Pratihara Nagabhata II defeated the Pala king…

maximilian-ii-of-bavaria.s: Maximilian II was King of Bavaria from 1848, when his father Ludwig I abdicated, until his death in 1864. He accepted liberal reforms after the revolution of 1848, and in German affairs he tried to keep Bavaria independent between Austria and Prussia.

miguel-de-cervantes.s: Miguel de Cervantes was a Spanish novelist, playwright and poet, the greatest writer of the Spanish Golden Age. He fought at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, where he lost the use of his left hand, and spent five years as a captive in Algiers.

mulay-hasan.s: Mulay Hasan was a Hafsid sultan of Tunis who came to the throne in 1526. Driven out by Hayreddin Barbarossa in 1534, he was restored the following year by the Emperor Charles V, whose expedition captured Tunis, and ruled as a Spanish vassal with a Spanish garrison at La Goulette.

muqaddimah.s: The Muqaddimah is the introduction to the universal history of Ibn Khaldun, completed in its first form in 1377. In it he set out a theory of history in which dynasties rise through the group solidarity, or asabiyya, of hardy tribal peoples and decline as luxury erodes it,…

madrasa-al-shammaiyya.s: The Madrasa al-Shamma'iyya is a college in the medina of Tunis, founded by the Hafsid ruler Abu Zakariya Yahya I in the mid-13th century near the Zaytuna Mosque. It is generally regarded as the first madrasa in Ifriqiya, and it introduced to the Hafsid lands the endowed…

masal-al-jumh.s: Ma'sal al-Jumh is a site in central Arabia, west of modern Riyadh, where kings of Himyar left rock inscriptions recording military expeditions into the interior. One was made by Abikarib As'ad and his son Hassan Yuha'min in the 5th century, and another by Ma'dikarib Ya'fur in…

madikarib-yafur.s: Ma'dikarib Ya'fur was a Christian king of Himyar in south Arabia, who probably came to power around 519 as a client of Kaleb of Aksum. An inscription of 521 at Ma'sal al-Jumh in central Arabia records his campaign there.

malkikarib-yuhamin.s: Malkikarib Yuha'min was a king of Himyar in south Arabia in the late 4th century. Inscriptions from his reign, from about 380, show that the royal court abandoned the old polytheistic cults in favour of a single god, Rahmanan, the Merciful, Lord of Heaven.

martyrdom-of-arethas.s: The Martyrdom of Arethas is a Greek hagiographical text describing the massacre of the Christians of Najran in 523 under the Himyarite king Yusuf and the Aksumite expedition against him. It centres on Arethas, the elderly leader of the Najran Christians, who was executed with…

muza.s: Muza was an ancient port on the Red Sea coast of south-western Arabia, near modern Mocha in Yemen. The 1st-century Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes it as a busy harbour of Arab shipowners and merchants trading with Africa and India, exporting myrrh and importing cloth,…

merobaudes-poet.s: Flavius Merobaudes was a Latin poet and Roman general of the 5th century. He wrote panegyrics for the general Aetius and was honoured with a statue in the Forum of Trajan in 435.

merobaudes-general.s: Flavius Merobaudes was a Roman general, probably of Frankish origin, who served the emperors Valentinian I and Gratian. In 375 he helped proclaim the child Valentinian II emperor, and he held the consulship in 377 and 383.

madhvacharya.s: Madhvacharya was a Hindu philosopher from near Udupi on the coast of Karnataka who founded the Dvaita, or dualist, school of Vedanta. Against Advaita, he taught that God, identified with Vishnu, is eternally distinct from souls and matter.

madurai-sultanate.s: The Madurai Sultanate was a Muslim kingdom in the southern Tamil country, founded in 1335 when the governor Jalal-ud-din Ahsan Khan rebelled against the Delhi Sultanate. Its sultans killed the Hoysala king Veera Ballala III near Tiruchirappalli in 1343.

melkote.s: Melkote is a hill town in Mandya district, Karnataka, and a major centre of Sri Vaishnavism. The philosopher Ramanuja lived there for about twelve years in the early 12th century, and its Cheluvanarayana Swamy temple and hilltop Yoga Narasimha temple remain important places of…

marquis-de-bussy.s: Charles Joseph Patissier, Marquis de Bussy-Castelnau, was a French commander in India under Joseph François Dupleix. From 1751 he placed and kept Salabat Jung on the throne of Hyderabad with a French force, gaining the Northern Circars for France in 1753.

michel-raymond.s: Michel Raymond was a French soldier of fortune who commanded a large French-trained corps in the service of Nizam Ali Khan of Hyderabad. His force fought at Kharda in 1795.

mahbub-ali-khan.s: Mir Mahbub Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, was the sixth Nizam of Hyderabad, succeeding as an infant in 1869 and ruling until his death in 1911. During his minority the chief minister Salar Jung I continued his reforms.

mubariz-khan.s: Mubariz Khan was a Mughal noble and governor of Hyderabad who was appointed by the court in Delhi to oppose the growing independence of Nizam-ul-Mulk in the Deccan. He was defeated and killed by Nizam-ul-Mulk at the Battle of Shakar Kheda in October 1724, a victory that…

muzaffar-jung.s: Muzaffar Jung was a grandson of Asaf Jah I who claimed the throne of Hyderabad after 1748 with French support. Allied with Chanda Sahib, he won at Ambur in 1749, and after his uncle Nasir Jung's death in December 1750 he became Nizam.

maule-river.s: The Maule is a river of central Chile that flows from the Andes to the Pacific Ocean at Constitución. Tradition holds that it marked the southern limit of the Inca Empire, where Inca expansion stopped in the face of Mapuche resistance in the late 15th century.

miguel-cabello-de-balboa.s: Miguel Cabello de Balboa was a Spanish priest and chronicler who worked in Ecuador and Peru. His Miscelánea antártica, completed in 1586, includes a history of the Inca rulers with dates for their reigns, which modern scholars, notably John Rowe, used to build the standard…

madiun-affair.s: The Madiun Affair was a communist uprising in September 1948 centred on the town of Madiun in East Java, during Indonesia's war of independence against the Netherlands. Leftist troops and supporters of the Communist Party, whose leader Musso had recently returned from the…

muhammadiyah.s: Muhammadiyah is an Indonesian Islamic organisation founded in Yogyakarta in 1912 by Ahmad Dahlan. A modernist movement, it called for a return to the Qur'an and hadith, criticised practices it saw as unorthodox and promoted modern education.

marquis-de-tracy.s: Alexandre de Prouville, Marquis de Tracy, was a French soldier sent by Louis XIV as lieutenant general for France's American colonies. He reached Quebec in 1665 with the Carignan-Salières Regiment, the first large body of regular troops in New France, and built forts along the…

mahmud-shah-ii-of-johor.s: Mahmud Shah II was sultan of Johor from 1685 to 1699 and the last ruler descended from the sultans of Malacca. He came to the throne as a child, and his reign was remembered for its cruelty.

mahmud-shah-iii-of-johor.s: Mahmud Shah III was sultan of Johor and Riau from 1761 to 1812, succeeding as a child. Power at his court lay largely with the Bugis viceroys, whose war with the Dutch led to the Dutch occupation of Riau in 1784.

memory-of-the-world-programme.s: The Memory of the World Programme is an initiative launched by UNESCO in 1992 to protect the world's documentary heritage and make it accessible. Its international register lists manuscripts, archives, books, films and recordings judged to be of world significance, such as the…

muhammad-haidar-dughlat.s: Muhammad Haidar Dughlat was a Central Asian prince, soldier and historian of the Dughlat family and a cousin of the Mughal emperor Babur. His Persian history, the Tarikh-i Rashidi, written in the 1540s, records the Moghul khans of Central Asia and is a main source for the…

mutambuka.s: Mutambuka was Omugabe, or king, of Nkore in the mid-nineteenth century, one of the rulers under whom the kingdom became an expanding power. He raided neighbouring Buhweju, Igara and the successor chiefdoms of Mpororo for cattle and drew them into tributary relations.

martin-of-aragon.s: Martin, called the Humane, was king of Aragon from 1396 to 1410 and also king of Sicily from 1409. The last ruler of the house of Barcelona in the male line, he lost his only legitimate son, Martin the Younger, in 1409 and died the next year without naming an undisputed heir.

majolus-of-cluny.s: Majolus was abbot of Cluny from 954 to 994, under whom the abbey's influence spread across Burgundy, Provence and Italy, and was close to the emperors Otto I and Otto II. In 972 he was captured in the Alps by Muslim raiders from Fraxinetum and held for ransom; the outrage led…

montmajour-abbey.s: Montmajour Abbey is a former Benedictine monastery on a rocky hill, once an island in the marshes, near Arles in Provence, founded in 948. It became a rich and powerful abbey and a pilgrimage centre, with a Romanesque church, cloister and crypt, and a fortified keep added in…

munuza.s: Munuza was a Berber governor of the Muslim conquerors of Iberia, based at Gijón in Asturias in the early eighth century. According to the Asturian chronicles, the Visigothic noble Pelagius rebelled against him, and after the Muslim defeat at Covadonga Munuza fled and was…

munich-secession.s: The Munich Secession was an association of artists founded in 1892 by painters, among them Franz von Stuck, who broke away from the official Munich Artists' Association in protest at its conservative exhibitions. The first of the secessions in the German-speaking world, it…

maastricht-treaty.s: The Maastricht Treaty, formally the Treaty on European Union, was signed in the Dutch city of Maastricht in February 1992 and came into force in November 1993. It created the European Union, introduced European citizenship and set out the path to economic and monetary union…

mala-strana.s: Malá Strana, the Lesser Town, is a historic quarter of Prague on the left bank of the Vltava, below Prague Castle. It was founded as a town by Ottokar II in 1257 and rebuilt after fires and wars, so that its palaces, gardens and churches, notably St Nicholas, are largely Baroque.

mawanda-of-buganda.s: Mawanda was kabaka of Buganda in the early eighteenth century. He extended the kingdom eastwards towards Busoga and strengthened royal control by appointing chiefs who owed their posts to the king rather than to the clans.

mawokota.s: Mawokota is one of the original core counties of the Kingdom of Buganda, south-west of Kampala, today in Mpigi District of Uganda, bordering Lake Victoria. With Busiro and Kyadondo it formed the area where, according to historians, a group of clans first accepted a common…

mengo.s: Mengo is a hill in Kampala, the capital of Uganda, and the site of the Lubiri, the palace of the kabakas of Buganda, from the 1880s. The name came to stand for the government of Buganda itself.

masindi.s: Masindi is a town in western Uganda, north-east of Lake Albert. In the nineteenth century it was a royal centre of Omukama Kabalega of Bunyoro.

murchison-falls.s: Murchison Falls is a waterfall on the Victoria Nile in north-western Uganda, where the river forces its way through a gap only a few metres wide before flowing into Lake Albert. Samuel Baker named it in 1864 after Sir Roderick Murchison, president of the Royal Geographical…

melville-herskovits.s: Melville Herskovits was an American anthropologist who founded the first major African studies programme in the United States at Northwestern University in 1948. His two-volume "Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom" (1938) was based on fieldwork in the 1930s, and his "The…

margrethe-ii.s: Margrethe II was Queen of Denmark from 1972 until her abdication on 14 January 2024 in favour of her son, Frederik X. The constitutional change of 1953 allowed her, as eldest daughter of Frederick IX, to inherit the throne.

montesquieu.s: Montesquieu, Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de La Brède et de Montesquieu, was a French magistrate and political philosopher of the Enlightenment. His Persian Letters of 1721 satirised French society, and The Spirit of the Laws of 1748 compared forms of government and argued…

michel-le-tellier.s: Michel Le Tellier was a French statesman who served as secretary of state for war from 1643 to 1677 and later as chancellor of France. He began the reform of the French army, bringing its officers and supply under royal control, a work continued by his son, the Marquis de…

moliere.s: Molière, the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was a French playwright and actor, regarded as the greatest master of French comedy. Supported by Louis XIV, his company performed at court and in Paris.

monastery-of-the-cross.s: The Monastery of the Cross is an Eastern Orthodox monastery in Jerusalem, built in the eleventh century by the Georgian monk Giorgi-Prokhore on the traditional site where the tree for Christ's cross grew. For centuries it was a centre of Georgian learning in the Holy Land, and…

megali-idea.s: The Megali Idea, or Great Idea, was the aim of Greek nationalism to unite all Greek-inhabited lands in one state, with Constantinople as its capital. Named in a speech by Ioannis Kolettis in 1844, it guided Greek policy for nearly eighty years and led to the gain of Thessaly,…

magnus-barefoot.s: Magnus Barefoot, or Magnus III, was king of Norway from 1093 to 1103. He led expeditions to the Orkneys, the Hebrides and the Isle of Man to assert Norwegian rule, and in 1098 his fleet defeated the Normans off Anglesey, killing Hugh of Montgomery, Earl of Shrewsbury.

meilyr-brydydd.s: Meilyr Brydydd was a Welsh court poet, the earliest of the Poets of the Princes whose work survives. He served Gruffudd ap Cynan, king of Gwynedd, and wrote an elegy on his death in 1137, as well as a deathbed poem asking to be buried on Bardsey Island.

menai-strait.s: The Menai Strait is the narrow tidal channel, about 25 kilometres long, that separates the island of Anglesey from the mainland of north-west Wales. It protected Anglesey, the granary of the kingdom of Gwynedd, and in November 1282 an English force crossing it on a bridge of…

merfyn-frych.s: Merfyn Frych ('the Freckled') was king of Gwynedd from 825 until his death in 844. He came to power after the death of Hywel ap Rhodri Molwynog, and Welsh tradition links his origins with the Isle of Man.

manuel-i-komnenos.s: Manuel I Komnenos was Byzantine emperor from 1143 to 1180. He pursued ambitious policies in Italy, the Crusader states and the Balkans, and his victory over Hungary at Sirmium in 1167 brought Syrmia and Dalmatia under Byzantine control.

mary-of-hungary-queen-of-naples.n: Mary of Hungary, Queen of Naples
mary-of-hungary-queen-of-naples.s: Mary of Hungary was a daughter of Stephen V of Hungary who married Charles II of Naples and became queen of Naples. After the death of her brother Ladislaus IV in 1290 she claimed the Hungarian throne for her family, and the claim passed through her son Charles Martel to her…

martyrdom-of-the-holy-queen-shushanik.n: Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik
martyrdom-of-the-holy-queen-shushanik.s: The Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik is a hagiography written in the late fifth century by the priest Iakob Tsurtaveli, the oldest surviving work of Georgian literature. It tells of Shushanik, an Armenian princess married to Varsken, the pitiakhsh of southern Kartli, who…

mithridates-i-of-iberia.s: Mithridates I was a king of Iberia in the first century CE and a client of Rome. A Greek inscription found at Mtskheta records that in 75 CE the Emperor Vespasian strengthened the fortifications of the city for him, describing the king as a friend of Caesar and of the Romans.

messiah-handel.s: Messiah is an English-language oratorio by George Frideric Handel, with a text compiled from the Bible by Charles Jennens. Composed in 1741, it received its first performance in Dublin on 13 April 1742, at a charity concert in the Music Hall on Fishamble Street.

menahem.s: Menahem was king of Israel from about 752 to 742 BCE. He seized the throne by killing Shallum in Samaria and, according to the Books of Kings, paid the Assyrian king 1,000 talents of silver, raised by a levy of fifty shekels on each wealthy man, to secure his rule.

maria-montessori.s: Maria Montessori was an Italian physician and educator who developed the Montessori method of teaching. She opened her first Casa dei Bambini (Children's House) in a working-class district of Rome in 1907, basing it on children's self-directed activity with specially designed…

monza.s: Monza is a city in Lombardy, northern Italy, just north-east of Milan. It was a residence of the Lombard queen Theodelinda, whose cathedral holds the Iron Crown of Lombardy, and its royal villa was a summer residence of the House of Savoy.

marche.s: The Marche is a region of central Italy between the Apennines and the Adriatic Sea, with its capital at Ancona. Most of it belonged to the Papal States from the Middle Ages until 1860, when Piedmontese troops occupied it on their way south to meet Garibaldi, and a plebiscite…

march-on-rome.s: The March on Rome was the mass mobilisation by which Benito Mussolini's National Fascist Party came to power in Italy in October 1922. While Fascist squads converged on the capital, King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign a decree of martial law and on 29 October invited…

melisende-queen-of-jerusalem.s: Melisende was Queen of Jerusalem from 1131 to 1153, the eldest daughter of Baldwin II. She ruled jointly with her husband Fulk of Anjou and, after his death in 1143, with her son Baldwin III, until he forced her from power in 1153.

melisende-psalter.s: The Melisende Psalter is an illuminated psalter made in the scriptorium of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem around 1131–1143, probably for Queen Melisende. Its miniatures and carved ivory covers combine Byzantine, Western European and Eastern Christian styles, and…

montfort-castle.s: Montfort Castle is a ruined crusader fortress in the hills of western Upper Galilee, in present-day Israel. The Teutonic Knights acquired the site in 1220 and built it as their headquarters, which they called Starkenberg.

manasseh-of-judah.s: Manasseh was king of Judah for about half a century in the 7th century BCE, the son of Hezekiah. He remained a loyal vassal of Assyria and is named among the tributaries of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and his reign saw economic recovery after Sennacherib's invasion.

micah-prophet.s: Micah was a Hebrew prophet from Moresheth in the Shephelah of Judah, active in the late 8th century BCE under the kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. The Book of Micah, one of the twelve minor prophets, condemns the oppression of the poor and foretells the destruction of Samaria…
