mizpah-in-benjamin.s: Mizpah in Benjamin was an ancient town north of Jerusalem, usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh. The Bible describes it as a gathering place of the tribes and a border fortress between Judah and Israel.

makkhali-gosala.s: Makkhali Gosala was an Indian ascetic of the 5th century BCE, the best-known leader of the Ajivika movement. A contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira, he taught in Magadha and neighbouring kingdoms that all events are fixed by fate and that souls pass through a long,…

madra-kingdom.s: The Madras were an ancient people of the Punjab in north-western India, named in Vedic texts, the Mahabharata and Buddhist sources, with their capital at Sakala, modern Sialkot. In the epic, Madri, the wife of Pandu, and her brother Shalya are Madras.

magadhi-prakrit.s: Magadhi Prakrit was the Middle Indo-Aryan vernacular of ancient Magadha in eastern India. It is associated with the speech of the Buddha and Mahavira, appears in the eastern versions of the inscriptions of Ashoka, and is used for some lower-class characters in classical…

magahi.s: Magahi is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by more than 12 million people, mainly in southern Bihar and neighbouring parts of Jharkhand in India. It descends from Magadhi Prakrit, the ancient language of the kingdom of Magadha, and belongs to the Bihari group together with…

mahanandin.s: Mahanandin was, according to the Puranas, the last king of the Shishunaga dynasty of Magadha, reigning in the 4th century BCE. The Puranas say that Mahapadma Nanda, the founder of the Nanda dynasty, was his son by a Shudra woman and overthrew the old dynasty around 345 BCE,…

mysore-dasara.s: Mysore Dasara is the ten-day festival of Navaratri and Vijayadashami celebrated at Mysore in Karnataka, India, and the state festival of Karnataka. The Wodeyar kings continued the royal Mahanavami festival of the Vijayanagara Empire, beginning with Raja Wodeyar in 1610, to…

madurai-nayak-dynasty.s: The Madurai Nayak dynasty ruled much of present-day Tamil Nadu from 1529 to 1736. Its founders were governors for the Vijayanagara Empire who became independent after Vijayanagara's defeat in 1565, ruling from Madurai and later Tiruchirappalli.

madhavrao-i.s: Madhavrao I (1745–1772) was Peshwa of the Maratha Empire from 1761 to 1772. Coming to office soon after the disaster of Panipat, he restored Maratha power in the Deccan and the north, defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad and led repeated campaigns against Hyder Ali of Mysore,…

maria-carolina-of-austria.s: Maria Carolina of Austria (1752–1814) was queen of Naples and Sicily as the wife of Ferdinand IV, whom she married in 1768. A daughter of Maria Theresa and sister of Marie Antoinette, she dominated government, removed the minister Tanucci and, after her sister's execution,…

marie-antoinette.s: Marie Antoinette (1755–1793) was queen of France as the wife of Louis XVI. A daughter of Maria Theresa of Austria, she married the future king in 1770 to seal the Franco-Austrian alliance and became a target of popular hostility for her extravagance and opposition to reform.

monastery-of-irache.s: The Monastery of Irache is a Benedictine abbey near Estella in Navarre, one of the oldest monasteries of the kingdom, documented from the early eleventh century. Lying on the pilgrim road to Santiago, it kept a hospital for pilgrims and held large estates, and its Romanesque…

monastery-of-leyre.s: The Monastery of Leyre (San Salvador de Leyre) is a monastery in eastern Navarre near Yesa, one of the oldest and most important in Spain. In the tenth and eleventh centuries it was closely linked to the kings of Pamplona, who were buried there and endowed it with great estates.

muniadona-of-castile.s: Muniadona of Castile (c. 995–1066), also called Mayor, was the daughter of Count Sancho García of Castile and the wife of Sancho III of Navarre.

magnus-lagabotes-land-law.s: Magnus Lagabøte's Land Law (Landsloven) was the national law code issued for Norway by King Magnus VI in 1274, replacing the separate laws of the regional assemblies. With a town law issued soon after, it was among the earliest law codes in Europe valid for a whole kingdom.

magnus-eriksson.s: Magnus Eriksson (1316–1374) inherited the crown of Norway and was elected king of Sweden in 1319 as a three-year-old, uniting the two kingdoms under one king. His reign saw the Black Death and a national law code for Sweden around 1350.

magnus-erlingsson.s: Magnus Erlingsson (1156–1184) was king of Norway from 1161, a son of the powerful nobleman Erling Skakke and a grandson of King Sigurd the Crusader through his mother. With church support he was crowned in Bergen in 1163 or 1164, the first coronation in Scandinavia.

mithridates-v-of-pontus.s: Mithridates V Euergetes was king of Pontus from about 150 to about 120 BCE. He allied with Rome, sending ships in the Third Punic War and troops against Aristonicus in the war over Pergamon, and was rewarded with Greater Phrygia, which Rome later took back.

men-deity.s: Men was a moon god worshipped widely in Anatolia, especially in Phrygia and Pontus, in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. He was shown as a young man in a Phrygian cap with a crescent moon behind his shoulders.

mithridates-iii-of-pontus.s: Mithridates III was king of Pontus from about 220 to about 185 BCE, son of Mithridates II and the Seleucid princess Laodice. Little is known of his reign, but he continued his family's ties with the Seleucid dynasty.

mitridate-re-di-ponto.s: Mitridate, re di Ponto is an opera seria in three acts by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, written when he was fourteen and first performed in Milan on 26 December 1770. The libretto by Vittorio Amedeo Cigna-Santi is based on Racine's tragedy Mithridate.

mithridate-play.s: Mithridate is a tragedy in five acts by the French playwright Jean Racine, first performed in Paris in January 1673. It portrays the last days of Mithridates VI of Pontus, defeated by Rome, and his rivalry with his sons Xiphares and Pharnace for the love of Monime.

mafra-national-palace.s: Mafra National Palace is a huge baroque palace, basilica and Franciscan friary at Mafra, north-west of Lisbon, built for King John V from 1717 and paid for with Brazilian gold. Designed by João Frederico Ludovice, it is one of the largest palaces in Europe and includes a…

manifestis-probatum.s: Manifestis probatum is the papal bull issued by Pope Alexander III on 23 May 1179 that recognised Afonso I (Afonso Henriques) as king of Portugal and the kingdom as a vassal of the Holy See. Afonso had used the royal title since about 1139 and Alfonso VII of León had accepted…

meifod.s: Meifod is a village in the Vyrnwy valley of Montgomeryshire, mid Wales. Its church, associated with Saint Tysilio, was the mother church of medieval Powys and a burial place of its princes, including Madog ap Maredudd in 1160.

muhanga.s: Muhanga, formerly Gitarama, is a town in the Southern Province of Rwanda, west of Kigali. It was the home base of Grégoire Kayibanda and the Hutu party Parmehutu.

mibambwe-iv-rutarindwa.s: Mibambwe IV Rutarindwa was king of Rwanda from 1895 to 1896, the chosen heir and co-ruler of Kigeli IV Rwabugiri. Soon after his accession the faction of the queen mother Kanjogera turned against him, and in the Coup of Rucunshu in 1896 he was overthrown and died with his…

margaret-maid-of-norway.s: Margaret, Maid of Norway, was the daughter of King Eric II of Norway and the granddaughter of Alexander III of Scotland, and was recognised as Queen of Scots after his death in 1286. The Treaty of Birgham of 1290 arranged her marriage to the future Edward II of England, but…

malcolm-ii-of-scotland.s: Malcolm II was King of Scots from 1005 to 1034. His victory over the Northumbrians at the Battle of Carham around 1018 secured Lothian and the Tweed frontier, and the British kingdom of Strathclyde came under Scottish control during his reign.

margaret-tudor.s: Margaret Tudor was the elder daughter of Henry VII of England and queen of James IV of Scotland, whom she married in 1503 under the Treaty of Perpetual Peace. After James's death at Flodden she was regent for her son James V and remained active in Scottish politics.

melrose-abbey.s: Melrose Abbey is a ruined Cistercian abbey in the Scottish Borders, founded by David I in 1136, the first Cistercian house in Scotland. It grew rich from sheep farming and the wool trade, and the heart of Robert the Bruce is believed to be buried there.

muhammad-al-idrisi.s: Muhammad al-Idrisi was an Arab geographer and cartographer, born probably in Ceuta, who worked at the court of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily in Palermo. In 1154 he completed the Tabula Rogeriana, or Book of Roger, a description of the known world with a world map divided…

maio-of-bari.s: Maio of Bari was the chief minister of William I of Sicily, holding the title emir of emirs from 1154. The son of a judge of Bari, he dominated the royal government and was hated by the barons, who blamed him for the loss of the North African territories to the Almohads.

martin-i-of-sicily.s: Martin I, called Martin the Younger, was King of Sicily from 1390 to 1409, the son of Martin I of Aragon. He restored royal authority over the Sicilian barons, and in 1409 he won the Battle of Sanluri in Sardinia, breaking the power of Arborea, but died of fever at Cagliari…

mark-rutte.s: Mark Rutte is a Dutch politician who led the liberal People's Party for Freedom and Democracy and served as Prime Minister of the Netherlands from 2010 to 2024, the longest tenure in the country's history, heading four coalition governments. His last cabinet fell in 2023 over…

meigle.s: Meigle is a village in Strathmore, Perthshire, Scotland, with one of the most important collections of early medieval carved stones in Europe. More than two dozen Pictish symbol stones, cross-slabs and grave monuments, mostly of the eighth to tenth centuries, were found at its…

mot-god.s: Mot is the god of death in the religion of Ugarit and Canaan, whose name means death. In the Baal cycle he swallows the storm god Baal, bringing drought, until the goddess Anat cuts him down and Baal returns to life; the two gods then fight to a standstill.

meher-kapisi.s: Meher Kapısı, the Gate of Mithra, is a Urartian rock niche cut into a hillside near Van in eastern Turkey under Ishpuini and Menua around 800 BCE. Its long inscription lists the gods of the Urartian pantheon, headed by Haldi, Teisheba and Shivini, and the sacrifices of cattle…

malmesbury-abbey.s: Malmesbury Abbey is a former Benedictine abbey in Malmesbury, Wiltshire, south-west England, founded in the seventh century. Under Aldhelm, its abbot in the late seventh century, it became a leading centre of learning, and King Æthelstan was buried there in 939.

mul-of-kent.s: Mul was a West Saxon prince, the brother of King Cædwalla, who helped him conquer Kent in 686 and was installed as its ruler. In 687 the people of Kent rose against him and burned him to death with a dozen companions.

marklin.s: Märklin is a German toy company founded in 1859 by Theodor Friedrich Wilhelm Märklin in Göppingen, Württemberg, at first making tin accessories for dolls' houses. In 1891 it introduced standard track gauges for clockwork model railways, and it became one of the world's…

milan-stojadinovic.s: Milan Stojadinović was a Serbian economist and politician who was prime minister of Yugoslavia from 1935 to 1939. He stabilised the economy, expanded trade with Germany and moved the country closer to Germany and Italy, while founding the Yugoslav Radical Union.

miroslav-krleza.s: Miroslav Krleža was a Croatian writer and the leading figure of twentieth-century Croatian literature. His novels, plays and essays, including The Return of Philip Latinowicz (1932) and the Glembay cycle, criticised bourgeois society and nationalism.

minoan-civilisation.s: The Minoan civilisation was a Bronze Age civilisation on Crete, named by Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos. From about 2000 BCE it built great palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, used the Linear A script and traded widely across the Aegean and…

maha-bandula.s: Maha Bandula was a Burmese general of the Konbaung dynasty who led campaigns in Manipur and Assam and on the frontier of British Bengal. In the First Anglo-Burmese War he commanded the Burmese armies against the British, was defeated near Yangon in December 1824, and was…

ming-rui.s: Ming Rui was a Manchu general of the Qing dynasty, a relative by marriage of the Qianlong Emperor, who commanded the third Qing invasion of Burma in 1767–1768. After advancing towards Ava, his army was cut off and destroyed by Burmese forces near Maymyo in early 1768, and he…

mingun-pahtodawgyi.s: The Mingun Pahtodawgyi is a huge unfinished brick stupa at Mingun, on the west bank of the Irrawaddy north of Mandalay, begun by King Bodawpaya in 1790. Intended to be the largest stupa in the world, it was abandoned at about a third of its planned height of 150 metres, and an…

mpanzu-a-kitima.s: Mpanzu a Kitima was a Kongolese prince who contested the succession to King João I of Kongo in 1509 against his half-brother Afonso. Supported by opponents of Christianity, he was defeated in battle at the capital, Mbanza Kongo, a victory that Afonso attributed to the…

mpemba.s: Mpemba was one of the principal provinces of the Kingdom of Kongo in west-central Africa, lying in the heart of the kingdom south of the capital, Mbanza Kongo. Kongo tradition links the founding royal line to the older polity of Mpemba Kasi.

mithra.s: Mithra is an ancient Indo-Iranian deity of covenant, truth and light, closely associated with the sun. Venerated in the Avesta and honoured throughout the Iranian world, he appears as Miiro on the coins of the Kushan emperors and as Mihr in later Persian tradition.

mangraisat.s: The Mangraisat is a law code of Lan Na attributed to Mangrai, founder of Chiang Mai, though it survives only in later manuscripts and how much dates from his reign is uncertain. It regulates matters such as land, irrigation, debt, marriage, theft and fines for injuries, and is…

maravarman-kulasekara-pandya-i.s: Maravarman Kulasekara Pandya I was a Pandya king of Madurai who reigned for some four decades from 1268, the height of the Later Pandyan Empire. He defeated the last Chola king, Rajendra III, and the Hoysala Ramanatha, and sent an army to Sri Lanka.

marcus-garvey.s: Marcus Garvey was a Jamaican political activist who founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914 and led a mass movement of black pride and Pan-Africanism, based in New York from 1916. In the early 1920s his organisation negotiated to settle African Americans in…

marcus-vipsanius-agrippa.s: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa was a Roman general and statesman, the closest friend, son-in-law and chief lieutenant of Augustus. He commanded the fleets that won at Naulochus in 36 BCE and Actium in 31 BCE, ended the Cantabrian Wars in north-western Hispania in 19 BCE and built…

mertola.s: Mértola is a town in the Alentejo region of southern Portugal, on a hill above the Guadiana. As Myrtilis Iulia it was a river port of Roman Lusitania, where in 440 the Suebic king Rechila forced the Roman commander Censorius to surrender.

mpu-prapanca.s: Mpu Prapanca was a Buddhist court poet of the Majapahit kingdom in Java, author of the Old Javanese poem Nagarakretagama (Desawarnana), completed in 1365. Written in praise of King Hayam Wuruk, the poem describes the royal capital, the king's progresses through East Java and…

malaysia-agreement.s: The Malaysia Agreement was the treaty signed in London on 9 July 1963 by Britain, the Federation of Malaya, North Borneo, Sarawak and Singapore, providing for the creation of Malaysia. It set out safeguards for the Borneo states, including control over immigration, and…

malaysian-new-economic-policy.s: The New Economic Policy (NEP) was an affirmative-action and development programme adopted by Malaysia in 1971, after the racial riots of 13 May 1969. It aimed to eradicate poverty and to restructure society so that the Bumiputera, chiefly Malays, would own at least 30 per cent…

manding.s: Manding, or Manden, is the historical heartland of the Mandinka people on the upper Niger, on the border of modern Mali and Guinea, around Kangaba and Niani. Its chiefdoms were united by Sundiata Keita in the 13th century to form the Mali Empire, and after the empire's decline…

mansa-sulayman.s: Mansa Sulayman was ruler of the Mali Empire from about 1341 to 1360, the brother of Mansa Musa. His reign kept the empire near its height, and the traveller Ibn Battuta, who visited his court in 1352–1353, described its ceremonial, justice and security.

matthias-holy-roman-emperor.s: Matthias was Holy Roman Emperor from 1612 to 1619 and King of Hungary and Bohemia, a son of Emperor Maximilian II. As archduke he challenged his brother Rudolf II and in 1608, backed by the estates of Hungary, Austria and Moravia, forced Rudolf to cede him those lands.

mikulov.s: Mikulov, German Nikolsburg, is a town in South Moravia near the Austrian border, known for its castle, its vineyards and its historic Jewish community, long the seat of the chief rabbi of Moravia. The castle was held by the Dietrichstein family from 1575.

moravian-compromise.s: The Moravian Compromise was a set of laws adopted in 1905 that reorganised the Moravian Diet and its electoral system along national lines. Voters were enrolled in separate Czech and German registers, each electing a fixed share of the seats, and school administration was…

moravian-silesian-land.s: The Moravian-Silesian Land was one of the four lands of interwar Czechoslovakia, created in 1928 by merging Moravia with Czech Silesia, with its capital at Brno. Part of its territory was annexed by Germany in 1938.

madiun.s: Madiun is a city in East Java, Indonesia, on the Madiun river in the interior of the island. In the late sixteenth century it was the centre of an east Javanese principality that resisted the rise of Mataram and fell to Panembahan Senapati around 1590.

medism.s: Medism was the Greek term for collaborating with or siding with the Persian Empire, whose people the Greeks often called Medes. It was a charge of treason during and after the Persian Wars of the fifth century BCE, levelled at Thebes and other states that submitted to Xerxes…

manjakamiadana.s: Manjakamiadana was the queen's palace, the largest building of the Rova, the royal compound of the Merina rulers in Antananarivo. Built in timber for Ranavalona I by Jean Laborde around 1840, it was encased in stone between 1867 and 1873 to designs by the missionary James…

menabe.s: Menabe was a Sakalava kingdom on the west coast of Madagascar, founded in the seventeenth century by the Maroserana dynasty. Its rulers built their power on cattle, warfare and trade, and relatives of the dynasty founded the northern Sakalava kingdom of Boina.

manuel-gonzalez-flores.s: Manuel González Flores was a Mexican general and president from 1880 to 1884, a close ally of Porfirio Díaz, who held the office between Díaz's first and second terms. His government extended railways and telegraph lines but faced charges of corruption and riots over a new…

mariano-escobedo.s: Mariano Escobedo was a Mexican general of the liberal side in the Reform War and the French intervention. Commanding the republican Army of the North, he besieged Emperor Maximilian at Querétaro and accepted his surrender in May 1867.

mexican-revolution.s: The Mexican Revolution was the series of revolts and civil wars that began in November 1910 with Francisco Madero's call to rise against Porfirio Díaz. After Díaz fell, revolutionary leaders including Carranza, Obregón, Villa and Zapata fought Victoriano Huerta and then one…

miguel-miramon.s: Miguel Miramón was a Mexican conservative general who headed the conservative government during the Reform War from 1859 to 1860, one of the youngest men to hold the presidency. Defeated by the liberals, he went into exile and later returned to serve Emperor Maximilian.

medinet-madi.s: Medinet Madi is an archaeological site in the south-western Faiyum of Egypt, the ancient town of Dja, later Narmouthis. Its temple to the cobra goddess Renenutet and the crocodile god Sobek was begun by Amenemhat III and completed by Amenemhat IV, and is the best-preserved…

medjay.s: The Medjay were a people of the Eastern Desert of Nubia, known from Egyptian texts from the Old Kingdom onwards. In the Middle Kingdom they served as scouts and auxiliaries for the Egyptian army and are associated with the archaeological Pan-Grave culture.

mentuhotep-iii.s: Mentuhotep III was a king of the Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt, son and successor of Mentuhotep II, who reigned about twelve years around 2000 BCE. He inherited a united and stable kingdom, built temples in the Theban region and sent an expedition under the official Henenu across…

mentuhotep-iv.s: Mentuhotep IV was the last king of the Eleventh Dynasty of Egypt, reigning for a few years around 1990 BCE and omitted from later king lists. He is known mainly from inscriptions in the Wadi Hammamat, where his vizier Amenemhat led a large quarrying expedition.

mirgissa.s: Mirgissa was a large Egyptian fortress of the Middle Kingdom at the Second Cataract of the Nile in Lower Nubia, probably the Iken of Egyptian texts. Built in the Twelfth Dynasty, it had a mud-brick slipway for dragging boats past the rapids and served as a trading post with…

moscow-mathematical-papyrus.s: The Moscow Mathematical Papyrus is an ancient Egyptian mathematical text of the Middle Kingdom, probably of the Thirteenth Dynasty, now in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow. Its 25 problems include the correct calculation of the volume of a truncated pyramid.

molpoi.s: The Molpoi were a guild of singers at Miletus devoted to the cult of Apollo Delphinios. Their head served as the city's eponymous magistrate, and an inscribed list of these officials survives from 525/524 BCE onward.

myrcinus.s: Myrcinus was an ancient town of the Edonians in Thrace, near the lower Strymon river and the later site of Amphipolis. Darius I gave it to Histiaeus of Miletus as a reward for guarding the Danube bridge during the Scythian campaign, but his general Megabazus warned the king of…

mavura-mhande.s: Mavura Mhande was a ruler of the Mutapa kingdom, installed by the Portuguese in 1629 after they defeated Nyambo Kapararidze. In return he signed a treaty that made Mutapa a vassal of Portugal, admitted missionaries and opened the country's gold mines to Portuguese traders.

mahasi-sayadaw.s: Mahasi Sayadaw was a Burmese Theravada Buddhist monk and meditation master. His method of insight, or vipassana, meditation, based on noting bodily and mental events, was taught at a centre in Rangoon from 1949 and spread across Asia and the West.

min-aung-hlaing.s: Min Aung Hlaing is a Myanmar general who became commander-in-chief of the armed forces in 2011. He oversaw the military operations against the Rohingya in 2017, for which UN investigators called for him to be tried for genocide, and on 1 February 2021 he led the coup that…

majdanek-concentration-camp.s: Majdanek was a Nazi concentration and extermination camp on the outskirts of Lublin in German-occupied Poland, opened in 1941. Some 78,000 prisoners, about 59,000 of them Jews, died there, most notoriously in the mass shootings of the 'Harvest Festival' in November 1943.

mefo-bills.s: Mefo bills were promissory notes devised by Hjalmar Schacht to finance German rearmament in secret from 1934. Issued by armaments firms to a dummy company, the Metallurgische Forschungsgesellschaft (Mefo), and guaranteed by the Reichsbank, they kept military spending off the…

marie-of-the-incarnation-ursuline.s: Marie of the Incarnation, born Marie Guyart, was a French Ursuline nun and mystic who arrived at Quebec in 1639 and founded the first school for girls in North America, teaching French and Native pupils. She learned Algonquian and Iroquoian languages and wrote dictionaries and…

medieval-inquisition.s: The Medieval Inquisition was a series of papal tribunals established from the 1230s to combat heresy, above all the Cathars and Waldensians of southern France and northern Italy. Staffed mainly by Dominican and Franciscan friars, it questioned suspects, recorded testimony and…

mount-everest.s: Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth, rising to about 8,849 metres in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Known in Nepali as Sagarmatha and in Tibetan as Chomolungma, it was named by the British after the surveyor George Everest.

maori-language-act-1987.s: The Māori Language Act 1987 made te reo Māori an official language of New Zealand and gave the right to speak it in legal proceedings. It also created the Māori Language Commission to promote the language.

mixed-member-proportional-representation.s: Mixed-member proportional representation, or MMP, is an electoral system in which voters elect constituency members and also vote for parties, with list seats allocated so that each party's share of parliament matches its share of the party vote. Developed in post-war West…

minh-huong.s: The Minh Hương were descendants of Chinese, many of them Ming loyalists, who settled in Vietnam after the fall of the Ming dynasty in 1644. Registered as a separate community, they intermarried with Vietnamese, adopted local customs and served as merchants, officials and…

marcus-petreius.s: Marcus Petreius was a Roman soldier who commanded the army that defeated Catiline at Pistoria in 62 BCE. A loyal legate of Pompey, he fought against Caesar in Spain in 49 BCE and then in Africa.

mastanabal.s: Mastanabal was a Numidian prince, one of the three legitimate sons of King Masinissa. When Scipio Aemilianus divided the royal functions after Masinissa's death in 148 BCE, Mastanabal received responsibility for justice.

michael-aung-thwin.s: Michael Aung-Thwin is a historian of Myanmar, long a professor at the University of Hawaii. In his studies of the Pagan Kingdom he argued that the growth of tax-free religious land gradually weakened the state, and in The Mists of Ramanna (2005) he questioned the traditional…

mahipala-ii.s: Mahipala II was a king of the Pala dynasty of Bengal in the second half of the eleventh century. According to the Ramacharita he imprisoned his brothers Shurapala and Ramapala, and soon afterwards he was killed in the revolt of the Kaivartas under their leader Divya, who…

mahendravarman-ii.s: Mahendravarman II was a king of the Pallava dynasty who reigned briefly, around 668 to 670, after his father Narasimhavarman I, the conqueror of Vatapi. His short reign saw the Chalukyas recover under Vikramaditya I and renew their war with the Pallavas, and he was succeeded…

manavanna.s: Manavanna, also called Manavamma, was a Sri Lankan prince who spent years in exile at the Pallava court of Kanchipuram. With the help of Pallava armies sent by sea by Narasimhavarman I, he eventually won the throne of Anuradhapura in the late seventh century, founding a line…

manigramam.s: The Manigramam was a merchant guild of medieval South India, recorded in inscriptions from the eighth century onwards. It traded across the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea: a ninth-century Tamil inscription at Takua Pa in southern Thailand names it, and the Kollam copper…

mattavilasa-prahasana.s: Mattavilasa Prahasana, 'The Farce of Drunken Sport', is a one-act Sanskrit comedy written in the early seventh century by the Pallava king Mahendravarman I. It mocks a drunken Kapalika ascetic, a greedy Buddhist monk and a Pashupata, who quarrel over a lost skull begging bowl…

marcantonio-colonna.s: Marcantonio Colonna was an Italian nobleman and commander of the Colonna family. He led the papal galleys in the fleet of the Holy League at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, where the Ottoman navy was defeated, and was given a triumphal entry into Rome.

maximilian-henry-of-bavaria.s: Maximilian Henry of Bavaria was archbishop-elector of Cologne from 1650 and prince-bishop of Liège and Hildesheim. He allied with Louis XIV of France, and in Liège his Regulation of 1684 abolished the political power of the craft guilds and placed the city under princely control.

meuse-inferieure.s: Meuse-Inférieure was a department of the French Republic and Empire from 1795 to 1814, named after the lower Meuse and centred on Maastricht. It covered parts of the former Prince-Bishopric of Liège and of the Dutch and Austrian lands, roughly today's Dutch and Belgian Limburg.

manfred-king-of-sicily.s: Manfred was a son of Emperor Frederick II and king of Sicily from 1258 to 1266. Opposed by the papacy, he allied with Epirus and Achaea against Nicaea, sending knights to the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259.

maria-ii-zaccaria.s: Maria II Zaccaria was a Genoese noblewoman, widow of Pedro de San Superano, who ruled the Principality of Achaea from 1402 to 1404. She was succeeded by her nephew Centurione II Zaccaria, the last Latin prince of Achaea, who lost the remaining lands to the Byzantines in 1430.

marino-sanudo-torsello.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello was a Venetian statesman and geographer who travelled widely in the eastern Mediterranean. His Secreta fidelium crucis proposed a crusade with an economic blockade of Egypt, and his history of Romania describes the Frankish states of Greece, including…

marquisate-of-bodonitsa.s: The Marquisate of Bodonitsa was a small crusader state in central Greece, created after the Fourth Crusade to guard the pass of Thermopylae. Held by Italian families including the Pallavicini and later the Zorzi of Venice, it acknowledged the princes of Achaea as suzerains and…

matilda-of-hainaut.s: Matilda of Hainaut was princess of Achaea from 1313 to 1318, the daughter of Isabella of Villehardouin and Florent of Hainaut and the last of the Villehardouin line. Married to Louis of Burgundy, she was later deprived of the principality by the Angevins of Naples and died in…

melingoi.s: The Melingoi were a Slavic tribe that settled on the slopes of Mount Taygetus in the Peloponnese in the early Middle Ages. They kept considerable autonomy under the Byzantines and the Franks, who built fortresses such as Mistras to control them, and were gradually assimilated…

miron-costin.s: Miron Costin was a Moldavian boyar, chronicler and poet. He continued Grigore Ureche's chronicle of Moldavia from 1595 to 1661 and wrote a work on the origin of the Moldavians, arguing for their Roman descent.

moldova-river.s: The Moldova River is a river of north-eastern Romania, about 210 km long, which rises in the Eastern Carpathians of Bukovina and flows south-east to join the Siret near the town of Roman. According to tradition the frontier march founded on its banks in the fourteenth century…

moldovita-monastery.s: Moldovița Monastery is an Orthodox convent in Suceava County, north-eastern Romania, whose church was built in 1532 by Prince Petru Rareș of Moldavia. Its walls, inside and out, were covered with frescoes in 1537, including a celebrated Siege of Constantinople.

moldova.s: Moldova is a landlocked country in eastern Europe between Romania and Ukraine, with its capital at Chișinău. Its core is the land between the Prut and the Dniester, the eastern half of the medieval Principality of Moldavia, annexed by Russia in 1812 as Bessarabia.

mirza-hasan-shirazi.s: Mirza Hasan Shirazi was an Iranian Shi'i jurist, the leading religious authority of his time, who taught at Samarra in Ottoman Iraq. In December 1891 a ruling attributed to him declared the use of tobacco forbidden while a British company held the Iranian tobacco monopoly, and…

mirza-hosein-khan-sepahsalar.s: Mirza Hosein Khan Sepahsalar, also titled Moshir od-Dowleh, was a reforming minister of Qajar Iran. After years as envoy in Istanbul, where he observed the Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, he became prime minister in 1871 and tried to create a cabinet government, modernise the army…

mirza-reza-kermani.s: Mirza Reza Kermani was an Iranian radical, a follower of the pan-Islamist Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, who shot dead Naser al-Din Shah at the shrine of Shah Abdol-Azim near Tehran on 1 May 1896, on the eve of the shah's jubilee. He had earlier been imprisoned and tortured for his…

mohammad-ali-shah-qajar.s: Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar was shah of Iran from 1907 to 1909. Hostile to the new constitution, he had the Persian Cossack Brigade bombard the Majlis in June 1908, starting a civil war in which constitutionalists held out in Tabriz.

mohammad-shah-qajar.s: Mohammad Shah Qajar was shah of Iran from 1834 to 1848, a grandson of Fath Ali Shah and son of Abbas Mirza. Guided by his minister Haji Mirza Aqasi, he besieged Herat in 1837–1838 but withdrew under British pressure after Britain occupied Kharg Island.

morgan-shuster.s: William Morgan Shuster was an American lawyer and financial administrator appointed treasurer-general of Iran by the Majlis in 1911 to reorganise the country's finances. His energetic reforms, including a treasury gendarmerie, alarmed Russia and Britain, and a Russian…

mozaffar-ad-din-shah-qajar.s: Mozaffar ad-Din Shah Qajar was shah of Iran from 1896 to 1907, succeeding his assassinated father Naser al-Din Shah. Short of money, he took large Russian loans and granted concessions, including the D'Arcy oil concession of 1901.

mahaviracharya.s: Mahaviracharya was a Jain mathematician of the ninth century who worked at the court of the Rashtrakuta emperor Amoghavarsha I. About 850 he wrote the Ganitasarasangraha, a comprehensive Sanskrit treatise on arithmetic, algebra and geometry.

manyakheta.s: Manyakheta, modern Malkhed in the Kalaburagi district of Karnataka, was the capital of the Rashtrakuta empire from the reign of Amoghavarsha I in the early ninth century until 972. It was then sacked by the Paramara king Siyaka II of Malwa, and the Western Chalukyas who…

mercedarians.s: The Mercedarians, the Order of Our Lady of Mercy, are a Catholic religious order founded in Barcelona about 1218 by Peter Nolasco to ransom Christians held captive by Muslims. Their members took a special vow to offer themselves as hostages if needed to free captives.

mariano-melgarejo.s: Mariano Melgarejo was a Bolivian general who seized power in 1864 and ruled as president until 1871. His erratic rule became a byword for caudillo misgovernment: he decreed the sale of indigenous communal lands, provoking revolts, and signed treaties that conceded territory…

movement-for-socialism-bolivia.s: The Movement for Socialism (MAS) is a Bolivian left-wing party that grew out of the coca growers' unions of the Chapare and was led by Evo Morales. It won the presidency in 2005 and governed from 2006 to 2019 and again from 2020 to 2025, nationalising hydrocarbons and…

mauricio-hochschild.s: Mauricio Hochschild was a German-born mining entrepreneur who became one of Bolivia's three 'tin barons', alongside Simón Patiño and the Aramayo family. His company controlled a large share of Bolivian tin and other mineral exports until the nationalisation of the great mines…

manuel-bulnes.s: Manuel Bulnes was a Chilean general and president. He commanded the army that won the Battle of Yungay in 1839, destroying the Peru–Bolivian Confederation, and served two terms as president from 1841 to 1851.

ma-ying-jeou.s: Ma Ying-jeou is a Taiwanese politician of the Kuomintang who was mayor of Taipei and president of the Republic of China from 2008 to 2016. He pursued closer economic ties with the People's Republic, opening direct flights and signing a trade framework agreement in 2010.

marco-polo-bridge-incident.s: The Marco Polo Bridge Incident was a clash between Chinese and Japanese troops near the Lugou Bridge south-west of Beijing on the night of 7 July 1937. Fighting spread after negotiations failed, and Japan sent reinforcements to north China.

marcist-revolution.s: The Marcist Revolution was an uprising that began in Guayaquil on 6 March 1845 against Juan José Flores, the Venezuelan-born general who had dominated Ecuador since its foundation in 1830. Led by Guayaquil merchants and liberals, it forced Flores to leave the country.

manuel-enrique-araujo.s: Manuel Enrique Araujo was a Salvadoran physician and president from 1911 to 1913. His government founded the National Guard, a rural police force, and was remembered for its relative tolerance and reforms.

mara-salvatrucha.s: Mara Salvatrucha, or MS-13, is a criminal gang formed in the 1980s by young Salvadoran immigrants in Los Angeles, many of them refugees from the civil war. After mass deportations from the United States in the 1990s it spread to El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala, where it…

mauricio-funes.s: Mauricio Funes was a Salvadoran television journalist who became the first president from the FMLN, the former guerrilla movement, serving from 2009 to 2014. His government expanded social programmes and apologised for state crimes during the civil war.

melendez-quinonez-dynasty.s: The Meléndez–Quiñónez dynasty was the family group that held the presidency of El Salvador from 1913 to 1927: the brothers Carlos and Jorge Meléndez and their brother-in-law Alfonso Quiñónez Molina. Ruling through the official National Democratic Party and controlled…

mart-laar.s: Mart Laar is an Estonian historian and politician who was prime minister from 1992 to 1994 and from 1999 to 2002. His first government carried out radical market reforms, including rapid privatisation, free trade and a flat income tax, which became a model for other…

mantsala-rebellion.s: The Mäntsälä rebellion was a failed uprising by members of the Lapua Movement in February and March 1932, which began when armed activists broke up a Social Democratic meeting at Mäntsälä in southern Finland. The rebels demanded the resignation of the government, but the army…

marimekko.s: Marimekko is a Finnish textile, clothing and design company founded in Helsinki in 1951 by Armi and Viljo Ratia. Its bold printed fabrics, above all Maija Isola's Unikko poppy pattern of 1964, became internationally famous in the 1960s, helped by Jacqueline Kennedy wearing its…

martti-ahtisaari.s: Martti Ahtisaari (1937–2023) was a Finnish diplomat and Social Democratic politician who served as president of Finland from 1994 to 2000. As a United Nations official he led the transition to Namibian independence in 1989–1990, and he later mediated in Kosovo in 1999, in Aceh…

marsilio-ficino.s: Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a Florentine philosopher and priest, the leading Neoplatonist of the Renaissance. Supported by Cosimo de' Medici and later Lorenzo, he translated the complete works of Plato into Latin, published in 1484, as well as the Corpus Hermeticum and…

masaccio.s: Masaccio (1401–1428) was a Florentine painter, the first great painter of the Italian Renaissance. In a short career he applied Brunelleschi's linear perspective and a new sculptural naturalism in works such as the Holy Trinity fresco in Santa Maria Novella and the frescoes of…

manuel-estrada-cabrera.s: Manuel Estrada Cabrera (1857–1924) was a Guatemalan lawyer who ruled the country as president from 1898 to 1920, one of the longest dictatorships in Central American history. He favoured foreign companies, granting the United Fruit Company and its railway affiliate major…

miguel-angel-asturias.s: Miguel Ángel Asturias (1899–1974) was a Guatemalan novelist, poet and diplomat who received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1967. His novel El Señor Presidente, published in 1946, portrayed life under the dictatorship of Manuel Estrada Cabrera, while Men of Maize and his…

miguel-garcia-granados.s: Miguel García Granados (1809–1878) was a Guatemalan soldier and politician who led the Liberal Revolution of 1871 with Justo Rufino Barrios, overthrowing the conservative government of Vicente Cerna. As provisional president from 1871 to 1873 he expelled the Jesuits and began…

manuel-bonilla.s: Manuel Bonilla (1849–1913) was a Honduran general and politician who was president from 1903 to 1907 and again from 1912 until his death. Overthrown in 1907, he returned to power after an invasion in 1910–1911 backed by the banana entrepreneur Samuel Zemurray and the American…

mandal-commission.s: The Mandal Commission was a body set up by the Janata government of India in 1979 under B. P.

manmohan-singh.s: Manmohan Singh (1932–2024) was an Indian economist and Congress politician who was prime minister from 2004 to 2014. As finance minister from 1991 to 1996 he launched the liberalisation of the Indian economy, dismantling industrial licensing and opening the country to foreign…

mars-orbiter-mission.s: The Mars Orbiter Mission, also called Mangalyaan, was India's first interplanetary mission, launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation in November 2013. It entered orbit around Mars on 24 September 2014, making India the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit and the…

mizoram.s: Mizoram is a state in north-eastern India, bordering Myanmar and Bangladesh, with its capital at Aizawl. An armed revolt led by the Mizo National Front began in 1966, fed by resentment of the Assam government's handling of a famine in the Mizo hills.

minox.s: The Minox is a subminiature camera designed by the Riga-born engineer Walter Zapp and first manufactured in 1938 by the state electrical works VEF in Riga. Small enough to fit in the palm and using film 9.5 millimetres wide, it became famous as a spy camera used by…

mosquito-coast.s: The Mosquito Coast is the Caribbean lowland of eastern Nicaragua and north-eastern Honduras, home to the Miskito people and Creole and Garífuna communities. From the seventeenth century the Miskito kings were allied with Britain, which maintained a protectorate over the coast.

matagalpa.s: Matagalpa is a city in the central highlands of Nicaragua and capital of the department of the same name, at the heart of the country's main coffee-growing region. Coffee spread there from the 1870s, encouraged by laws that transferred indigenous communal land to private…

momotombo.s: Momotombo is a conical stratovolcano rising to about 1,300 metres on the northern shore of Lake Managua in western Nicaragua. Earthquakes and eruptions in the early seventeenth century led to the abandonment of the first colonial city of León, at its foot, in 1610.

mireya-moscoso.s: Mireya Moscoso is a Panamanian politician who was president of Panama from 1999 to 2004, the country's first woman president. The widow of the three-times president Arnulfo Arias, she led his Arnulfista Party and presided over the transfer of the Panama Canal on 31 December 1999.

manuel-noriega.s: Manuel Noriega was a Panamanian general who, after heading military intelligence under Omar Torrijos, became commander of the Panama Defence Forces and de facto ruler of Panama from 1983 to 1989. Long a CIA informant, he was indicted in the United States for drug trafficking…

manuel-pardo.s: Manuel Pardo was a Peruvian businessman and politician, founder of the Civilista Party, who was president of Peru from 1872 to 1876, the first civilian elected to the office. He sought to use guano revenue for railways, education and productive investment, but his government…

mario-vargas-llosa.s: Mario Vargas Llosa was a Peruvian novelist and essayist, a leading figure of the Latin American literary boom, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010. His novels include The Time of the Hero (1963), Conversation in the Cathedral (1969) and The Feast of the Goat (2000).

miguel-grau-seminario.s: Miguel Grau Seminario was a Peruvian naval officer who commanded the ironclad Huáscar in the War of the Pacific. For months in 1879 he raided the Chilean coast and held off a stronger navy, gaining a reputation for chivalry by rescuing Chilean sailors after sinking the…

minceta-tower.s: The Minčeta Tower is the large round fortress at the highest, north-western corner of Dubrovnik's city walls. Begun as a four-sided tower in 1319, it was rebuilt in 1463–1464 after the fall of Constantinople, to plans by the Florentine architect Michelozzo, and completed by…

muse-bihi-abdi.s: Muse Bihi Abdi is a Somaliland politician and former air force officer who was president of Somaliland from 2017 to 2024. A commander in the Somali National Movement, he led the ruling Kulmiye party to victory in the 2017 election.

marikana-massacre.s: The Marikana massacre took place on 16 August 2012 near the Lonmin platinum mine at Marikana in North West Province, South Africa, when police opened fire on striking miners, killing 34. Ten people, including police officers, had been killed in the preceding days.

multi-party-negotiating-forum.s: The Multi-Party Negotiating Forum was the body that negotiated the end of apartheid in South Africa in 1993, after the breakdown of CODESA. Meeting at Kempton Park, it brought together 26 parties and organisations, survived the assassination of Chris Hani, and agreed the…

marino-faliero.s: Marino Faliero was Doge of Venice from 1354 to 1355. An experienced commander and diplomat, he was elected in old age and within months plotted with commoners to overthrow the patrician government and make himself prince.

mark-the-evangelist.s: Mark the Evangelist is the traditional author of the Gospel of Mark and, by Christian tradition, founder of the church of Alexandria. In 828 two Venetian merchants smuggled relics said to be his out of Alexandria to Venice, where the Basilica of San Marco was built to house them.

murano.s: Murano is a group of islands in the Venetian lagoon, about 1.5 kilometres north of Venice. In 1291 the republic ordered glassmakers to move their furnaces there, partly to reduce the risk of fire in the city, and Murano became the centre of Venetian glass-making, famous for…

maha-yazawin.s: The Maha Yazawin (Great Chronicle) is the first national chronicle of Burma, compiled by U Kala and completed around 1724 under the Restored Toungoo dynasty. It traces Burmese kingship from legendary Buddhist origins to the early 18th century and became the basis for the later…

mahadhammayaza-dipati.s: Mahadhammayaza Dipati was the last king of the Toungoo dynasty of Burma, reigning from 1733 to 1752. His weak government could not stop Manipuri raids or the rebellion of the Mon in Lower Burma, whose Restored Hanthawaddy kingdom captured Ava in 1752.

minyekyawdin.s: Minyekyawdin was king of the Restored Toungoo dynasty of Burma from 1673 to 1698. His long reign was a period of peace at home and on the frontiers, in which the administrative system built by his predecessors continued to function, though the court's control of manpower and…

maxima-caesariensis.s: Maxima Caesariensis was one of the provinces created in Roman Britain by the reforms of Diocletian around 300. It covered south-eastern Britain, with its capital at Londinium (London), which was also the seat of the vicarius of the Diocese of the Britains.

magnentius.s: Magnentius was a Roman usurper who seized power in the West in January 350 after the murder of Emperor Constans, ruling Gaul, Britain, Spain, Italy and Africa. He was defeated by Constantius II at the Battle of Mursa in 351, one of the bloodiest battles of the century, and…

mendip-hills.s: The Mendip Hills are a range of limestone hills in Somerset, England, south of Bristol. Their lead and silver deposits were mined by the Romans within a few years of the conquest of 43 CE, with lead pigs stamped as early as 49 CE.

myos-hormos.s: Myos Hormos was a port on the Red Sea coast of Egypt, at Quseir al-Qadim north of modern Quseir. Founded under the Ptolemies, it became under Roman rule one of the main harbours for trade with Arabia and India, linked by a desert road to Coptos on the Nile.

marcus-junius-brutus.s: Marcus Junius Brutus was a Roman senator who, with Gaius Cassius Longinus, led the conspiracy that killed Julius Caesar on the Ides of March 44 BCE. Claiming to defend the Republic, he left Italy and raised forces in the eastern provinces.

marcus-aemilius-lepidus-triumvir.s: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus was a Roman politician and ally of Julius Caesar who formed the Second Triumvirate with Mark Antony and Octavian in 43 BCE. He was given Africa to govern, but after trying to take Sicily from Octavian in 36 BCE he was stripped of his powers.

marcus-furius-camillus.s: Marcus Furius Camillus was a Roman statesman and general of the early fourth century BCE. He captured the Etruscan city of Veii in 396 BCE after a long siege, and Roman tradition credited him with saving Rome after the Gallic sack of about 390 BCE.

magnitogorsk.s: Magnitogorsk is an industrial city in the southern Urals of Russia, built from 1929 around a huge iron and steel works beside Magnitnaya, the 'magnetic mountain' of iron ore. Constructed at great speed during Stalin's first Five-Year Plan, partly by forced labour, it became a…

mikhail-kalinin.s: Mikhail Kalinin was a Bolshevik revolutionary of peasant origin who served as formal head of state of Soviet Russia from 1919 and of the Soviet Union from 1922 until 1946. As chairman of the Central Executive Committee and later of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet he held a…

middle-atlas.s: The Middle Atlas is a mountain range in central Morocco, part of the Atlas system, running north-east from the High Atlas towards the Taza gap. Its forested heights and plateaus, home largely to Amazigh (Berber) tribes, overlook the plains of Fez and Meknes.

muhammad-al-qaim.s: Muhammad al-Qa'im bi-amr Allah was the founder of the Saadi dynasty of Morocco. A sharif from the Draa valley, he was proclaimed leader of the holy war against the Portuguese by the tribes of the Sus in 1510, with the backing of Sufi brotherhoods.

mithridates-ii-of-parthia.s: Mithridates II was king of the Parthian Empire from about 124 to 91 BCE. He restored Parthian power after the defeats of his predecessors by the Saka, subdued the nomads and settled many of them in Sakastan, and pushed the western frontier to the Euphrates.

massagetae.s: The Massagetae were an ancient Iranian nomadic people of the steppes east of the Caspian Sea, generally counted among the Saka. Herodotus relates that their queen Tomyris defeated and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BCE, and he describes their horsemanship, bronze and…

maeandrius.s: Maeandrius was the secretary of Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, and took control of the island after his master's murder around 522 BCE. According to Herodotus he offered the Samians equal rights but kept power for himself.

melissus-of-samos.s: Melissus of Samos was a Greek philosopher of the Eleatic school and a statesman of his island in the fifth century BCE. Following Parmenides, he argued that reality is one, eternal, unchanging and infinite.

manasses-chronicle.s: The Manasses Chronicle is a verse world history written by the Byzantine author Constantine Manasses in the twelfth century. Its Middle Bulgarian translation, made for Tsar Ivan Alexander in the 1340s, survives in an illuminated manuscript in the Vatican Library with 69…

michael-ii-asen.s: Michael II Asen was tsar of Bulgaria from 1246 to 1256, a son of Ivan Asen II and Irene Komnene Doukaina. He came to the throne as a child, and during his reign the Empire of Nicaea took much of Thrace and Macedonia.

michael-shishman.s: Michael Shishman was tsar of Bulgaria from 1323 to 1330 and founder of the Shishman dynasty, the last ruling house of medieval Bulgaria. Previously despot of Vidin, he was elected by the boyars, fought the Byzantines and later allied with Andronikos III.

manuchihr-iii.s: Manuchihr III was Shirvanshah, ruler of Shirvan in present-day Azerbaijan, from about the 1120s to about 1160. Allied with the Georgian kingdom, he married Tamar, a daughter of King David IV the Builder.

muyeol-of-silla.s: Muyeol, born Kim Chunchu, was king of Silla from 654 to 661, the first king from the 'true bone' rank. As a diplomat he secured an alliance with Tang China in 648, and as king he joined the Tang in destroying Baekje in 660, with Kim Yu-sin commanding the Silla army.

michu-of-silla.s: Michu was king of Silla from 262 to 284, according to the Samguk sagi. A descendant of Kim Alji, he was the first member of the Kim clan to take the throne, which had earlier passed between the Bak and Seok clans.

munmu-of-silla.s: Munmu was king of Silla from 661 to 681, son of King Muyeol. With Tang China he completed the conquest of Baekje and destroyed Goguryeo in 668, and then fought the Silla–Tang War, which ended in 676 with Silla controlling the peninsula south of the Taedong River.

mekong-delta.s: The Mekong Delta is the region of southern Vietnam where the Mekong River divides into many channels before reaching the South China Sea. In the early centuries CE it was the heart of Funan, whose port at Oc Eo has yielded Roman and Indian objects.

mikhail-tukhachevsky.s: Mikhail Tukhachevsky was a Soviet military commander who led Red Army fronts in the Russian Civil War and the Polish–Soviet War of 1920. As chief of staff and deputy commissar of defence he pressed for the mechanisation of the army and helped develop the theory of deep…

muara-takus.s: Muara Takus is a Buddhist temple compound in Kampar Regency, Riau province, on the island of Sumatra in Indonesia. Within a walled enclosure stand several brick and sandstone stupas, the largest the Candi Mahligai, whose dating is debated.

miluo-river.s: The Miluo is a river in north-eastern Hunan, China, flowing west into the Xiang River near Dongting Lake. According to tradition, the poet and Chu minister Qu Yuan drowned himself in it in about 278 BCE in despair at the fall of the Chu capital to Qin, and the Dragon Boat…

maha-thammaracha-ii.s: Maha Thammaracha II was king of Sukhothai in the later fourteenth century, the son of Li Thai. Faced with repeated attacks by Borommaracha I of Ayutthaya on the northern towns, he submitted in 1378 and became a vassal of Ayutthaya, ending Sukhothai's independence.

maha-thammaracha-iii.s: Maha Thammaracha III, also known as Sai Lue Thai, was king of Sukhothai from about 1398 to 1419, as a vassal of Ayutthaya. He tried to restore Sukhothai's standing and strained against its overlord, but lacked the strength to break free, and the centre of the kingdom shifted…

maha-thammaracha-iv.s: Maha Thammaracha IV was the last king of Sukhothai, ruling from 1419 to 1438 as a vassal of Ayutthaya after King Intharacha settled a succession dispute in his favour. He ruled mainly from Phitsanulok.

michael-vickery.s: Michael Vickery was an American historian of Cambodia and mainland Southeast Asia. He wrote widely on early Khmer history, on the Khmer Rouge period in Cambodia 1975–1982, and on Thai history.

masnavi.s: The Masnavi, or Masnavi-ye Ma'navi, is a long Persian poem by Jalal al-Din Rumi, composed in Konya in the last years of his life. In six books of some 25,000 rhyming couplets, it teaches Sufi doctrine through stories, fables and commentary on the Qur'an.

mesud-i.s: Mesud I was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from 1116 to 1156, the son of Kilij Arslan I. He made Konya the settled capital of a reunited state, fought the Danishmendids and the Byzantines, and during the Second Crusade in 1147 his forces routed the German army of Conrad…

majid-bin-said.s: Majid bin Said was the first Sultan of Zanzibar, ruling from 1856 to 1870. On the death of his father Said bin Sultan his realm was divided: Majid took Zanzibar and the African dominions while his brother Thuwaini took Oman, a division confirmed by British arbitration in 1861.

madrid-protocol-of-1885.s: The Madrid Protocol of 1885 was an agreement signed on 7 March 1885 by Britain, Germany and Spain. Britain and Germany recognised Spanish sovereignty over the Sulu archipelago, and Spain gave up its claims to North Borneo, where the British North Borneo Company had been…

muhammad-pulalun.s: Muhammad Pulalun was Sultan of Sulu in the mid-nineteenth century. After Spanish expeditions destroyed the Balangingi strongholds in 1848 and stormed Jolo in 1851, he signed a treaty in 1851 acknowledging Spanish sovereignty over Sulu.

metamorphosis-insectorum-surinamensium.s: Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium is an illustrated book by the German-born naturalist and artist Maria Sibylla Merian, published in Amsterdam in 1705. Based on her stay in Suriname from 1699 to 1701, its sixty plates show the life cycles of insects together with the…

maroons.s: Maroons were Africans and their descendants in the Americas who escaped slavery and formed independent communities, usually in forests, swamps or mountains beyond colonial control. Large maroon societies arose in Suriname, Jamaica, Brazil, Colombia and elsewhere, and some won…

matawai.s: The Matawai are a Maroon people of Suriname, descended from Africans who escaped from the plantations in the eighteenth century and settled along the Saramacca River. Closely related to the Saramaka, they made a peace treaty with the colonial government in 1767 that recognised…

moengo.s: Moengo is a town on the Cottica River in eastern Suriname, built as a company town for bauxite mining by Suralco, the Surinamese subsidiary of Alcoa, which developed the deposits from the late 1910s. For decades it was a centre of the industry that dominated the Surinamese…

moiwana-massacre.s: The Moiwana massacre was the killing of at least 39 inhabitants of the Ndyuka Maroon village of Moiwana in eastern Suriname, most of them women and children, by soldiers of the National Army on 29 November 1986, during the interior war against the Jungle Commando. In 2005 the…

mpumalanga.s: Mpumalanga is a province of north-eastern South Africa, bordering Eswatini and Mozambique, created in 1994 from the eastern part of the former Transvaal and given its present name in 1995. Its capital is Mbombela.

matterhorn.s: The Matterhorn is a pyramid-shaped mountain of the Alps, 4,478 metres high, on the border between Switzerland and Italy above Zermatt. One of the last great Alpine peaks to be climbed, it was first ascended by Edward Whymper's party on 14 July 1865, when four climbers died on…

max-frisch.s: Max Frisch was a Swiss novelist, playwright and architect from Zurich. His novels Stiller and Homo Faber and his plays The Fire Raisers and Andorra examine questions of identity, guilt and conformity, and he was a sharp critic of Swiss complacency.

morogoro.s: Morogoro is a city in eastern Tanzania at the foot of the Uluguru Mountains, about 190 kilometres west of Dar es Salaam on the Central Line railway. It is an agricultural centre and the seat of the Sokoine University of Agriculture.

mount-kilimanjaro.s: Mount Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano in north-eastern Tanzania near the Kenyan border and, at 5,895 metres, the highest mountain in Africa. Its summit, Uhuru Peak on the Kibo cone, still carries glaciers that are rapidly shrinking.

manuel-gamio.s: Manuel Gamio was a Mexican anthropologist and archaeologist, often called the father of modern Mexican anthropology. His study of the population of the Teotihuacan Valley, published in 1922, combined archaeology, history and ethnography, and his excavations exposed the…

mahavyutpatti.s: The Mahavyutpatti is a Sanskrit–Tibetan dictionary compiled in imperial Tibet in the early ninth century, under royal patronage, to standardise the translation of Buddhist texts. Its thousands of entries fixed the Tibetan equivalents of Sanskrit terms, giving Tibetan…

me-agtsom.s: Me Agtsom, also called Tride Tsugtsen, was emperor of Tibet from 705 to 755, coming to the throne as an infant under the regency of his grandmother Thrimalö. In 710 he married the Tang princess Jincheng.

muscovy-company.s: The Muscovy Company was an English trading company chartered in 1555 after Richard Chancellor's voyage to the White Sea opened direct contact with the court of Ivan IV. One of the first major joint-stock companies, it held a monopoly of English trade with Russia, enjoyed…

mahmud-shah-ii-of-malwa.s: Mahmud Shah II was the last sultan of the Khalji dynasty of Malwa, reigning from 1511 to 1531. Dependent on his Rajput minister Medini Rai, he was defeated and captured by Rana Sanga of Mewar in 1519 but released and restored to his throne.

malik-muhammad-jayasi.s: Malik Muhammad Jayasi was a Sufi poet from Jais in Awadh who wrote in the Awadhi language. His epic Padmavat, completed in 1540, tells in allegorical form the story of the Sinhalese princess Padmavati, queen of Chittor, and Alauddin Khalji's desire for her.

mandalgarh.s: Mandalgarh is a hill fort and town in the Bhilwara district of Rajasthan, on the plateau north-east of Chittor. Contested for centuries between Mewar, the sultans of Malwa and the Mughals, it was one of the main strongholds of eastern Mewar.

mirabai.s: Mirabai was a Rajput princess and Hindu mystic poet of the bhakti movement, devoted to the god Krishna. Born into the Rathore family of Merta, she is traditionally said to have married Bhoj Raj, son of Rana Sanga of Mewar, and after his early death to have rejected the…

makerere-university.s: Makerere University in Kampala is Uganda's oldest and largest university. Founded in 1922 as a technical school, it became Makerere College, the leading centre of higher education in British East Africa, a college of the University of London from 1949 and part of the…

mobutu-sese-seko.s: Mobutu Sese Seko was the ruler of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which he renamed Zaire, from 1965 to 1997. An army officer, he seized power in a coup in November 1965 and ruled as an authoritarian president backed by Western powers during the Cold War, promoting a…

manie-maritz.s: Manie Maritz was a Boer general who led the Maritz Rebellion of 1914. A commando leader in the Second Boer War, he later joined the Union Defence Force, but when South Africa entered the First World War on Britain's side he went over to the Germans in South West Africa with…

maritz-rebellion.s: The Maritz Rebellion was a rising of Afrikaners in 1914–1915 against the Union government's decision to invade German South West Africa on Britain's side in the First World War. Led by Manie Maritz, Christiaan de Wet, Christiaan Beyers and Jan Kemp, some 12,000 rebels took up…

mines-and-works-act-1911.s: The Mines and Works Act of 1911 was a law of the Union of South Africa under which regulations reserved skilled jobs in the mines for white workers, the first of the industrial colour bar laws. When the courts struck down the regulations in 1923, Hertzog's Pact government…

mohamed-bin-zayed-al-nahyan.s: Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is the ruler of Abu Dhabi and has been president of the United Arab Emirates since May 2022. A son of the founding president Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, he became crown prince of Abu Dhabi in 2004 and was the country's de facto leader during the…

mohammed-bin-rashid-al-maktoum.s: Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum is the ruler of Dubai and has been vice-president and prime minister of the United Arab Emirates since 2006. A son of Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum, he served as the federation's first defence minister from 1971 and drove Dubai's growth into a…

mubadala-investment-company.s: Mubadala Investment Company is a sovereign wealth fund owned by the government of Abu Dhabi. Founded in 2002 as Mubadala Development Company and merged with the International Petroleum Investment Company in 2017, it invests worldwide in sectors such as energy, technology,…

margaret-thatcher.s: Margaret Thatcher was a British Conservative politician and the first woman prime minister of the United Kingdom, serving from 1979 to 1990. Her governments privatised state industries, curbed trade union power, deregulated finance and won the Falklands War in 1982; her…

michael-faraday.s: Michael Faraday was an English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the principle behind electric generators and transformers. Largely self-educated, he worked at the Royal Institution in London, where he also made major discoveries in electrochemistry,…

mahanaim.s: Mahanaim was a town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, mentioned in the Hebrew Bible. It served as the capital of Saul's son Ish-bosheth while David ruled in Hebron, and as David's refuge during the rebellion of Absalom; its exact location is uncertain, though Tell edh-Dhahab…

manikya-lal-varma.s: Manikya Lal Varma was an Indian independence activist from Mewar and a leader of the praja mandal movement in the princely states of Rajputana. He founded the Mewar Praja Mandal in 1938 and, after Udaipur joined the union in April 1948, became prime minister of the United…

matsya-union.s: The Matsya Union was a short-lived state of the Indian Union formed on 18 March 1948 by merging the princely states of Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur and Karauli in eastern Rajputana, with Alwar as its capital. Named after the ancient Matsya kingdom of the region, it joined the…

mewar-praja-mandal.s: The Mewar Praja Mandal was a people's association founded in 1938 by Manikya Lal Varma in the princely state of Mewar (Udaipur) to campaign for civil liberties, responsible government and relief from feudal dues. Banned by the state soon after its foundation, it was part of…

marbury-v-madison.s: Marbury v. Madison was a case decided by the Supreme Court of the United States in 1803 under Chief Justice John Marshall.

marshall-plan.s: The Marshall Plan, officially the European Recovery Program, was an American programme of aid to Western Europe after the Second World War, proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in 1947.

martin-luther-king-jr.s: Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and the best-known leader of the civil rights movement. Advocating non-violent protest, he led the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955–1956 and campaigns in Birmingham and Selma, gave the I Have a Dream speech at the March on…

mask-of-warka.s: The Mask of Warka, also called the Lady of Uruk, is a marble sculpture of a female face from Uruk, dating from about 3100 BCE and found in 1939. Probably part of a composite cult statue with inlaid eyes and eyebrows, it is one of the earliest naturalistic representations of…

meskiaggasher.s: Meskiaggasher was the first king of the First Dynasty of Uruk according to the Sumerian King List, which calls him a son of the sun god Utu, credits him with a reign of 324 years and says that he entered the sea and disappeared. He is not attested in contemporary inscriptions…

marcos-perez-jimenez.s: Marcos Pérez Jiménez was a Venezuelan army officer who ruled Venezuela as a dictator from 1952 to 1958. A member of the junta that overthrew the elected president Rómulo Gallegos in 1948, he oversaw large public works financed by oil revenue while repressing opposition through…

mene-grande.s: Mene Grande is a town on the eastern side of Lake Maracaibo in the Venezuelan state of Zulia. In 1914 the Zumaque I well, drilled there by the Caribbean Petroleum Company, an affiliate of Royal Dutch Shell, opened the first commercially significant oilfield in Venezuela.

manuel-de-amat-y-junyent.s: Manuel de Amat y Junyent was a Catalan soldier who served as governor of Chile from 1755 to 1761 and viceroy of Peru from 1761 to 1776. He reorganised the colonial militias after Spain's losses in the Seven Years' War, carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 and built…

martin-de-porres.s: Martin de Porres was a lay brother of the Dominican order in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman from Panama. Known for his care for the sick and the poor, he became one of the most popular saints of Latin America and was canonised in 1962 as the first…

maximus-metropolitan-of-kiev.s: Maximus, Metropolitan of Kiev, was a Greek churchman who headed the Orthodox Church of Rus' as Metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus' from 1283 to 1305. After Kiev was devastated by the Mongols, he moved the seat of the metropolitan to Vladimir in 1299, bringing the head of the…

mstislav-mstislavich.s: Mstislav Mstislavich, called the Bold (Udatny), was a Rus' prince who ruled Novgorod at intervals from 1210 to 1217 and later Galicia. Allied with Konstantin of Rostov, he defeated Yuri and Yaroslav of Vladimir at the Battle of Lipitsa in 1216.

maba-people.s: The Maba are a people of the Ouaddaï region of eastern Chad, speakers of a Maban language, who formed the ruling core of the Wadai Sultanate founded in the early seventeenth century. Their aristocracy supplied the sultan's heavy cavalry and many officials.

manasollasa.s: The Manasollasa is a Sanskrit encyclopaedic work compiled in 1129 under the Western Chalukya king Someshvara III. In a hundred chapters it covers the duties of kings, government, warfare, architecture, painting, music, dance, cuisine, sport and entertainment, giving a detailed…

mao-gong-ding.s: The Mao Gong ding is a Western Zhou bronze cauldron, discovered in Qishan, Shaanxi, in the 1840s, that bears the longest known inscription on an ancient Chinese bronze, of nearly 500 characters. It records a king's charge to his kinsman the Duke of Mao, granting him authority…

mount-li.s: Mount Li (Lishan) is a mountain near Xi'an in Shaanxi, China, with hot springs at its northern foot. According to tradition King You of Zhou was killed there in 771 BCE when the Marquis of Shen and the Quanrong sacked his capital.

mount-qi.s: Mount Qi (Qishan) is a mountain in western Shaanxi, China, above the plain of Zhouyuan, the early homeland of the Zhou people. Tradition says that Gugong Danfu led the Zhou there, and excavations around Zhouyuan have found palace foundations, inscribed oracle bones and hoards…

mohammad-ali-khan-zand.s: Mohammad Ali Khan Zand was a son of Karim Khan Zand, the founder of the Zand state in Iran. After his father's death in 1779 his uncle Zaki Khan proclaimed him and his brother Abu al-Fath Khan joint rulers while holding real power himself.

mohammad-hasan-khan-qajar.s: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar was chief of the Qajar tribe of Astarabad and a leading contender for power in Iran after the death of Nader Shah. Holding Mazandaran and much of the north, he fought Karim Khan Zand and Azad Khan Afghan, but was defeated and killed in 1759.

mthethwa-paramountcy.s: The Mthethwa Paramountcy was a Nguni state near the coast of what is now KwaZulu-Natal, which under Dingiswayo dominated neighbouring chiefdoms, including the Zulu, in the early 19th century. It competed with the Ndwandwe for land, cattle and the Delagoa Bay trade.

mbuyazi.s: Mbuyazi was a son of the Zulu king Mpande and a rival of his half-brother Cetshwayo for the succession. His supporters, the iziGqoza, were believed to have Mpande's favour.

mgungundlovu.s: Mgungundlovu was the royal capital of the Zulu king Dingane, built around 1829 in the Emakhosini valley in KwaZulu-Natal. In February 1838 the Voortrekker leader Piet Retief and his party were killed there on Dingane's orders.

mhlangana.s: Mhlangana was a son of the Zulu chief Senzangakhona and a half-brother of Shaka. In September 1828 he and his brother Dingane assassinated Shaka at Dukuza.

mljet.s: Mljet is a Croatian island in the southern Adriatic, west of Dubrovnik. Listed by Constantine VII among the islands of the Narentines, it later came under the Republic of Ragusa in the 14th century and remained part of it until 1808.

minbu.s: Minbu is a town on the west bank of the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar, opposite Magway. Its district, watered by irrigation canals fed from the hill streams, was with Kyaukse one of the two great rice granaries of the dry zone that supported the kingdoms of Pagan, Ava,…

mat-kilau.s: Mat Kilau was a Malay warrior and one of the leaders of the Pahang uprising against British rule in 1891–1895, alongside Dato Bahaman. After the revolt failed he was believed dead, but in 1969 an elderly man in Pahang revealed himself as Mat Kilau, and the state government…

mesara-plain.s: The Mesara is the largest plain of Crete, in the south of the island between the Asterousia mountains and the foothills of Mount Ida. Farmed since the Neolithic, it supported the Minoan palace of Phaistos and the early tholos tombs of the region, and later the Greek and Roman…

madanapala.s: Madanapala was the last important king of the Pala dynasty of eastern India, reigning in the mid-12th century. By his time the Palas had lost Bengal to the Sena dynasty and held only parts of Bihar, and his death around 1161 is taken as the end of Pala rule.

mahipala-i-pala.s: Mahipala I was king of the Pala dynasty of Bengal and Bihar from about 988 to 1038. He revived Pala power after a century of decline by recovering northern and eastern Bengal, and he restored Buddhist monasteries.

mahipala-i-gurjara-pratihara.s: Mahipala I was king of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty of Kannauj in the early 10th century. Around 916 the Rashtrakuta king Indra III invaded and sacked Kannauj, but Mahipala recovered his capital, apparently with help from the Chandela king Harsha.

mosbach.s: Mosbach is a town on the edge of the Odenwald near the Neckar in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, known for its timber-framed old town. From 1410 to 1499 it was the seat of the Palatinate-Mosbach line of the Wittelsbachs, after which it returned to the Electoral Palatinate.

mannheim.s: Mannheim is a city in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, at the meeting of the Rhine and Neckar. Founded as a fortress town by Elector Frederick IV of the Palatinate in 1606 and laid out in a grid of lettered blocks, it became the residence of the Electors Palatine in 1720.

mahmud-badaruddin-i.s: Mahmud Badaruddin I was Sultan of Palembang in southern Sumatra from 1724 to 1757. His reign was the high point of the sultanate, enriched by pepper and by tin from Bangka sold to the Dutch East India Company.

mahmud-badaruddin-ii.s: Mahmud Badaruddin II was Sultan of Palembang in southern Sumatra, who resisted both the British during their occupation of Java and the returning Dutch. He defeated a Dutch expedition in 1819, but a larger force took Palembang in 1821 and exiled him to Ternate, where he died.

mahendravarman-i.s: Mahendravarman I was king of the Pallava dynasty of Kanchipuram in the early 7th century. He fought the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II, excavated the first rock-cut temples of the Tamil country and wrote the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana.

mamallapuram.s: Mamallapuram, or Mahabalipuram, is a coastal town in Tamil Nadu, India, that was a port of the Pallava dynasty and is named after King Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla. Its monuments, a World Heritage Site, include the monolithic rathas, cave temples, the great relief of…

mitra.s: Mitra is a Vedic god of friendship, contracts and alliances, usually invoked together with Varuna in the Rigveda and closely related to the Iranian Mithra. A 14th-century BCE treaty between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza of Mitanni invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra…

majhgawan-diamond-mine.s: The Majhgawan diamond mine near Panna in Madhya Pradesh, India, is a kimberlite pipe that has been the country's only large mechanised diamond mine in modern times. Diamonds of the Panna belt were worked for centuries and were a source of wealth for the rulers of Panna.

mahamati-prannath.s: Mahamati Prannath was a religious teacher from Jamnagar in Gujarat who led the Pranami sect, a Krishna-centred devotional movement founded by his guru Devchandra. He travelled widely, preaching against religious division, and settled at Panna as guru of the Bundela ruler…

montmartre.s: Montmartre is a hill in the 18th arrondissement in the north of Paris, crowned by the basilica of Sacré-Cœur. On 18 March 1871 the attempt by Adolphe Thiers's government to remove the National Guard's cannons from the hill set off the uprising of the Paris Commune, and the…

montagne-sainte-genevieve.s: The Montagne Sainte-Geneviève is a hill on the Left Bank of the Seine in the 5th arrondissement of Paris. It was the centre of Roman Lutetia, with its forum, and later took its name from the abbey of Saint Genevieve, the city's patron saint.

meena.s: The Meena, also written Mina, are a community of Rajasthan and neighbouring regions of India and one of the state's largest scheduled tribes. Tradition holds that Meena chiefs ruled parts of the Jaipur region, including Amber, before the Kachhwaha Rajputs took it in the…

monitore-napoletano.s: The Monitore Napoletano was the official newspaper of the Parthenopean Republic, published in Naples twice weekly from February to June 1799. Edited by Eleonora Fonseca Pimentel, it reported the acts of the republican government, explained its reforms and urged the patriots to…

mansoor-ali-khan-pataudi.s: Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi was an Indian cricketer who became India's youngest Test captain in 1962, at the age of 21. Despite losing the sight of one eye in a car accident, he led India in 40 Tests and guided it to its first overseas Test series win, in New Zealand in 1968.

marxism-leninism.s: Marxism–Leninism is the communist ideology developed in the Soviet Union from the ideas of Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin and codified under Joseph Stalin in the late 1920s. It holds that a vanguard party should seize power, rule a one-party state in the name of the working…

merck-group.s: Merck is a German chemical and pharmaceutical company based in Darmstadt and one of the oldest such firms in the world. It traces its origins to the Engel pharmacy in Darmstadt, acquired by the Merck family in 1668, and began industrial production of alkaloids and other…

mohegan.s: The Mohegan are an Algonquian-speaking Native American people of south-eastern Connecticut. In the 1630s their sachem Uncas broke away from the Pequot and allied with the English colonists, fighting beside them in the Pequot War of 1637.

mopsus.s: Mopsus is a legendary seer of Greek tradition, said to be a son of Manto and grandson of Tiresias, who defeated Calchas in a contest of prophecy and led migrants into southern Anatolia after the Trojan War. Cities of Pamphylia and Cilicia, such as Perge and Mopsuestia,…

marmara-ereglisi.s: Marmara Ereğlisi is a town on the northern shore of the Sea of Marmara in Tekirdağ Province, European Turkey. It occupies the site of ancient Perinthus, a Samian colony that resisted Philip II of Macedon in 340 BCE and later, renamed Heraclea, became the capital of the Roman…

monte-sannace.s: Monte Sannace is an archaeological site near Gioia del Colle in Apulia, southern Italy, the remains of one of the largest settlements of the Peucetians. Inhabited from the Iron Age, it flourished between the 6th and 3rd centuries BCE, when it was enclosed by stone walls and…

matala.s: Matala is a village and bay on the south coast of Crete, Greece, west of the Mesara plain. In antiquity it served as a harbour for Phaistos and later for Gortyn.

mardonius.s: Mardonius was a Persian general, nephew and son-in-law of Darius I. He led an expedition to Thrace and Macedonia in 492 BCE and commanded the land forces left in Greece by Xerxes after Salamis in 480 BCE.

mount-cithaeron.s: Mount Cithaeron is a mountain range in central Greece, about 1,400 metres high, forming the border between Boeotia and Attica. Its passes carried the roads from Athens to Thebes and Plataea, and the Greek army camped on its slopes before the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE.

mayflower.s: The Mayflower was an English merchant ship that carried about 102 passengers, among them the Separatists later called the Pilgrims, from Plymouth in England to New England in 1620. Bound for the Hudson River region, it reached Cape Cod in November and the settlers founded…
